News.title: 'Princess Diana's brother Earl Spencer has thrown down the gauntlet to King - how he responds will be telling'
News.content:
Does anyone seriously believe King Charles, a man whom countless people have described over the years as being seriously affected by Princess Diana’s death, regardless of their disaster of a marriage, would say such “monstrous” words?

The pointed language used by Earl Spencer is so outlandish and hyperbolic that even the most committed Republicans would struggle to get on board. But this war of words, which is already spiralling wildly out of control, endangers the very fabric of the monarchy.

And all in the week that Prince Harry has turned up to cosplay being a royal, with 48 hours of public engagements as he strives to rehabilitate his own image now he’s parked up in Britain once again.

View 3 Images Earl Spencer insists he is "telling the truth" about explosive claims in his new book (Image: BBC)

‌



Forget the notion of “your truth” - ridiculously peddled by Oprah Winfrey following her interview with Harry and Meghan after their explosive exit from royal life - there is only one truth here. Princess Diana’s brother Earl Spencer has abandoned his self-imposed shackles from publicly talking about his sister’s experiences within the royal family - all in good time to publicise his book and cash in ahead of the 30th anniversary of Diana’s death.

How convenient then that he has suddenly lifted the lid on private conversations with the then Prince Charles, where he allegedly “sounded giddily elated” upon the tragic news of the death of the mother of his children. Spencer knows the framing around it has the potential to inflict the most damage.

Claiming Charles's “pent-up contempt” for his former wife, and adding that the King sounded almost gleeful - comparing his tone to that of “a lottery winner” - at the very moment the nation was collapsing into grief, is simply staggering. Spencer has laid down the gauntlet to the King his own version of "recollections may vary" is anything but a rebuttal of his version of events.

View 3 Images King Charles responded to Earl Spencer's claims in an unprecedented statement (Image: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA via AP)

‌



These aren't simply unflattering anecdotes about a phone call 30 years ago, they are a direct challenge to the version of events the monarchy has quietly relied on for years - that Charles was a grieving father doing his best amid impossible pressure, not a man irritated by his ex-wife's popularity.

If the public believes Spencer over the Palace, it doesn't just tarnish a moment in history; it corrodes the trust that underpins the King's own reign, at a time when Charles is already contending with health concerns and a slimmed-down, ageing monarchy, and how he will respond to his estranged son’s homecoming.

For an institution that survives on the idea of quiet dignity and closing ranks, those days are over. What happens next will be for the King to decide.

News.title: US left ‘on brink of war’ with China over report of nukes moving in Middle East
News.content:
US left ‘on brink of war’ with China over report of nukes moving in Middle East

A US analyst used an AI chatbot that wrongly identified a Chinese ship's cargo as nuclear weapons components - and it almost started a war between the two countries

View Image A plan to intercept the ship was underway, reports claim (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The United States "almost started a war" against China after an AI chatbot wrongly concluded a Chinese ship was carrying nuclear weapons components, according to a new report.

‌



The incident happened this spring, when the vessel was spotted in the Middle East in the midst of America's war with Iran. The US was preparing to board the vessel and planes were circling, with plans to intercept the ship underway.

‌



But, once officials had a more detailed look into the intelligence report that led to the large-scale response, they realised it had been generated with the help of AI, CNN reports.

‌



An analyst is said to have used a chatbot that wrongly identified the nature of the Chinese ship's cargo, suggesting the vessel was transporting components of a nuclear weapons programme.

Trump's forces preparing for war around the moon as US unveils space weapons READ MORE :

What exactly the vessel was transporting remains unclear to this day, with one source telling CNN that the intelligence report was "entirely false" but "almost started a war" between the US and China.

‌



It is also unclear whether the AI chatbot used by the US analyst was one that is commercially available or one that has been developed by the US government.

However, a former senior US official who has knowledge of the AI systems used by the country's military said the internal tools are "mostly just copies of the commercial stuff wearing lipstick".

The AI bot reached its almost catastrophic conclusion after fusing together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings. AI was once again then used by the analyst to list the findings into an intelligence report.

Article continues below

Mirror Online has approached the Pentagon and US Special Operations Command Pacific for comment.

An "Artificial Intelligence Acceleration Strategy" was released in January by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth which aims to accelerate the military's use of AI. Hegseth said this will "unleash experimentation and eliminate bureaucratic barriers".

But the incident in spring is not isolated, a source told CNN, while another said "AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster".

News.title: Earl Spencer hits back at Palace and claims King Charles went 'ballistic' in row after Diana's death
News.content:
Earl Spencer hits back at Palace and claims King Charles went 'ballistic' in row after Diana's death

In a new interview with the BBC, Princess Diana's brother has claimed he is "telling the truth" after Buckingham Palace hit back at claims in his new book that the King said of his former wife after her death "rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough"

Earl Spencer fumes 'I'm telling the truth' in bombshell BBC interview

Princess Diana's brother says he is "telling the truth" about claims King Charles said the royal family would “forget her soon enough" following her tragic death in 1997.

‌



Earl Spencer accused the then-then Prince Charles of launching into a furious tirade against him in a phone call in the days after the princess was killed in a Paris car crash, alongside her lover Dodi Fayed. The Earl said he told the King how he strongly disagreed with the decision made by the royals to have princes William and Harry - aged just 15 and 12 - walk behind their mother’s coffin during her funeral procession.

‌



Buckingham Palace issused a strongly worded rebuke just over an hour after Spencer’s claims emerged in a newspaper serialisation of his new book on Thursday, saying the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

‌



View 3 Images Earl Spencer has insisted he is "telling the truth" after explosive allegations in his new book (Image: BBC)

"I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said," the Earl said, s peaking to the BBC today. Pressed on whether he disagreed with Buckingham Palace disputing his version of events, Spencer hit back saying they had not issued a formal denial of the phone call alleged to have taken place.

“They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary," he said. The late Queen Elizabeth II issued a now famous statement, including the line “recollections may vary”, in the aftermath of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s claims following their exit from the monarchy, that unnamed members of the family “had concerns” over the colour of their unborn son Archie’s skin colour.

‌



Reacting to the rebuttal from the palace, Earl Spencer said: “Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?” Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: “I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

“I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that.”

View 3 Images Princess Diana's brother spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg (Image: BBC)

‌



In further extracts published on Thursday, Spencer also claimed the King “sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". The Earl told the BBC that while he did not keep contemporaneous notes of the conversations with the King, or keep a diary, he told close family members at the time “because it was so monstrous".

Royal sources today told The Mirror that Spencer’s explosive claims are “utter nonsense”. Well placed palace insiders also reacted with dismay that Diana’s brother has chosen to use the monarch as “a punching bag” to publicise his tell-all memoir on his sister’s life, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.

One source, who worked for the royal family for a decade said: “(The allegations) couldn't be further from the truth of a man (King Charles) who was deeply affected by Diana’s death.” The source added: “To claim anything other than he was overwhelmingly concerned for the wellbeing of his son’s futures, without their mother, is simply contumelious.”

‌



View 3 Images The King in Scotland earlier this week (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

In a two minute 39 second clip of the upcoming BBC interview with presenter Laura Kuenssberg, Spencer alleged the King “went ballistic” and “ranted for a while”, accusing his family of not having an adequate sense of duty. He added: “And then he stopped and I thought, oh now, now he's gonna pull himself together and say something more appropriate. And then, he said, 'we'll forget her soon enough'.”

Spencer said he couldn't say exactly what went through his mind at that moment as he was “just so stunned”, adding: “I just, after a stunned silence, I said, I cannot believe you just said that. And I hung up on him.”

Article continues below

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next Tuesday and is expected to be highly critical of the royal family. Buckingham Palace has declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

News.title: England squad: Palmer and Trent back as snubbed star's partner takes aim at Thomas Tuchel
News.content:
Thomas Tuchel has announced his latest England squad as the Three Lions all prepare for an extended, revamped three-week international break across late September and early October

Thomas Tuchel has named his 26-man England squad for the upcoming international break. Chelsea's Cole Palmer and Real Madrid's Trent Alexander-Arnold have received recalls.

Palmer has impressed under Xabi Alonso this season, scoring four times and adding two assists in five appearances. He is back in the Three Lions camp after missing the World Cup. Another face returning to the England fold is Alexander-Arnold, despite a difficult start to the season at Real Madrid, where he has been in and out of the XI alongside Denzel Dumfries.

Elsewhere, Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Liverpool's Rio Ngumoha have been selected by Tuchel, who were included in the four-person warm-up group before the World Cup earlier this summer. Lewis Hall also makes it following an excellent start to the season at Newcastle United, while Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite has earned a place as a reward for a solid start to the campaign.

News.title: Prince Harry says 'we're happy and kids in school' before launching new Invictus programme
News.content:
Prince Harry says 'we're happy and kids in school' before launching new Invictus programme

The Duke of Sussex played pickleball and spoke to students about prosthetics as he visited a school in Birmingham today as he launched an Invictus education programme

View 6 Images Prince Harry in Birmingham today (Image: Getty Images)

Prince Harry has admitted his brief return to the UK has been “eventful” on his first public appearance back in the UK. It came as the Duke of Sussex spoke during the outing, the first in public since arriving from the US with his family, but added: “It’s wonderful to be back on British soil.”

‌



Since the Sussexes landed back to start a new life in the UK, they have been involved in a public spat with Buckingham Palace about their status, and their children have moved schools after issues were raised by their security team about the school run.

‌



Prince William teams up with Bollywood legend for Earthshot Prize Awards as finalists announced READ MORE :

View 6 Images Prince Harry in Birmingham today (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



But at the inaugural Invictus Spirit Awards on Thursday night, he told Hello! Magazine: “The last two weeks have been… it’s been eventful.

“But, you know, we’re getting stuck into the work. Kids are in school. We’re happy. And as I said, it’s great to be back on British soil, and looking forward to Birmingham next year for the Invictus Games that’s coming up.”

Today, Harry made another public appearance when he played pickleball and was quizzed by schoolchildren while launching a new Invictus Games education scheme. He met students at Ninestiles, an Academy in Birmingham, the host city for his games for wounded soldiers next year.

‌



The event also marked the launch of the education scheme INSPIRE, which enables teachers to use stories in lessons from Invictus Games in subjects ranging from maths and English to PE and performing arts.

View 6 Images Harry tried his hand at pickleball (Image: Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP)

During the visit, he told pupils during a Q&A that the "people that inspire me are the people that get knocked down and get back up again" And urged them to strike a "balance" between mental health and physical health.

‌



Kicking off the visit, in the school gym he played several rallies of pickleball on two courts with Year 7 and Year 11 students. Harry joked his back was in pain after reaching for a low shot and cried out "nice" when one of the players won a point.

He bonded with nine-year-old Ryan, who was playing pickleball for the first time, and after winning a point, Harry said to the youngster: "I'll give you that one."

Afterwards, Ryan said about playing against the prince: "It was fun, and I won. He knows I did. Call him and tell him I won. It was a really fun game." Joining a class of youngsters studying STEM, Harry took part in a chat about the design and technology of prosthetics with former Invictus Games competitors Dr Dave Henson and Josh Boggi.

‌



View 6 Images The Duke of Sussex launched a Birmingham education programme today (Image: Aaron Chown/POOL PA via AP)

The lessons designed by teachers for students ranging from Early Years through to Key Stage 5 use the Invictus Games and the stories of its competitors to create curriculum-aligned resources across Maths, English, STEM, Art, Performing Arts, Sport and PSHE.

It is available through the Invictus Games Birmingham 2027 website, enabling teachers across the UK to bring the experiences and values of the Games into the classroom.

‌



Before the Duke entered the classroom, Lee Hazard, Director of Special Projects at Invictus Games, told the students that ' Prince Harry will be here' in a few minutes. One lad at the front piped up, saying: "Who is Prince Harry?" While another boy said: "He's the King's son".

View 6 Images Harry met with students at the Ninestiles School (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

Once in the classroom, Harry moved around the students, giving tips after being set the task of designing a prosthetic. He suggested to one group: “Think about branding, school branding on it. This is our prosthetic.” A second group of children said they were designing a prosthetic for running.

‌



Harry said: “If there were no rules, what would you do to give someone the best chance. How are you going to make the machine that gives them the extra oomph?"

When asked about balancing mental health and physical health, he said: "The two are inseparable. When you do physical exercise, it feels good and is good for your mental health.

He added: "Doing the physical stuff certainly helps with my mental health and that doesn't have to be going to the gym, doesn't have to be a sport, it could literally be putting your phone down, going for a walk.

‌



View 6 Images Harry spoke with students learning about prosthetics (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

He said: "Whether it's cycling, swimming, running, walking, getting out, putting your phone down, all of those things may be seriously benefit parts of your mental health. But try and find the balance. Everything in life is about balance."

Harry was also asked by a student to name someone who was his inspiration. He told the students: "It's not a single person, it's a whole group of people. And it's not always the people you probably think it is.

‌



Pointing to the Invictus Games competitors he said: "It's these guys. This this Invictus community of people who get knocked down but keep getting back up.

"The people who support them in that process. Of course, individually, it takes so much to get to where they are today. But I would take a guess that every single person here is here because of the support that they've been given by other people. So the people that inspire me are the people that get knocked down and get back up.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



"And there's other people that find the time in their day to be able to help other people. Because that feels good for them and that is something that they want to do.

"That's the kind of group, community inspiration that I think really moves the needle. So yes, you can still have that individual person that inspires you.

"But for me, being involved in this community for the last 12 years, they are the ones that inspire me every single day. And I get my annual fix by being around them. Does that answer your question?"

News.title: Funeral for couple found dead by kids in Spanish hot tub hears heartbreaking tributes
News.content:
Funeral for couple found dead by kids in Spanish hot tub hears heartbreaking tributes

Thomasina and Patrick Tobin had rented a villa in Cullera, near Valencia, but were found lifeless in a hot tub by their children in August

View 4 Images Patrick and Thomasina Tobin (Image: RIP.IE)

A London-based couple whose bodies were found in a hot tub at a Spanish villa by their children have been described as "much loved parents"

‌



Thomasina Tobin, 51, from Ireland, and Patrick Tobin, 48, from New Zealand, died in August at a villa they had rented in Cullera, near Valencia. Their bodies were tragically discovered by their teenage children, who raised the alarm.

‌



Their deaths are believed to be accidental and a funeral service for the pair took place in Ballintra, County Donegal, today. The funeral heard the Tobins' sudden passing has left an "immeasurable void in the lives of all who loved them".

‌



Rev Canon Patrick McGinn described the couple as welcoming and "so generous in every way", the Irish Mirror reports. He added both Mrs and Mr Tobin were "meticulous" and their children were "the most important part of their lives".

View 4 Images Thomasina Tobin has been described as a loving mum

Mystery over couple found dead in hot tub by kids as experts question key theory READ MORE :

Several items from the couple’s life together were brought up to the altar, including a photo of the couple and their children.

‌



Canon McGinn said: "This represents the family that Paddy and Thomasina created together and how [the children] were at the heart of their lives, Paddy being a devoted father, Thomasina being a loving mum. They created a lovely home together in Greenwich."

Mrs Tobin resembled her late mother, "with grit, determination, a tenacious person and she would stick with things even though they were really hard. And yet it was all completed with huge softness, love and kindness".

View 4 Images Patrick Tobin was a devoted father

‌



Mr McGinn described Mr Tobin as "quick, adventurous and constantly kept everyone on their toes". He added that the father loved sports and had tried a number of them, including rugby, hockey, cricket and surfing, the Irish Times reports.

Mr McGinn said: "We are all so sad for you who are heartbroken today. We really don’t know what to say. All we can do is huddle in grief around the remains of shattered dreams and what might have been. We can just hold you in our hearts today."

Mrs Tobin, who was originally from County Monaghan, worked as a quantity surveyor and was a senior executive with a project management consultancy in the construction industry, while Mr Tobin worked in the tech sector.

Article continues below

View 4 Images The couple reportedly became trapped in the hot tub (Image: Airbnb)

During today's funeral, Mrs Tobin's brother, John, thanked those who "have helped us along the way over the past number of weeks".

The couple were found dead by their children on August 24, with Spanish media reporting that post-mortem examinations showed both parents suffered fatal heart stoppages when they became trapped in the Jacuzzi.

News.title: Parts of Britain where house prices have fallen despite average cost rising - check your area
News.content:
Parts of Britain where house prices have fallen despite average cost rising - check your area

Buyers will on average pay more for homes across Britain though there are areas where people can snap up a property for upward of 20 per cent less than they could this time last year

View 4 Images Many regions saw falling house prices while many saw sharp increases (Image: Tim Graham/Getty Images)

There have been major shifts in the housing market with prices tumbling in some parts of Britain despite average prices rising on the whole.

‌



New figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) revealed average house prices rose by 1.4 per cent across the UK with the average property now setting buyers back on average £273,000. The year-on-year change means on average house pricess are now £4,000 more expensive than they were in July 2025.

‌



But regions that have typically seen an explosion in prices over the decades have dramatically fallen in contrast to now-booming property hotspots. London saw a 3.3 per cent decrease in the 12 months to July this year, making it 11 consecutive months where average prices have fallen in the capital.

‌



View 4 Images Property prices rose on average across the UK (Image: Cambridge News)

Thames Water is introducing more regular bills for thousands of customers READ MORE :

Cost of private rent across Britain rises to highest on record - check prices in your area READ MORE :

Inner London's Westminster, Kensington and Chelsea and Tower Hamlets were among those that saw the largest falls, though regions outside the capital did also see a reversal in trends. Rutland, Aberdeen and the Shetland Islands were also among the top 10 regions where prices have seen a noticeable decline.

Check our interactive map below to see the change in house prices where you live:

‌



Where have average house prices fallen most since July 2025?

View 4 Images London saw the biggest fall in house prices across Britain (Image: Getty Images)

City of Westminster - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of -20.7 per cent (median monthly wage: £4,384)

City of London - average price £710,652 representing an annual change of -17.4 per cent (median monthly wage: £4,850)

Tower Hamlets - average price £447,796 representing an annual change of -14.4 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,810)

Kensington and Chelsea - average price £1,232,640 representing an annual change of -14.1 per cent (median monthly wage: £4,381)

Camden - average price £815,159 representing an annual change of -10.1 per cent (median monthly wage: £4,120)

Hammersmith and Fulham - average price £738,048 representing an annual change of -9 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,950)

City of Aberdeen - average price £130,689 representing an annual change of -8.7 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,180)

Shetland Islands - average price £179,493 representing an annual change of -7 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,250)

Rutland - average price £298,916 representing an annual change of -6.5 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,040)

Lambeth - average price £536,623 representing an annual change of -6.3 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,780)

‌



In contrast, Northern Ireland saw the largest increase in average house prices across Britain with the eight of the top 10 largest increases been seen in the country. House prices on average increased to £874, representing a 1.6 per cent change in the 12 months since July last year.

Other sharp increases were also seen in the North West of England where prices rose by between 8.6 and 9.6 per cent. Average house prices increased to £215,000 in Wales and £196,000 in Scotland, representing a 2.6 per cent and 2.3 per cent change, respectively.

Where have average house prices risen the most since July 2025?

View 4 Images Many regions saw marked rises in house prices (Image: Cambridge News)

‌



Newry Mourne and Down - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 12.8 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,667)

Derry City and Strabane - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 12.4 per cent (median monthly wage: 2,625)

Fermanagh and Omagh - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 11 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,583)

Mid Ulster - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 10.5 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,650)

Lisburn and Castlereagh - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 9.7 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,933)

Trafford average price - £876,788 representing an annual change of 9.6 per cent (median monthly wage: £3,174)

Causeway Coast and Glens - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 9.6 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,542)

Armagh City, Banbridge and Craigavon average price - £876,788 representing an annual change of 9.2 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,700)

Antrim and Newtownabbey - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 8.8 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,800)

Burnley - average price £876,788 representing an annual change of 8.6 per cent (median monthly wage: £2,570)

But those hoping to get on the property ladder face fresh hurdles amid a warning from property website Zoopla that the average homebuyer needing to save an extra £18,200 in deposit funds to counter higher mortgage rates. Buyers in London will need a staggering £35,000 in additional cost compared to the £10,200 extra for those in the North East.

Average five-year fixed mortgages rates have risen from below 4 per cent in January to about 4.8 per cent earlier this month following uncertainty from the Iran war. The situation is not better in the rental market with people on average paying their landlords more.

Article continues below

Renting a home privately is on the rise across the country with people paying on average nearly £1,500 a month. On average, it costs £1,412 a month to privately rent a home in the year to August 2026 - it represents the highest amount on record and 3.9 per cent more than the same time last year.

News.title: Mel B's daughter among stars spotted in purple beanie at London Fashion Week
News.content:
Mel B's daughter among stars spotted in purple beanie at London Fashion Week

Phoenix Brown, Heartstopper star Jenny Walser and former Love Islander Jordan Hames were among the celebrities spotted wearing a limited-edition purple Grimace beanie at London Fashion Week

View 7 Images Phoenix Brown showed off her beanie before heading to the H&M&YOU&I event (Image: PinPep)

A host of celebrities have been spotted out and about wearing an unusual fashion accessory as they made their way to a range of shows that mark the beginning of London Fashion Week. Heartstopper actress Jenny Walser, TV presenter Charli Fisher and former Love Islander and model Jordan Hames were pictured n the capital wearing a purple beanie.

‌



Phoenix Brown – daughter of Spice Girl Mel B –was seen at the H&M&YOU&I event wearing the headpiece, which has a pair of cartoon eyes. The quirky, fully reversible purple and yellow hat draws inspiration from Grimace, the iconic McDonald's character who first burst onto the scene in 1971.

‌



View 7 Images Brown oozed cool as she headed inside (Image: PinPep)

‌



Jenny, best known for her roles as Tori Spring in the hit Netflix series and Louise Wrigley in Call The Midwife, were seen wearing the accessory ahead of the Mithridate Show at Space House on Thursday. Meanwhile, Charli modelled the beanie as she turned up for The Art of Belonging show at Asia House in central London.

Jordan, who shot to fame on the 2019 series of Love Island, showed off the eye-catching hat as he made his way to 180 The Strand, while stylist and designer Kyle De'Volle turned heads wearing the beanie as he rocked up at Dover Street Market for the BFC Jewellery Showcase.

The eye-catching beanie has been launched to mark the arrival of McHappy Day , a new fundraising day taking place across the UK with the aim of raising vital funds for Ronald McDonald House UK.

‌



7 View 7 Images Stylist Kyle De’Volle was also spotted wearing the Charity Beanie (Image: PinPep) 7 View 7 Images The hat topped off his all-denim outfit (Image: PinPep)

‌



Ella Joseph, CEO at Ronald McDonald House UK, said: "We are so excited to see the limited-edition Grimace Beanie getting such a warm reaction at London Fashion Week.

"As we head into Autumn, a beanie is a stylish essential, but it also contributes to McDonald's McHappy Day fundraising as all proceeds from every Beanie sold will be donated directly to Ronald McDonald House UK.

"Ronald McDonald House UK offers vital support for families with children in hospital by providing them free accommodation, within walking distance of their ward."

‌



7 View 7 Images Jenny Walser looked great as she stepped out ahead of the Mithridate Show (Image: WILL_IRELAND) 7 View 7 Images Charli Fisher wore the Beanie while heading to The Art of Belonging (Image: PinPep)

View 7 Images Ex-Love Islander Jordan Hames was also seen getting involved (Image: WILL_IRELAND)

‌



She added: "The 14 Ronald McDonald Houses across the UK give families access to community and a place that they can call home, helping to alleviate the practical and financial pressures that come with hospital stays.

"This means that with every purchase of a Grimace Beanie, customers can help make a real difference to families when they need it most."

Scheduled for Saturday 26th September, £1 from every qualifying main meal purchased at selected restaurants will go straight to the charity, bolstering its efforts to support families of seriously ill children throughout the UK.

Article continues below

Priced at just £5, the Grimace Beanie is available now at participating McDonald's restaurants or through the McDonald's App.

It's certainly a surprising addition to London Fashion Week, which will showcase Spring/Summer 2027 collections from some of the most influential names in the fashion industry.

The twice-yearly showcase ranks amongst the fashion industry's elite "Big Four" weeks, sitting alongside Paris, Milan and New York, and plays a crucial role in shaping worldwide style trends each season.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
News.content:
He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.

The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.

But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.

In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.

The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.

Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret.

But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.

Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.

He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.

Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.

Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".

At the conclusion of the hearing, the Lady Chief Justice said it had been a "serious day addressing serious matters".

She said a judgment will be issued at a later date.

News.title: Flight chaos caused by software defect in space of a millisecond, report says
News.content:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

News.title: Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July - the 16th conviction since the new offence was created in January.

Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.

At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".

She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.

James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.

The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.

News.title: Brother didn't match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
News.content:
The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and the police showed "no urgency" to clear his name.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Nicholas Brandram's sisters accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".

Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the investigation.

Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health deteriorated after his arrest and questioned why the police were not able to carry out DNA tests that could have proved his innocence.

News.title: 'Get in' - woman joins police chase by giving officer a lift in Nissan Micra
News.content:
A driver came to the aid of a police officer who was chasing a suspect on foot - telling him to "get in" after stopping her Nissan Micra and offering him a lift.

The officer had been pursuing Jacob Roberts, 25, who had reverse-rammed a police car twice and crashed into parked cars and a building while trying to escape.

Roberts sped away from officers who had smelled cannabis coming from his van, with the chase seeing him drive in an erratic manner, failing to stop at multiple junctions, mounting pavements and putting pedestrians at risk.

The driver helped PC Kerswell catch up to Roberts, who was arrested and later jailed for one year and two months for a number of driving offences.

While fleeing from police in his white van, Roberts had driven into a dead-end street in Abercwmboi, Rhondda Cynon Taf, where he ditched the car and tried to escape officers on foot.

Police bodycam footage captured the moment the officer then runs to a red Nissan Micra driven by an un-named female driver and tells her: "I need a lift."

"Get in," the woman replies.

As she gave chase the woman is heard asking the officer to direct her, saying: "Where to?"

The officer is seen jumping out of the car after spotting the suspect and takes out his taser and arrests him.

During a search officers found two cannabis cigarettes on him.

Roberts, from Mountain Ash, was jailed for one year and two months for dangerous driving and disqualified from driving for three years.

He was sentenced at Merthyr Tydfil Crown Court on 16 September, where he pleaded guilty to dangerous driving, driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance, failure to stop after a road accident, criminal damage to property, and possession of controlled Class B drugs.

Kerswell said: "Roberts was already banned from driving when he committed these offences - he showed complete disregard for all other road users, including pedestrians.

"I hope it acts as a deterrent for others who think of driving dangerously.

"It's lucky that no one was seriously injured during this pursuit. We hope this sentence will give Roberts time to reflect on his actions."

News.title: Tenko and Coronation Street actress Stephanie Cole dies aged 84
News.content:
Solihull-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, after making her stage debut at the age of 17 â playing the 90-year-old medium Madame Arcati in Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.

She went on to enjoy a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film and was perhaps best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.

The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.

Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the women's health, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman.

During this same period, Cole also played the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow" in the Ronnie Barker-starring Open All Hours.

She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God.

But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, as one of her proudest moments. The series also starred Maggie Smith and Julie Walters.

Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman.

News.title: Men lose appeal for harrassing BBC journalist over A Very British Cult documentary
News.content:
The men were attempting to overturn their convictions from February, when they were each sentenced to 200 hours of community service and given restraining orders banning them from contacting or approaching Nye or her partner for 10 years.

They were also banned from entering the London borough where the couple live for a decade.

A year after the initial broadcast of the BBC programmes about the organisation, the Lighthouse group began a campaign of peaceful, and legal, protests outside BBC offices in London, against Nye and the BBC.

"While there were elements of peaceful protest and freedom of expression, their conduct, as we have already identified, was not proportionate to the proper exercise of those rights and went beyond what was acceptable and indeed became criminal", the judge said.

After an interaction with Nye in July 2024, Kamra gave evidence that he was "dissatisfied" and that questions he had for Nye were still not answered.

The group decided to visit her home address, which they found using a private investigator and said that they had looked up BBC guidance of doorstepping.

"The appellants therefore appreciated that there was a line which their conduct must not cross", said Pounder.

"What happened descended into bullying and oppressive conduct", he added, deeming that the behaviour of the three men was not reasonable.

During the first visit to Nye's home address on 29 August, the group had distributed leaflets they had printed to Nye's neighbours.

The judge said the contents were "not confined to criticism of journalism".

"They identified her to those living in the immediate neighbourhood and associated her with serious allegations concerning racism, dishonesty and the concealment of child sexual abuse by family members," he explained.

"That is materially different from distributing critical literature outside the headquarters of a public broadcaster."

The court heard Kamra later returned to the property to post a handwritten letter saying "we will be back", which "materially reinforced" Nye's concerns, Pounder said.

Deichler, Kamra and Singh visited her property again a week later, on 5 September, before they were later arrested.

The three men maintained that they were performing citizen journalism and were at her property to obtain a doorstep interview, as part of their own documentary, and that they were acting in the public interest.

Judge Pounder accepted that they saw themselves as citizen journalists, but underlined their behaviour was not reasonable, as he pointed to their "deliberate acquisition of a private address, attendance of home, distribution of inflammatory literature, indication return visit and subsequent return".

Giving evidence for the second time, from behind a curtain, Nye told the court of her fear when the three accused went to her property.

It was "extremely" distressing, Nye said.

Their actions had resulted in Nye installing CCTV, panic alarms, direct lines with the police and carrying rape alarms, the court heard.

The three men had also claimed that their attendance outside Nye's home was an expression of their religious beliefs.

Pounder said there was no doubt that their views were "sincerely held", telling them that it had been concluded that a prayer they said outside her door was "an incidental part of their attendance at the address".

The Bible they wanted to give her, Pounder said could have been posted to her via the BBC.

On top of their original convictions, the judge has ordered the three men to each pay an additional Â£1,000.

News.title: Ex-Brookside star who fled after fraud trial arrested in Spain
News.content:
A former TV soap actor has been arrested in Spain after skipping bail before his trial for a Â£13.6 million fraud that conned would-be models.

Philip Foster, 51, who played Christian Wright in the Liverpool soap, is wanted and must serve an eight-and-a-half year jail sentence after being convicted of fraud and money laundering last year.

He ran an operation involving sham modelling agencies that exploited the dreams of aspiring young models and their parents for more than eight years.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) said that after jumping bail, Foster was convicted and sentenced in his absence at Sheffield Crown Court in February 2025. He was arrested by officers on Thursday in Alicante.

Extradition proceedings to return him to the UK are now under way, the NCA said.

A National Trading Standards (NTS) investigation found that more than 6,000 victims parted with large sums of money on the false promise of securing paid modelling work in the fraud that Foster ran from his base in Marbella.

News.title: Twenty women had breasts removed unnecessarily during cancer treatment, NHS trust admits
News.content:
Dozens of affected women and their families contacted us after we reported concerns about serious failings at the trust's breast cancer unit. These included:

A high number of mastectomies compared with other NHS trusts

Operations that were carried out "too quickly"

Outsourcing of some treatment to private clinics run by the trust's breast cancer clinical lead - an arrangement that one independent expert said created "a clear conflict of interest

Patients described the shock they had felt on being told a mastectomy (the removal of all or part of a breast) could have been avoided, as well as the psychological and physical pain that many still live with.

We also met former patients who have come together to support each other and call for a public inquiry.

CDDFT is now carrying out an internal review of breast cancer cases between January 2023 and February 2025, alongside the cases of 640 former patients who contacted a dedicated helpline.

Of 514 cases reviewed by the trust so far, 315 patients have been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died.

It says that cases have also been identified where cancer diagnoses were missed or delayed. Some of these patients subsequently saw their cancer spread.

Russell has told BBC's Today programme that the trust will meet in the coming week to decide whether to extend the scope of the review, and look at up to 10,000 cases dating back as far as 2015.

He says the trust has been taking advice from patients' groups, clinical experts and legal representatives, and it will have to take "a really balanced view". Any decision, he adds, will be made public.

The National Crime Agency says it is now working with Durham Police to investigate allegations by former patients and determine if any criminal offences have taken place.

News.title: Sisters of 'Putney pusher' suspect say DNA will clear his name
News.content:
The results of a DNA test will clear the name of Nicholas Brandram, the suspect in the "Putney pusher" case, his sisters have told the BBC.

The banker was arrested in June, nine years after a woman was pushed in front of a moving bus by a jogger on Putney Bridge in May 2017. He gave a DNA sample to police two months ago but never received the results, his sisters said.

Brandram was found dead in his west London home on Tuesday. His family have insisted he was innocent and said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the Met investigation.

The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, but did not respond to this specific claim.

News.title: British Steel plan lacks credibility, MPs say
News.content:
The government has no credible plan for the future of British Steel, MPs have claimed.

A report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST) had not set out how British Steel, which runs its main plant in Scunthorpe and has operations in Teeside, would become profitable.

MPs warned steel tariffs could drive firms out of business or to move abroad.

A spokesperson for DBIST said it welcomed the report and would review the recommendations, adding securing the long-term future of the UK steel sector "was in the national interest".

A 26-page report, external, published on Friday, said the government was unable to provide clear estimates of how much the overall nationalisation could cost.

It had projected costs to reach Â£642m by 30 June this year, but the government later said it had only been Â£555m.

In April last year, the government passed an emergency bill to take control of British Steel amid reports the then-owner Jingye was planning to switch off two blast furnaces in Scunthorpe.

The Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill became law in July, taking the company into public ownership.

The government then published its steel strategy in March this year, which included an ambition for 50% of steel used in the UK to be made in Britain.

The strategy confirmed electric arc furnaces as the future of British steelmaking, replacing traditional blast furnaces, which resulted in job losses at steelworks including Port Talbot.

It also highlighted concerns that British Steel's 4,052 workers face uncertainty and the steel strategy is still vague about when the 50% target would be achieved.

The report said: "Without a credible long-term plan, uncertainty and costs for workers, industry and taxpayers will continue to increase."

News.title: Football club apologises for United 93 shirt advert
News.content:
A football club has apologised after it published images of a new clothing line with "United 93" printed on the back - the call sign of one of the aircraft hijacked on 9/11.

The clothing was supposed to make reference to Oxford United's founding year of 1893.

However, it said it had been released "without understanding of the historical context and associations".

United Airlines Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, killing all 44 people on board after being hijacked on 11 September 2001. A docudrama film titled United 93 was made about the tragedy and released in 2006.

Oxford United was founded in 1893 as an amateur club called Headington and now plays in League One - the third tier of the English football pyramid.

In a statement, the club said its Campus Clothing range had been withdrawn and it "sincerely apologised" for the error.

"It should not have reached the point of sale and we take full responsibility for not undertaking proper due diligence," it said.

"We have removed the collection with immediate effect and are reviewing our approval processes to ensure nothing like this happens again."

The 9/11 attacks saw 19 Al Qaeda members hijack four commercial passenger planes in the US.

Two of them were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City, resulting in them both collapsing.

Another plane struck the Pentagon, near Washington DC, while the fourth plane - United 93 - crashed in rural Pennsylvania. It was believed to be destined for the US Capitol Building, also in Washington DC.

The attacks killed 2,977 people and injured tens of thousands more.

News.title: Teenager jailed for life over ambush murder
News.content:
A teenager who travelled more than 150 miles from Leeds to London to stab a man has been jailed for at least 25 years for his murder.

Sulaiman Tajzai, 18, ambushed shop worker Farmanullah Sherzad outside the 26-year-old's home in Westminster on 27 March, stabbing him at least 10 times.

Sentencing him at the Old Bailey to a life term, Judge Angela Rafferty KC said he had held a grudge against Sherzad "based on a false suggestion of misconduct" and had been "effectively stalking him down like prey".

Describing the attack as "exceptionally violent", she told Tajzai: "It is not said on your behalf, nor could it be, that you had any justifiable or excusable grievance against this man."

News.title: UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs
News.content:
Although the UK has, over the years, produced some of the world's most successful artists, that kind of success has rarely been repeated at Eurovision.

Over the past 15 years, the UK has only come higher than 15th place on one occasion - when Sam Ryder came second with his song Space Man in 2022. He was beaten by Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra.

And next year's event, being held in Burgas in Bulgaria, will mark 30 years since the UK last won the contest, when Katrina and the Waves scored 227 points with their song Love Shine A Light.

Many countries choose their entry through a publicly televised selection process.

The last time this was done in the UK was with the show Eurovision: You Decide in 2019. Michael Rice was selected, but went on to come last at the contest in Tel Aviv, Israel.

Speaking to the BBC, Dame Caroline referred to the televised selection process that has previously taken place, but questioned how acts were put forward to take part.

"Clearly there have been different approaches tried over the years," she said. "But who decides who makes it into that shortlist? I think all these things are worth looking at."

She added: "We need to look at what the process is and what other processes have been tried."

Two men deported by the United States to Equatorial Guinea were arbitrarily arrested after police covered their heads with a bag, beat them and held them at gunpoint in a hotel-turned-detention center, their lawyers and rights groups said on Friday.

Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian national, and Samson Birhane from Eritrea are among over 40 people who have been deported by the United States to Equatorial Guinea, a small oil-rich state in central Africa. Lawyers said they believed their arbitrary arrests were retaliation for the men raising alarm about the conditions of their detention and the police violence they had endured.

The two men are being held in a hotel on the outskirts of Malabo that the country’s longtime President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo has turned into a prison for asylum seekers sent from the U.S. under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration. Earlier this year, The Associated Press obtained exclusive access to the hotel.

The Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries other than their own under a series of obscure agreements. Advocates say the transfers are part of a broader U.S. crackdown to deter immigration.

U.S. judges had protected most of those deported to Equatorial Guinea from being returned to their countries of origin. Nevertheless, 12 people have been sent back to their countries of origin, according to their lawyers, including four Ethiopians earlier this month.

Those who remain in detention at the Bamy Hotel have faced violence from authorities, who tried to confiscate everyone’s phones, their lawyers said.

“Over the past months, we have observed escalating cases of police violence,” said Isabella Mosselmans, director of Global Litigation Council, an organization which is part of a coalition representing the individuals detained in Malabo. “On July 31, masked Equatorial Guinean police officers broke into a number of the hotel rooms of five people (...) and grabbed them by the neck and tackled them to the ground and handcuffed them and threatened them at gunpoint.”

The authorities tried to pressure Soliman and Birhane to agree to be returned to their countries, their lawyers said, and tried to take away their phones. Videos of Soliman protesting against the treatment by the authorities and being held at gunpoint by a police officer in the hotel have been published in international media.

Police arrested Soliman and Birhane on Sept. 11, accusing them of breaking a mirror. Officers later brought the men back to the hotel with bags over their heads and beat them in front of other detainees, according to the lawyers.

The lawyers for Soliman and Birhane said they have not been able to reach the two men since the authorities took them to La Luna police station. Both the men had lived in the United States for decades before being deported.

“Amnesty International believes that the police officers targeted them in reprisal for reporting the authorities' violent threats to coerce them to agree to return to their countries of origin,” the rights group said in a statement on Friday. “Since then, the two men have been held in an overcrowded police cell, in inhumane conditions, unable to speak to their lawyer.”

Immigration lawyers say the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their countries of origin. Equatorial Guinea is one of at least eight other African nations to have entered into such an agreement with the United States.

Equatorial Guinea is one of Africa's richest countries because of its oil resources, but U.S. officials say it is also plagued by corruption and human rights abuses.

Critical voices are almost nonexistent in the country, where rights groups and the U.S. State Department have accused the government of detaining, torturing and even killing people who speak out.

U.S. companies are among the country's largest foreign investors, and the military receives U.S. funding for training.

Fifa president Gianni Infantino has been urged to provide an additional minimum of $10 million (£7.5m) to all 211 member federations over the next three years from existing reserves.

The presidents of Uefa and Concacaf wrote to Infantino on Friday, noting their analysis indicated this sum represented a "conservative" figure of what the organisation could give each national body. They stated Fifa is set to end the year with reserves reaching $6 billion (£4.5bn).

This request follows friction over Infantino’s proposal to secure private investment for a business entity managing competitions, such as the men’s and women’s World Cups.

Infantino had offered significant funding boosts for member associations (MAs) if that project was swiftly accepted. However, Uefa’s president Aleksander Ceferin and Concacaf president Victor Montagliani, whose confederation covers North and Central America alongside the Caribbean, maintained that distributing such funds did not depend on obtaining private backing.

"Releasing part of these reserves would demonstrate that MAs should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits," they wrote in correspondence seen by the Press Association.

open image in gallery Aleksander Ceferin (left) is ramping up the pressure on Infantino (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

"Development is an institutional responsibility of Fifa – not a matter of individual discretion. We therefore propose that our confederations jointly complete this analysis and agree on the amount of Fifa’s reserves that should be released directly to the MAs, with recommendations on disbursements put forward for consideration through FIFA’s proper governance process at the next Fifa Council meeting."

Ceferin and Montagliani pointed out that even after paying 10m dollars to each association, reserves would remain above $1.5 billion (£1.1bn) throughout the 2027-30 cycle.

"Once a clearer picture of Fifa’s financial position at year-end is available, the Fifa Council can determine if a larger distribution is possible, and whether an equivalent distribution should follow in 2031-34," they wrote.

The confederation leaders stated this support should be supplementary to amounts Fifa is already committed to providing through the FIFA Forward scheme.

Infantino shelved the private investment plan on 1 August after Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation rejected the proposal.

Uefa maintains it lacks confidence in Infantino despite the scheme’s withdrawal and intends to identify an alternative candidate to oppose him in upcoming presidential elections.

On 27 August, Uefa requested an independent review into the formulation of the private funding plan, following a similar request made by Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt on the Fifa Council.

Uefa has also initiated legal action in US courts to obtain documents concerning the proposal, which Fifa has been permitted to contest.

FIFA has been asked for comment.

England bowler Brydon Carse will face no charges after an investigation into an alleged assault was closed by Derbyshire Police.

Carse was handcuffed by officers after a celebratory night out with Durham team-mates on August 23 and it was later confirmed he had been arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly, before being “de-arrested” after agreeing to depart.

Derbyshire Police said they were investigating an alleged assault in connection with the incident but have now determined no further action will be taken.

open image in gallery Brydon Carse in action for England (Robbie Stephenson/PA). ( PA Archive )

In a statement, Derbyshire Police said: “An investigation into reports of an assault in Derby city centre has been closed.

“Officers attended Molly Malones in the Wardwick, Derby, in the early hours of Sunday 23 August. A man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and was then de-arrested after his details were taken by officers.”

Subsequent enquiries were made pursuing the allegations of an assault but, after the alleged victim was identified and spoken to, no further action was taken, police said.

The matter is now in the hands of the independent Cricket Regulator, which will assess if Carse has a disciplinary issue to answer to relating to his conduct.

Carse has continued playing for Durham since the episode took place, helping his side win the Division Two title of the Rothesay County Championship, but he has been overlooked by England.

He was immediately removed from the squad ahead of the second Test against Pakistan, then left out of the final match too. While officially considered available for selection for the ongoing white-ball series against Sri Lanka, he was left on the sidelines once again.

open image in gallery Brydon Carse has helped Durham win the Division Two title (Mike Egerton/PA). ( PA Wire )

Speaking earlier this week, England’s limited-overs head coach Brendon McCullum called for his side to be mindful of their off-field responsibilities and added: “I’ve spoken to Carsey a lot and it’s the same message – you need to make good decisions off the field that allow you to be able to be the best version of yourself.

“As far as Carsey is concerned, it’s a good chance for him now to get his house in order and then push for selection for the next opportunity that arises.”

Test captain Joe Root also had his say ahead of the Lord’s Test when he described himself as “hacked off” by the growing list of alcohol-related incidents involving England players.

On Carse, he said: “I don’t think I’m speaking out of turn in saying he’s very upset, very apologetic and understands his actions. I’m sure when he gets his chance, he will say that himself.”

Holiday cottage owners have warned that they may be forced to close their businesses if proposed tax hikes on holiday lets go ahead.

The government has reportedly drawn up plans to introduce a tax for holiday cottages ahead of Andy Burnham’s first Budget, classing them as second homes rather than businesses.

The move could add thousands of pounds to the cost of running them, with tourism bosses warning that owners may be forced to sell up with a “catastrophic knock-on effect” on local businesses.

Molly and Matthew James, who run Croft Farm Holiday Cottages near Perranporth in Cornwall, told The Independent that the move would leave them between “a bit of a rock and a hard place” as they were already struggling to make ends meet after Storm Goretti tore down 43 trees on their property, which they are still dealing with months on.

open image in gallery Matthew and Molly James have run Croft Farm Holiday Cottages since 2013 ( Supplied )

When Ms James saw news of the proposed tax on holiday homes, she said she “didn’t know how to process it.”

“I think we’d have to close, but I also think we would struggle to sell, so I don’t really know what we’d do,” she said. “So we can’t sell because to try and find a buyer for something like this is quite tricky, we can't sell them off individually because they're not residential.

“We sleep 27 across the five cottages, that's 27 beds that have been under high demand this summer, that's 27 per week spending power not being used in our local economy.”

The visitor economy sector makes up 15 per cent of the Cornish economy, according to Cornwall Opportunities, with £2 billion of visitor spend annually.

The couple have been running the holiday let since 2013 after they moved their children down from Bristol for a different life.

While they managed to build up a steady business over seven years, they said that “every single penny went” after Covid lost them custom and the cost of maintenance has increased year on year since.

“These last six years have been insane,” Ms James said. “We are a small business, but our turnover is under the VAT threshold and therefore you'd think there'd be some support there, but although it's not a massive amount, we have got business rates this year.”

“We love being part of the holiday industry,” Ms James said. “98 per cent of the people are absolutely lovely and it's really nice sharing your time with them, and sharing our space. We're really lucky to have a beautiful space here and even post Storm Goretti, it's still a stunning location next to some of the most beautiful beaches that we really want people to come and enjoy.”

Director of Toad Hall Cottages agency James Norton, which represents over a thousand properties across the south-west, said that local businesses in the area would be affected if the holiday home sector crumbled.

open image in gallery The couple’s cottage is not far from Perranporth beach ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

“We've had council tax premiums, we've had rises in business rates, we had the furnished holiday abolition, we've had obviously national insurance increases as an employer which has affected everyone around her. We've also had increased fire regulations,” he told The Independent. “There's been so many things that that just sound like words on paper, but when you look at what they actually mean, it's really decimating the industry.

“We're losing a lot of holiday cottage owners for whom it's just not economically viable anymore, and I think there's a misconception that lots of these people earn good money from having a holiday let and the truth of it is most of them just about cover their mortgage and quite a few of them don't even do that.”

He added that if the holiday let industry declined, “there will be a catastrophic knock-on effect for the tourism businesses in the area.”

“It's the people that own and run the restaurants, the bakeries, the butchers, the shops round here whether it's clothes shops, toy shops, you know it's far ranging.”

A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

Hikers hoping to visit St. Mary's Glacier in Clear Creek County Colorado might find themselves disappointed since the geological feature recently melted.

St. Mary's Glacier is a perennial snowfield that, according to scientists, is a remnant of glaciers. At least it was, until it melted.

Jeremy Elder, a resident of Idaho Springs, told the Aspen Times that he lives approximately five miles from the geological site and, when he visited on Monday, found the snowfield had completely disappeared.

“I was surprised to see absolutely nothing,” he told the paper. “Not seeing any snow up there — it was honestly pretty sad to see that. It’s been such a hot summer, and with the weak snowpack last winter, I feel like all those things contributed. It’s just getting hotter and hotter, and we’re seeing the direct effects here.”

The snowfield has been around for hundreds of years and survived even the heat of summer, holding out just long enough to be rejuvenated by winter snowstorms. But now the beloved patch of snow is no more thanks to human-driven climate change.

St. Mary’s Glacier in Colorado. The area is a perennial snowfield that completely melted for the first time in recorded history in September 2026 ( Getty Images )

The melt likely isn't a terrible shock to anyone who was watched the snowfield shrink over the course of the last century.

Jordan Lipp, of Golden, told the Aspen Times that he's visited the area more than 100 times in the past 30 years, and said he actually anticipated — based on his observations of the snowfield's shrinking — that this would be the summer it disappeared completely.

He told the paper that he visited the snowfield to ski on September 12, but found there had been so much melt that only "two tiny pieces of snow" were left. Four days later, he returned to St. Mary's and found it completely bare.

St. Mary's Glacier's melting is of course not occurring in isolation. It, like many glaciers and snowfields across the planet, is at the mercy of human-driven climate change.

Glaciers across the world have have been shrinking every year for the past 39 years, according to the NOAA.

In Colorado, average annual temperatures have increase by about 2.3 degrees Fahrenheit between 1980 and 2022, according to the Colorado Climate Center.

Jonathan Ingraham, the outdoor editor for the Rocky Mountain Journal, was among those who visited the site post-melt.

“The first thought that ran through my mind yesterday was that this glacier and the snowfield probably had been the first time it had been melted out. It was just a little of awe and surreal,” he told Fox31.

While snowstorms will no doubt dump snow back into the area later this year, it remains to be seen if the snowfield will continue on as a perennial snowfield or become a seasonal fixture that melts away in summer.
