Earl Spencer has insisted he is “telling the truth” about a claim in his new book that the King told him that his sister Diana would be forgotten “soon enough” following her death.

In an interview with the BBC, the Earl said he was left “stunned” by Charles’ response to his former wife’s fatal car crash and that his words were “monstrous”, adding: “Those are exactly the words he said.”

Asked about Buckingham Palace’s response to his claims, Earl Spencer told the BBC: “Is he (Charles) furious, or is he embarrassed? Because I can tell you, here and now, those are exactly the words he said.

“I’ve only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. I was hyper-alert to what he was saying, and those are precisely the words he said, and I promise that to you now, genuinely, that is what he said.

“I don’t hear him saying he didn’t say that.”

open image in gallery Earl Spencer (left), Prince William, Prince Harry and the then Prince of Wales, waiting as the hearse carrying the coffin of Diana, Princess of Wales prepares to leave Westminster Abbey following her funeral service ( PA )

A spokesman for the palace hit back on the claims after they first emerged on Wednesday, saying “fraternal grief can cloud reason”.

King Charles has been engulfed in a third day of controversy following a series of bombshell allegations made by Earl Spencer in a tribute book to his older sister, Diana, Princess of Wales.

The keenly awaited memoir Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is being serialised in the Daily Mail before it is published next Tuesday.

On Friday, the Earl detailed the day of Diana’s funeral and claimed there had been a “lack of obvious care for Harry”, who had walked behind his mother’s coffin.

He wrote: “He needed Diana’s hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him. But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control.

“I have often looked back, reckoning that a more caring hand at such points as this would have helped him enormously in the future. Instead, he seemed so very alone in his despair and torment.”

In one of the most shocking allegations, the Earl claimed that the King had sounded “giddily elated… like a lottery winner” when he rang following her death in 1997.

open image in gallery Earl Spencer insisted to the BBC that he is ‘telling the truth’ ( BBC )

He also revealed comments Charles supposedly made about his ex-wife in a row over funeral preparations, in which he was said to have told Diana’s brother that “we’ll forget her soon enough”.

One excerpt read: “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated – like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.”

The Earl added: “He let me know he had informed William and Harry of their mother’s death, first thing that morning, in their bedrooms at Balmoral.

“It all sounded strangely matter-of-fact, given the enormity of the disaster.

“Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”

He also wrote about how he fought plans for William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk behind their mother’s coffin during the funeral procession.

The Earl is said to have insisted to the King that Diana would not have wanted her young sons to have made the difficult public walk.

“He went nuts. ‘That’s the problem with your family. They’ve got no bloody sense of duty!’ he started, before descending into a general rage,” Earl Spencer wrote.

open image in gallery Buckingham Palace responded to the claims, saying ‘fraternal grief can cloud reason’ ( PA )

“Prince Charles continued his stream of anger, without me interrupting. Then he stopped.

“I assumed the pause signalled an effort to bring himself under control, but then he unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured’, he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough!’”

The allegations sparked an “unprecedented” response from Buckingham Palace, which hit back before the serialisation, saying “fraternal grief can cloud reason”.

A Buckingham Palace spokesman said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”

Earl Spencer says the book has been written to correct “untruths” told about his older sister, who he says was “contemplating ending it all” and drove “more than once” to the cliffs at Beachy Head in East Sussex.

He also revealed details about Diana’s unhappy marriage to Charles and her wish to call off the engagement prior to their wedding in 1981, and claimed that the late Queen Elizabeth II considered restoring his sister’s Her Royal Highness title, which she lost when she divorced Charles.

The revelations come amid a difficult time for the royal family, who have been surrounded by controversy following a string of scandals.

It also follows the recent return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who the King has insisted are no longer working members of the royal family.

Rogue drones are targeting Britain’s military bases almost daily, leaving the UK vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran, The Independent can reveal.

Some 340 security incidents involving drones were reported at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026, data obtained under freedom of information laws show. In 2025, there were a total of 250 incidents recorded – double the 126 recorded the year before.

Experts warn the alarming increase reflects the government’s woeful lack of security and unreadiness to combat hostile threats at a time of intense escalation from Vladimir Putin, as well as aggression from Iran.

The MoD would not give details of who it suspected was behind the threats, but experts say hostile actors working on behalf of Moscow or Tehran were the obvious culprits. The stark figures, obtained under freedom of information laws, come as Poland warned that Putin is planning a drone attack on a Nato country.

open image in gallery Donald Tusk warns that Putin is planning a hybrid drone and missile attack on a Nato country ( Reuters )

Former Tory defence minister and former Army captain Tobias Ellwood said the large sharp uptick in detected drone incidents in the UK showed that the British military is viewed “as a target” and said the government is “asleep” to such threats.

He added: “Here in the UK we are doing nothing about protecting our critical national infrastructure, as well as military bases, and it’s such an easy way to disrupt.

“At the moment these are just rogue drones, and they’re passive, but it’s not a huge step to then add a kinetic dimension to them to make them introduce lethality.

“All this points to the fact that we are not taking the rise in threat levels that our European cousins are addressing seriously at all.”

Mr Ellwood said Russia and Iran were “100 per cent” responsible for many of those incidents. “They are absolutely active in Britain in plotting, mapping, and then recruiting useful idiots to prosecute this targeting.

“It could be criminal gangs as well, but they would then be supported by Russia. Russia is by far the obvious culprit here... It’s not China’s style. They tend to do things in a different way.”

It comes amid growing concerns over the UK’s ability to defend itself and intense pressure on Labour to boost defence spending and prioritise national security.

open image in gallery A 'no drone zone' sign near His Majesty's Naval Base Clyde in Scotland ( Getty )

Polish prime minister Donald Tusk warned on Friday that Moscow was planning hybrid strikes with drones or missiles targeting Nato countries supporting Ukraine.

“There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction,” he added.

UK chief of the defence staff, Sir Richard Knighton, cautioned earlier this year that the UK is facing the highest level of threat from Russia since the Cold War. And security minister Angela Eagle also warned of the dangers posed by Iran after the UK “identified activity linked to the IRGC involving threats to life and intimidation on UK soil”.

The Ministry of Defence said the rise in incidents reflected improvements in reporting, better counter-drone detection technology, and enhanced awareness among military personnel.

But Mr Ellwood bit back and insisted the government must ramp up security.

He said: “To say [incidents] have gone up because people are getting better at reporting, that’s shocking. These numbers are huge, and it means that this has been going on a long time, and we’ve completely ignored it.”

He added that Britain was rightly stepping up support for Ukraine, but the consequences meant Russia will be seeking to retaliate and the UK can expect to see “aggravated intrusion into our airspace increase over the next months and years”.

“Sadly, we won’t really react and find the money to move on the scale we need to.”

Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow for strategy and national security at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said: “I think it is increasingly important for governments, European governments overall, to be open about drones.

“We are still in the dark as to who is operating those drones. We believe it was highly likely that Russia was running a campaign over Europe.

“At a time of heightened awareness of Russian activity, the fact that the government is effectively operating in a pre-war scenario and is telling people to get prepared, you want your communications to be simple, clean, and not confusing.

“I think the House of Commons Defence Committee pretty well summed it up in terms of whether we are ready for war, and their answer was no.”

open image in gallery Louise Sandher-Jones said the government was introducing several policies aimed at combatting hostile drone threats ( AFP/Getty )

Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, told The Independent the government “is taking the threat posed by hostile drones to defence sites extremely seriously” by investing in counter-drone systems and giving defence personnel new powers to defeat drones threatening defence sites.

“In February, we established new restricted airspace areas over 44 critical defence sites in the UK. This autumn, we will introduce restricted airspace areas over a further 160 sites,” she said.

“By the end of the year, the Armed Forces Bill will become law, giving our personnel the power to take out drones – whether in the air, on the ground, or in the water – posing a threat to any defence site without the need for assistance from the police.

“The government has quadrupled its spending on anti-drone kit since taking office, with the Defence Investment Plan investing £750m into counter-drone systems and protection for our armed forces, both at home and deployed overseas.”

open image in gallery The government says it has ramped up spending on counter-drone defences ( PA )

Retired Brigadier Ben Barry, who was formerly a Nato commander and director of the British Army Staff, said: “Yes, the armed forces are spending a lot of money on counter-drone systems, but you have to remember that will be divided between protecting the armed forces when they’re deployed on overseas operations and protecting bases and units in the UK.

“What are the likely explanations for the drones? Well, it could be hobbyists, it could be criminals looking for stuff to steal, it could be hostile state intelligence services, it could also be terrorists doing reconnaissance.

“Malign activity and attacks from Russia have increased over the last few years, and as Russia continues to struggle in Ukraine, it is likely to increase further.

“There’s quite clearly been hostile activity by Iran in the UK,” he added.

“Unless the defence budget is rapidly increased, the government’s going to find it very difficult to meet the pledges it’s made.”

The Ministry of Defence and Labour have been approached for comment.

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”

News.title: Global fund utilises AI to tackle malaria, TB, and HIV amid aid cuts
News.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is helping to soften the blow from aid cuts, according to one of the world’s biggest development funds.

The Global Fund, which raises and invests billions of pounds to reduce the burden of HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria globally says new AI-driven products like portable pregnancy scanners are helping to mitigate the funding gap.

“[We] have adapted pretty quickly to the changes in the funding environment; it has undoubtedly had negative impacts on health outcomes [...], but in some ways, the resilience of life-saving services has been remarkable,” Peter Sands, the executive director of the Global Fund, told The Telegraph.

The Global Fund is managing a $6 billion (£4.4bn) shortfall for the period 2026 to 2028 and has been forced to make difficult decisions to continue their work, it confirmed this week.

The gap comes as Western governments shift money from foreign aid to defence. The UK reduced its contribution to the fund by 15 per cent last year to £850 million, down from £1 billion.

But Mr Sands said investments in tools to tackle infectious diseases – including those driven by AI – are starting to pay off.

“Innovation is absolutely part of the answer when money is short. One of the few ways you can get to make the money go further is to have a better tool, a better way of doing things,” Mr Sands said.

News.title: Thomas Tuchel faces fight to win trust of England players
News.content:
“This is how it should be, this is what a World Cup is for, to connect with the people and to give them experiences that they will not forget. And this is the feedback that I get.”

Asked if he had received any negative feedback at all since the World Cup, Tuchel answered: “No. Not at all. Do you think that’s necessary? I had some quite bad stuff between Argentina and France. [But] No [not since I’ve been back in England].”

The FA publicly backed Tuchel after the defeat by Argentina, but the German has now revealed that he was privately told his job was safe well before that.

Even if England had lost to Mexico and failed to reach the last eight of the World Cup, Tuchel has claimed he would not have been sacked. He said: “There was a moment, a very special moment, before the Mexico game where we had a talk and my bosses told me ‘we know that anything can happen in a football match, we know that anything can happen in a match in Mexico, in a World Cup match, but don’t worry, we see what’s going on and we want to continue like this’.

“It was a beautiful moment for me as a coach. I felt this kind of freedom to take my choices and to just coach freely, and there was never a doubt in my mind that we would continue together and there was obviously never a doubt in their mind.”

England secured their best World Cup finish since 1966 by winning the bronze-medal game against France in a chaotic match in Miami.

“If you look at the 6-4 against France, people talk about it like it’s one of their nicest experiences ever, to watch a football match,” Tuchel said. “So maybe I have to compromise in my wish for control, for a little bit more chaos, embrace the chaos, and maybe it brings out the best.”

Warnings for Alexander-Arnold and Palmer

Tuchel has named his first England squad since the World Cup for four Nations League games against Spain, Czech Republic (home and away) and Croatia. He has recalled Cole Palmer and Trent Alexander-Arnold to his squad, but insists he has lost no sleep over not taking the pair to the World Cup.

News.title: Fiji declares national crisis as HIV epidemic escalates
News.content:
“The rollout has been slow and frustrating, and Fiji will pay for it in terms of lives lost,” said Prof Lisa Maher, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute in Sydney who is supporting Fiji’s response. “This is the only thing that will turn the epidemic around and stop people dying, and stop onward transmission of HIV to the general population.”

But the emergency declaration should provide political cover to introduce the needle and syringe programme, with a Cabinet subcommittee now created to remove barriers to action.

“The government is signalling that it is prepared to act in this particularly important and controversial area,” said Prof Maher. “It’s not coincidental that the draft bill [to legalise the distribution of needles and syringes for certain groups] now looks likely to go before parliament, after being blocked for 10 months… So it’s not just symbolic.”

Dr Jason Mitchell, head of Fiji’s HIV taskforce, added: “Since the government announced [the crisis], it has followed with some very rapid actions in progressing the needle and syringe programme. So that is being fast tracked through the necessary channels, and the government is determined to get that out in the next couple of weeks.

“We’ve gotten to the point where we really needed to take some really strong action,” he told The Telegraph. “This is the government realising that there have been challenges, and they need to step it up.”

It is hoped that the declaration will also turbocharge other elements of the response – for instance the scale-up of the post-exposure prophylaxis (Prep) scheme, which was introduced in May – as the virus gains a foothold in the broader population.

Although there has been a major focus on testing, treatment and education, UNAIDS still estimates that only 39 per cent of an estimated 9,100 people living with HIV in 2025 knew their positive status. Just 22 per cent were accessing antiretroviral treatment, and 117 people died in 2025, compared to 25 in 2021.

News.title: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing
News.content:
There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

News.title: Banton shows his worth as England cruise to series victory against Sri Lanka
News.content:
A patchy Test team and a one-day international side learning on the job should not obscure the fact that under Harry Brook, England have built a formidable T20 outfit.

Missing a slew of first-choice players, they dispatched Sri Lanka with a game to spare and an emphatic show of their depth in the format, with Sonny Baker and Tom Banton – two men still finding their feet in the side – to the fore. England have now won 20 of the 23 completed T20s since Brook took over last year, and six matches in a row this summer. It is easily their best format and, as Liam Dawson said, they have “match-winners throughout” and plenty of “freak” performers.

In this six-wicket win, Baker’s one for 15 limited England’s target to a paltry 146, which Banton, a natural opener who is being recommissioned in the middle order, helped knock off with 47 balls remaining. “Tonight was a special performance, very clinical,” said Brook.

News.title: Interest rate increase ‘likely’, warns Bank of England
News.content:
Andrew Bailey has said that interest rates are likely to rise if the Middle East war rages on, warning inflation is now on course to hit 4pc.

The Bank of England opted to hold borrowing costs at 3.75pc on Thursday, the sixth time in a row it has left them unchanged.

However, the Governor said a “material” increase in energy prices since July would push up inflation to twice the Bank’s 2pc target.

He warned the outlook for inflation “continues to be on the upside” and criticised the “seeming loss of urgency to find solutions” to the war in Iran.

Oil prices are back above $100 a barrel and analysts expect average gas and electricity bills to rise above £2,000 this winter as the conflict continues.

Mr Bailey said: “So far, higher global energy costs have had a limited effect on price and wage setting in the UK.

“But the longer this volatility persists, the bigger the impact it will have on inflation, and the more likely it is we will need to raise Bank Rate to ensure that inflation falls back to our 2pc target.”

Investors expect the Bank to raise interest rates as soon as November, which has pushed average mortgage rates to their highest level in three years.

The average five-year fixed mortgage deal has risen to 5.87pc, according to Moneyfacts, which is the highest level since November 2023 and up from 4.95pc before the Iran war.

Thursday’s rate hold leaves the Bank out of step with central banks around the world after the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank voted to raise borrowing costs this month.

However, economists said there had been a change in tone from policymakers over the threat posed by energy prices and whether this would feed into the wider economy.

The Bank of England predicted that inflation would hit 4pc early next year, just as most workers are negotiating pay rises.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said: “It seems as though a majority of the MPC is on the cusp of wanting to tighten policy.”

In a warning on the impending pain facing households, Mr Bailey told the Chancellor that energy bills would rise by 24pc early next year under the Ofgem price cap.

This will push up annual average bills by £413 to £2,136, which the Governor blamed on the war in the Middle East.

The Governor is required to write a formal letter to the Chancellor every time inflation is more than a percentage point above its 2pc target.

Official data showed inflation rose to 3.1pc in August.

Mr Bailey said: “The energy price shock has been the most important factor driving recent short-term movements in inflation.”

Despite expectations of higher rates, the FTSE 100 rose on Thursday at its steepest pace since July, climbing more than 1pc, as the Bank of England eased the pressure on the UK bond market.

Policymakers also confirmed a Telegraph report that the Bank will stop selling the long-dated bonds it amassed during the financial crisis and lockdown.

The Bank will continue actively selling £20bn of government bonds per year until the rest of the stockpile is wound down to zero in 2034.

The announcement triggered a sharp fall in the cost of borrowing for the Treasury, with the yield on 30-year UK gilts falling at the fastest pace since May.

News.title: Next-generation antivenom fights India’s deadliest snakes
News.content:
The process to make antivenom has barely changed in a century: snakes are milked, their venom is injected into horses, and their antibodies are harvested to form the basis of the product. The resulting treatments are difficult to administer, can trigger severe side effects, and the quality varies from batch to batch.

“The big four snakes contribute to 70 per cent of poisonous bites [in India]… so 30 per cent of poisonous snakes are not covered, even to begin with,” said Dr Yogesh Jain, a public health physician in Chhattisgarh state and a member of The Global Snakebite Taskforce.

“But there are huge quality and efficacy issues even against these 70 per cent of bites. We’re relying on a 100-year-old technique of getting antivenoms, and at least 50,000 people are dying every year,” he told The Telegraph.

“There’s a real need for new technology. We don’t have a safe and appropriate antivenom for the largest majority of people in rural India.”

Now, scientists are hopeful that they have developed a potential alternative.

In the latest study, published last week, researchers showed that an experimental antivenom cocktail with five components protected mice against lethal doses of antivenom in Indian cobras, even when delayed by up to 20 minutes – a scenario that mimics the real-world lag between a bite and treatment.

“If you go 10 years back, people didn’t think you could make sufficiently simple products with new, modern biotechnology that could cover all these different snake venoms,” said Prof Andreas Laustsen-Kiel, head of the Section of Biologics Engineering at the Technical University of Denmark and co-author of the paper.

“People simply believed it was too complex, too expensive to manufacture, and so on… But the data we are gathering is convincing enough to say this is something that could make a huge dent in the lost lives and limbs snakebite causes every year.”

The antivenom itself was based on lab-made nanobodies – antibodies derived from a group of animals including camels, llamas and some species of shark. Scientists believe their structure means they could be a more potent, more precise, more temperature-stable alternative to man-made monoclonal antibodies – and cheaper to manufacture.

“The latest study builds on an earlier discovery of nanobodies that can protect across a broad spectrum of African snakes,” said Prof Nicholas Casewell, director of the Centre for Snakebite Research and Interventions at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, who has previously collaborated with Prof Laustsen-Kiel.

“In this paper they have iterated and demonstrated that a narrow number of nanobodies can protect against Indian cobras and king cobras. This demonstration brings the nanobody technology closer to market,” he added.

But that is likely still years away, depending on how much funding the researchers can attract. The next steps – a larger animal study, scaling up manufacture, and launching human trials – are expensive.

“If money was no issue, we could probably be testing in humans in 1.5 to three years from now,” said Prof Laustsen-Kiel. “But since money is a big issue, it is more likely that human trials won’t be able to start until 2.5 to four years from now.

“But I really think that this [study shows] there’s no doubt that biotech can deliver better antivenoms. The question is whether people are willing to fund it,” he said.

Sports.title: Alex Neil stokes flames for 100th Dockers’ Derby with West Ham as Millwall boss issues Den warning before grudge match
Sports.content:

ALEX NEIL has stoked the flames ahead of Saturday’s fiery Dockers Derby by declaring: “We love being hated.”

The Millwall boss insists his squad embraces being written off as they prepare to host West Ham at a packed Den.



Neil is relishing the chance to turn over the Lions’ bitter rivals.

And he told SunSport: “We love the underdog scenario that people tend to taint us with.



“Our famous song sums us up in the fact that people might not like what we do, how we do it — but we literally don’t care.

“I think that the interpretation of Millwall and the reality when you’re actually in it is two very different things.

“It’s a real privilege for me to be in the position that I’m in with this club and to feel part of that.

“So as far as we’re concerned we focus on ourselves and what’s good for our fanbase and try to get the results that we can.”

The two London clubs have not met each other for more than 12 years — West Ham winning 2-1 in the Championship at Upton Park in February 2012.

Neil draws on his Glaswegian roots to illustrate the passion and deep generational hatred that fuels this rivalry.

The feud between the two clubs dates back more than a century to dockyard disputes on the River Thames.

And Neil completely understands how deeply entrenched the fixture remains for families across South and East London.

He said: “I think what ends up happening is it’s so entrenched in the community as much as anything else.

“Almost from birth a kid will either have a Millwall or West Ham shirt put on them. You’re indoctrinated before you can even speak or walk or see anything else.

“I’ve been to a few Old Firm derbies which is probably as close in terms of magnitude and importance.



“The biggest difference down here is the fact that the Old Firm derby happens on a regular basis — whereas this one hasn’t happened so often, which is why it’s being discussed so much.

“The biggest thing I’ve always taken from derbies is the atmosphere. You can literally feel the passion, determination and desperation.”

Managing the extreme temperature inside the stadium will be crucial for both teams if they are to avoid costly red cards.

Neil has demanded his players strike a delicate balance between fierce effort and composure on the pitch.

He wants total aggression in the tackle, but complete discipline in their decision-making during moments of high pressure.



The Lions boss explained: “It’s trying to find that middle ground. It’s about making sure we’re doing what our fans would expect to see from their team in terms of running, determination and having that passion.

“But at the same time we must also control our emotions, don’t be silly or put the team at a disadvantage by making bad decisions.

“You can’t lunge into things that put you in trouble. It’s about having that fire in your belly but maintaining a cool mind.

“When a player steps into my dressing room, they do their job and give absolutely everything for the team — and more importantly we never give up.”



Strict security measures and heavy police operations will be deployed around Bermondsey to ensure safety for both fanbases.

Millwall and West Ham have worked tirelessly behind the scenes with Metropolitan Police authorities to guarantee the high-profile fixture passes without major incident off the pitch.

Saturday marks the ONE HUNDREDTH meeting between the old foes with Millwall edging West Ham with 38 wins to 34.

The Irons have hit their stride after a slow start with four wins on the spin — and go into today’s game top of the Championship after seven games.



Nuno Espirito Santo’s side are huge favourites to return to the Premier League at the first time of asking.

But Neil believes the Den cauldron can bridge the gap between his side and the East Londoners’ multi-million pound line-up.

He said: “Every year teams come down from the Premier League and they’ve got squads that have been operating up there.

“Depending on how long they’ve been in the Premier League determines their infrastructure because the longer you’re up there, the more riches you’ve got to spend. They have been in the top league for 14 years.

“But what I will say is it doesn’t mean anything when you cross the white line.



“That’s the biggest message to our lads — the fact that it doesn’t matter what your squad’s worth. When you cross that white line, it’s going to be 11 versus 11 and we’ve got to treat the game that way.”

Millwall have endured a frustrating injury crisis in the opening weeks of the season and at one point had THIRTEEN players out.

Despite the depleted options, Neil has promised home fans that every single player wearing a Lions shirt will leave everything on the pitch.

Brydon Carse will not face any charges after an investigation

Brydon Carse will not face any charges after Derbyshire Police closed their investigation into an alleged assault following an incident involving the England cricketer at a nightclub in Derby.

Last month, Carse was handcuffed outside a nightclub in Derby and missed the second and third Tests of England's series against Pakistan.

The 31-year-old was celebrating with Durham players after their win at Derbyshire in the County Championship and was also seen talking to team-mate Matthew Potts with former England captain Ben Stokes also pictured in the background.

Since making his international Test debut in October 2024, Carse has been England's wicket taker with 58 wickets to his name, including 22 in last winter's Ashes.

While he was omitted from the England squad during the Pakistan series, he continued to play for Durham during the Derbyshire Police investigation in the County Championship.

Ryan Gerard leapfrogged Adam Scott and Filippo Celli to take a two-shot lead at the halfway stage of the BMW PGA Championship, as Rory McIlroy impressed on day two to finish four shots off the lead.

Scott and Celli had climbed to take a share of the clubhouse lead midway through the second round at 10 under par, but Gerard surged in the afternoon, posting a flawless bogey-free seven-under 65 to finish his day at 12 under.

Aaron Rai, who co-led coming into Friday's round, finished tied with Manuel Elvira for fourth, while his playing partners, McIlroy and Ryan Fox, trailed them by one shot, sharing sixth place with five other players at eight under par.

Some big names missed the cut on Friday at Wentworth, including European Ryder Cup stars Jon Rahm and Tommy Fleetwood, with the Spaniard enduring a torrid two days at Wentworth, going 11 over par through 36 holes.

Tyrrell Hatton and Matt Fitzpatrick had at times been in danger of missing the cut too on Friday, but both produced remarkable finishes, each chipping in on the 18th, with the former making an eagle, to cap off their second rounds in style.

Race to Dubai leader Patrick Reed was forced to withdraw due to injury on the ninth hole after going nine over par.

More to follow…

Sports.title: Gabriel edging closer to Man Utd exit after Barca talks
Sports.content:
JJ Gabriel and his representatives are in Barcelona for talks about a potential move to the Catalan club.

The 15-year-old is attracting interest from a number of Premier League clubs, as well as Real Madrid, Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich, after he and his team put in a formal request to leave United.

Despite the leadership at United being hopeful they can persuade the young star to stay at the club as he is contracted until the end of the season, it looks more and more likely Gabriel is edging closer to a move away from Old Trafford.

Gabriel and his representatives put in a formal request to be de-registered after the UEFA Youth League tie against Sabah last Thursday - a game United won 5-0 with Gabriel scoring a hat-trick.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Khan updates Sky Sports on Gabriel's decision to leave Manchester United

Gabriel, who was not named in any of England's youth squads announced on Friday despite representing England most recently at U17 level, has not trained with United since then.

There is a belief - owing to a precedent due to a FIFA loophole - that Gabriel could leave United for a club in Europe once he turns 16 [on October 6] if he obtains a European passport that he could get through either of his parents.

Image: Manchester United celebrate Gabriel's opener in the FA Youth Cup semi-final

However, any move for Gabriel would be subject to FIFA approval.

United head coach Michael Carrick was asked about Gabriel on Friday and reiterated his view that the matter needed to be handled carefully.

"I think he's a young boy, JJ, and I think it's important that we certainly don't play anything out here," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Carrick has urged care in the handling of Gabriel, after the 15-year-old requested to leave the club

"I think the exposure and the scrutiny and everything, you've got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything, so the situation will work itself out, whatever way it's going to work itself out. Making sure he's okay is the important thing."

Merson: Massive blow if Gabriel leaves

Sky Sports' Paul Merson:

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Paul Merson says teenage sensations Max Dowman and Gabriel need to be patient as they look to build their careers

"First of all, he's an unbelievable talent. The problem now is with the lad and probably his agents and his family - I don't know him so I'm only thinking from the outside.

"When you're watching Max Dowman at Arsenal and Rio Ngumoha getting given a chance at Liverpool and doing very well, he's probably thinking, 'I should be playing at Man Utd now as well'.

"This is the problem you're going to have with the kids of this day and age. They're so talented that they want to play straight away. When I was playing, it was unheard of at 16.

"It'll be a massive blow for Man Utd. Believe me, this kid is an unbelievable talent. They'll have every club in the world wanting him."

Sports.title: Will Celtic ease the pressure or Rangers narrow the gap?
Sports.content:
Will Derek McInnes complete the double against Celtic, or can Martin O'Neill recover from a nightmare week to move eight points clear of Rangers?

The Old Firm sides meet in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, seven days after the Ibrox side laid down a marker with an emphatic League Cup win.

While McInnes appears to have weathered an early storm at Rangers, O'Neill is looking for solutions after Celtic followed up that 3-0 defeat with a 3-1 loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League.

Only Celtic fans will be inside Parkhead at the order of the authorities amid a ticket allocation spat between the two Glasgow giants.

We look at some of the talking points ahead of what is sure to be another fascinating encounter...

Is pressure mounting on O'Neill?

It is amazing how quickly things can change in football.

Just a few months ago, O'Neill was at peak legendary Celtic status after saving their season to deliver a league and cup double.

They then capitulated against LASK and crashed out of the Champions League, but a winning domestic start kept the pressure off.

Image: Celtic have suffered back-to-back defeats

However, the League Cup defeat to Rangers, followed by their Europa League loss to Ferencvaros means Sunday could be seen as a must-win for the veteran boss - even if the 74-year-old does not think so.

Celtic are guaranteed to go into the international break top of the Scottish Premiership, but few Celtic fans would accept back-to-back defeats to their fiercest rivals. Especially when they have dominated domestically for so long.

O'Neill will be desperately seeking solutions ahead of Sunday's game after admitting their confidence has taken a hit.

Is McInnes out the woods?

While the pressure is mounting at Parkhead, it appears to be easing at Ibrox after a turbulent start for McInnes.

Failure to secure European football and a slow start domestically had many wondering if he was the right manager to deliver silverware.

Image: Rangers are looking for their fifth straight win

But then the results started to come, and a tactical masterclass against Celtic to reach the League Cup semi-finals has switched the momentum.

The former Rangers midfielder backed himself to bring success to the club and victory on Sunday would put them just two points behind Celtic in the Scottish Premiership.

But defeat would leave them eight points in arrears after just seven games. If that happens, the scrutiny would no doubt return.

Big selection issues for Celtic

Image: It was a tough night for Celtic against Ferencvaros

It is not just a selection headache, but a dizzying migraine facing O'Neill - with five key positions to ponder before Sunday's showdown.

You can only confidently predict six of his starting XI: captain Callum McGregor, talismanic midfielder Benjamin Nygren, top scorer Camilo Duran, fans' favourite Kieran Tierney, reliable defender Cameron Carter-Vickers and academy graduate Colby Donovan.

GK: Goalkeeper Sam Johnstone was less than convincing on his Old Firm debut last weekend and was replaced by previous No 1 Viljami Sinisalo against Ferencvaros on Thursday.

LCB: Liam Scales and Auston Trusty regularly trade places at left centre-back, but the former has started the last two matches in that position.

Image: Celtic's Liam Scales cleared a shot off the line at Ibrox but scored an own goal against the Hungarians

CM: Captain McGregor was left exposed as a solo sitting midfield player at Ibrox so O'Neill might be tempted to bring in Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain for Mika Baur to provide additional protection. He must weigh-up whether he sticks with one six and two eights or switches to two sixes and one 10.

RW: Haissem Hassan has impressed since signing from Real Oviedo this summer but was left out of the starting XI last Sunday. The Egyptian must surely be in contention - especially if Rangers are expected to defend three-vs-three at the back.

Image: Callum McGregor believes Sunday's game is the 'ultimate test' after a tough week

ST: Club-record signing Kasper Hogh has scored in just one of his seven matches for Celtic so far. He was left on the bench against Ferencvaros to allow Duran to operate in his more natural No 9 position and may find it difficult to dislodge the Colombian from there. If that were to be the case, it is a toss-up between James Forrest and Sebastian Tounekti for the left-wing berth.

Will Rangers stick or twist at Parkhead?

Image: Will Derek McInnes make changes for the Old Firm rematch?

McInnes got his game plan spot on at Ibrox, and Celtic could not live with his team.

He used left-back James Penrice as an auxiliary midfielder to flood the middle of the pitch - allowing Rangers to press Celtic man for man.

Djeidi Gassama and Min-Su Kim provided width and energy as wing-backs with Dujon Sterling, Emmanuel Fernandez and Olwethu Makhanya defending three-vs-three against Celtic's front line.

It was a bold decision that paid dividends as Celtic folded under the pressure.

Dan Neil snatched the starring role of midfield general from his Celtic counterpart McGregor, who was left isolated without a defensive-minded midfield partner.

Image: Dan Neil netted a double against Celtic as Rangers reached the League Cup semi finals

The former Sunderland man would probably have still been named player of the match even if he had not netted two famous derby goals.

But Celtic Park will be a different test, especially with no away fans.

McInnes opted for two strikers last Sunday, but he might plump for an extra body in the heart of midfield.

If he does switch, will it be Ryan Naderi or Kevin Kelsy in that No 9 role?

Image: Kevin Kelsy scored his first Rangers goal against Celtic

Kelsy scored his first Rangers goal last weekend and was a constant threat, Naderi provided the assist but is a doubt for Sunday's showdown with an ankle problem.

He also has the option of Bojan Miovski, a player who knows the intensity of playing at Celtic Park from his days with Aberdeen.

If McInnes gets it right, he will be the first manager since Walter Smith in 1991 to win his first two Old Firm games in charge.

What the managers said

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Celtic manager Martin O'Neill is not too concerned about their form ahead of Sunday's Old Firm clash with Rangers, live on Sky Sports

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill:

"We're far from rock bottom.

"We're still in the lead and if we could win this, we can extend the lead and if we don't, even by the international break, we're still going to be in front.

"We're going to try and put that right if we can. But I know the last time we had an international break was in March time and we played very poorly against Dundee United.

"So that was, if you can call it a wake-up call or a moment of quiet reflection or whatever the case may be. We turned it round. The players are capable of turning it round.

"It's a big game, whether it's played in September or March time.

"We need to be up for the game. Do we need to win the game? It would be nice to win it, it wouldn't be great if we lost.

"That would be three on the trot. Psychologically, it would be a blow. But we need to be up for it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rangers manager Derek McInnes insists there will be no complacency from his players against Celtic on Sunday, live on Sky, despite last weekend's Old Firm win

Rangers boss Derek McInnes:

"Just because you win the game doesn't mean it always says you've got the tactics right and, equally, when you lose a game, it doesn't mean it says you've got them wrong.

"I think sometimes tactics can get a wee bit overplayed. I do think you normally win games during the individual moments and the performance of players being really high and really strong.

"We look to do something similar in terms of our approach. We want to make sure the aggression's there, the confidence is there to play.

"The energy that we displayed last week, these are all the things that are more important than tactics.

"Hopefully the players go into the game and onto the pitch with that message loud and clear that a big performance is required.

"You don't win at Celtic Park unless everybody plays well. We've got to try and bring something similar and look for those improvements again.

"Once the ball rolls, it's a game of football that we need to concentrate on the detail, in and out of possession, what we're looking to try and do."

Sports.title: Somerset title hopes suffer major blow in Yorkshire defeat as Notts also lose
Sports.content:
Somerset's hopes of becoming county champions for the first time in their history took a major blow as they collapsed to a costly defeat at the hands of Yorkshire.

Top of the County Championship Division One table heading into the penultimate round of matches, Somerset saw rivals Warwickshire wrap up a two-day victory against Essex but failed to keep pace at Headingley.

Chasing 287 - the highest score of the match - they were bundled out for 101 on the final day. Resuming on 73-3 they collapsed horribly as their final seven wickets fell for 25 runs in less than 13 overs.

Ben Cliff took three of them as he finished with 3-29 after taking 8-76 in the first innings, while Ben Coad claimed 4-33 and Matthew Revis 2-7.

Image: Yorkshire's Ben Cliff celebrates taking 11 wickets in the match against Somerset (SWpix.com)

The 185-run defeat leaves Somerset chasing from behind heading into their season-ending fixture against Surrey and one step further away from ending their 135-year quest for the county game's top prize.

Notts beaten by Sussex

Warwickshire will take an 11-point lead into the final round with Nottinghamshire also suffering a heavy defeat, while Hampshire have been relegated.

Notts could only set Sussex 76 to win at Hove and, although they grabbed a couple of early wickets to reduce the hosts to 14-2, Sussex secured a seven-wicket win just after the lunch break.

2h ago 11.46 EDT United to refuse to de-register JJ Gabriel JJ Gabriel latest: the Press Association understands Manchester United will not accept Gabriel’s request to be de-registered and have sought to persuade the youngster to stay, but there remains a risk that the 15-year-old could use a Fifa loophole to walk away when he turns 16 on October 6. Gabriel would not be allowed to join another Premier League club if United do not cancel his registration, which runs until the summer, but as he qualifies for an EU passport via his Irish lineage there is a precedent that would allow him to sign for a European club after his birthday at the start of next month. On Friday, there were reports Gabriel had arrived in Barcelona, having also been linked with Real Madrid, Paris St Germain and Bayern Munich. Michael Carrick was asked: “I think he’s a young boy, JJ, and I think it’s important that we certainly don’t play anything out here. I think the exposure and the scrutiny and everything, you’ve got to be careful and be sensible and think of him as much as anything, so the situation will work itself out, whatever way it’s going to work itself out. Making sure he’s okay is the important thing.” Share

2h ago 11.43 EDT There’s been a Ukrainian response to Russia’s admission to the U-15 World Cup. Matvii Bidnyi, Ukraine’s minister of youth and sports said it “legitimised a terrorist state”. Bidnyi said, per the Press Association: “The international sports community must maintain unity and principled consistency, ruling out any concessions to the aggressor state. “The Fifa football festival in Azerbaijan featuring the Russian under-15 national team with official national symbols – is nothing less than the legitimisation of a terrorist state, even if framed as an unofficial festival format. It is a direct attempt to provide Russians with a platform to display state symbols and spread Russian propaganda. “While Russian youth are admitted to international football festivals, the aggressor state continues to commit crimes against Ukrainian children. According to Bring Kids Back UA, more than 20,000 cases of deportation and forced displacement of Ukrainian children by Russia have been verified, which underpins the ongoing International Criminal Court arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin. What ‘equal opportunities’ can we talk about when Russia has deprived our children of a normal childhood? “We express our gratitude to Iceland and Germany for refusing to participate in this festival. We call on other national associations to join this decision and make a clear stand. FIFA’s 2022 decision to suspend Russia from international competitions must remain inviolable across all levels – without any loopholes for unofficial tournaments.” Share

The letter says Fifa should have cash reserves of $6 billion after the World Cup and can afford such a “one-off release” — which would total $2.1 billion to the 211 federations — Uefa’s president Aleksander Ceferin and Concacaf’s leader Victor Montagliani tell Infantino in a letter seen by AP. 4h ago 09.34 EDT Oxford United apologise for 'United 93' clothing Oxford United have abandoned a new range of American style-sportswear after it inadvertently referenced the tragedy of September 11. The League One club launched its new ‘Campus Collection’ on Friday morning and had removed it from sale by lunchtime, after clothing designs were revealed to bear the slogan ‘United 93’. The U’s immediately published an apology that admitted to a lack of understanding of “the historical context and associations” related to the branding and made “sincere apologies for this error and any offence caused.” “Inspired by the style and culture of American sports”, the Campus Collection was originally trailed for launch by the club on 11 September of this year, the 25th anniversary of the atrocity that killed nearly 3,000 people. Concerns over sensitivity saw the launch then delayed, but when the online collection was finally made available for sale on Friday, images showed models wearing an NFL-style shirt with ‘United 93’ on the chest, in recognition of Oxford being founded in 1893. United 93 was one of four domestic passenger jets seized by al-Qaida terrorists on 11 September 2001. A mutiny by passengers prevented hijackers from using the plane to destroy a government building in Washington DC, and it ultimately crashed into a field, killing all 44 people on board. A film titled ‘United 93’ was also made about the tragedy. Read more from Paul MacInnes below. Oxford United apologise for launching ‘United 93’ clothing range around 9/11 anniversary Read more Share Updated at 10.48 EDT

4h ago 09.24 EDT We’ve had loads of emails today about the England squad and Thomas Tuchel’s position and future in charge of the national team. Rick Parfett is the latest to weigh in on fan feeling towards the German after the World Cup semi-final exit: double quotation mark The atmosphere of blame and anger around Tuchel feels reflective of wider societal dynamics – a conversation lacking in nuance, an inability to appreciate positive aspects, and a reflexive default to anger and frustration. The causes are complex, among others: stagnating living standards, social media financially rewarding outrage, and newspapers constantly needing a story. But it doesn’t feel reflective of reality and it’s deeply tiresome to see it take over our national psyche. Tuchel brought clarity to his selections – no more crowbarring three number 10s into the team alongside Kane – and some really joyful moments. One mistake shouldn’t be allowed to erase that, in my opinion. I think that’s a very measured email, Rick, with some good points. In my view, however, Tuchel should be not be completely absolved of blame for his in-game management of the Argentina game, especially late on. Share

6h ago 07.49 EDT Russia to return to Fifa competition in boys' Under-15 World Cup Russia are poised to compete in a Fifa event for the first time since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The country was listed on Friday among the entrants for the boys’ Under-15 World Cup and Festival which is being hosted in Azerbaijan next month. Russian national teams and club sides were banned from Fifa and Uefa competitions in the wake of the invasion. Though Fifa lifted the ban on Russia’s under-17s in 2023, this under-15 tournament marks the first time they will have actually played. Russia have been drawn in a group alongside Turkey, as well as Afghanistan, Djibouti, Sierra Leone and Sudan. The FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival is a new festival-style competitions for boys (2026), girls (2027) and both (2028 onwards) be open to all 211 Fifa Member Associations, regardless of size or footballing tradition. To align with the development needs of U-15 players, the matches are shorter in duration, played on smaller pitches, with teams comprising – for the 2026 edition at least – eight players. The Fifa council agreed last December that the under-15 event would be open to teams from all of its 211 member associations. In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) dropped its recommendation for global sports federations like Fifa to ban Russia. In February, the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, told Sky News the Russia ban had “not achieved anything” and had just created “more frustration and hatred”. Ukraine’s sports minister Matvii Bidnyi described Infantino’s remarks as “irresponsible” and “infantile”. He said: “They detach football from the reality in which children are being killed.” Press Association Share

6h ago 07.39 EDT Spurs are bad. I know that, you know that. But why? They are getting into attacking areas but are failing to make or take chances. Our data visual journalist Andrew Beasley breaks it down. double quotation mark Several metrics illustrate their attacking problems. 6h ago 07.26 EDT Gianni Infantino must leave the Fifa presidency “no ifs or buts”, according to Hans-Joachim Watzke, one of the vice-presidents of the German Football Association (DFB), as he spoke at a festival dedicated to artificial intelligence in Berlin on Thursday. The DFB was one of the few federations not to sign a letter of support for Infantino’s re-election as Fifa president in six months’ time. “He has to go, no ifs or buts,” said Watzke, who said that three points in particular counted against the Swiss. The first was the Fifa Peace Prize, launched by Infantino and awarded in December 2025 to the US president, Donald Trump, to whom Infantino is close, during the draw for the 2026 World Cup. Infantino “created this prize himself, and he decided on it himself,” said Watzke. “You can’t just invent something on your own and then announce it, it’s madness,” said Watzke. Watzke also condemned the controversial handling of the Folarin Balogun red card during this year’s World Cup which was hosted in the US, Canada and Mexico. The American forward was sent off in the last 32 but his automatic one-match suspension was lifted after a phone call from Trump to Infantino. “It can’t be that when someone gets sent off, the head of state calls the Fifa president, and, remarkably, the whole thing is immediately overturned. That’s madness,” said Watzke. The third issue was the project, unveiled on 28 July and dropped four days later, to create a commercial company that would have been open to private investors and became a focal point of the rebellion against Infantino. “It’s completely insane,” said Watzke. “Nobody knew about it, his vice-presidents in Fifa knew nothing, the [Fifa] council knew nothing.” The DFB president Bernd Neuendorf said earlier in the week that it was also time for Infantino to depart. “The relationship of trust with Gianni Infantino, under this FIFA leadership, has of course been completely shattered,” he said in an interview with RTL/ntv television. “It’s important that this Infantino system comes to an end.” For now, Infantino is the only candidate for the FIFA presidency in the election scheduled for 18 March 2027, with candidacies open until 18 November. FA chair Hewitt demands Infantino release records of failed World Cup plan Read more Share

6h ago 07.22 EDT This time tomorrow we will be 8 minutes away from kick-off at The Den where West Ham and Millwall will renew their rivalry. The Metropolitan police have been granted special powers to tackle violence as the south and east London teams meet again for the first time in 14 years. double quotation mark There is nothing to glorify here. This will be the 100th competitive meeting, if discontinued, minor tournaments are included, and anyone failing to see the logic behind the rivalry can be forgiven. The sides are not on each other’s doorstep and Millwall are south of the Thames, meaning Crystal Palace and Charlton are more obvious enemies. Yet it is not really about football. The tribalism runs deep, dating back to when the clubs were formed by rival shipbuilding firms at docks on the Isle of Dogs in east London, and is more down to hooligan elements than anything that happens on the pitch. There have been many occasions when the nastiness has spiralled out of control. Hooliganism was rife in English football during the 1970s and 1980s and Millwall and West Ham had fearsome firms. Trouble erupted when the sides met at the Den for a testimonial for the Millwall defender Harry Cripps in 1972. The toxicity grew and a Millwall fan, Ian Pratt, died after a clash with West Ham fans at New Cross station in 1976. It is worth keeping in mind when people try to hype up this fixture. Stories about who was top dog on the terraces back in the day are not that interesting. Read more from Jacob Steinberg below. Fear and loathing linger as Millwall and West Ham resume ferocious rivalry Read more View image in fullscreen Police remove fans who began fighting during the West Ham and Millwall game at Upton Park in 1978. Sports.title: Tuchel should listen to ‘the 0.1%’ and learn from England’s World Cup mistakes | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel should be listening to the 0.1%. As he unveiled his first England squad since the World Cup, he said 99.9% of supporters he bumped into did not talk about his substitutions during the Argentina game. According to him, the conversation is far more positive. Memories are shared of the knockout wins over Mexico and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It seems those who want to take the England head coach to task over the retreat in the semi-final in Atlanta are in the minority.

This is, of course, hard to quantify. Is it really 99.9%? We can take Tuchel at face value, but relying on anecdotal evidence goes two ways. A lot of fans are not ready to move on yet. The national mood is far more downbeat than Tuchel imagines and he is kidding himself if he thinks people have forgiven the way England folded after going 1-0 up against Argentina early in the second half.

Tuchel wants to look forward as he prepares for the start of the Nations League. He was stung by the criticism after the defeat by Argentina. He was proud of England beating France to claim the bronze medal three days later. The head coach faced the media at Wembley on Friday and joked about his bosses at the Football Association telling him off for his defensive changes against Argentina. Switching to serious mode, he insisted the narrative should be directed by the 6-4 win over France.

The problem with focusing on the future is that Tuchel’s squad for Spain, Czechia and Croatia has to be viewed in the context of everything that happened at the World Cup. Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney have been dropped from the 26 selected in the summer. However, Tuchel suggested his initial intention was to maintain continuity from the World Cup. Injuries led to a shift, depriving England of Dean Henderson, Dan Burn, John Stones, Reece James, Djed Spence and Jordan Henderson, leaving room for players whose presence lends a sense of renewal to the process.

Hauling Trent Alexander-Arnold out of cold storage is an intriguing if slightly perplexing move. Why now? Does Tuchel actually trust the Real Madrid defender? Would Alexander-Arnold, who had not been selected since June 2025, be here if Spence, James or even Ben White were fit? The former Liverpool right-back has been in fitful form for José Mourinho’s Madrid and has never established himself with England. For Alexander-Arnold the challenge is to make sure he remains in the picture in November. Tuchel, who does not intend to use the 27-year-old as a midfielder, told the newcomers that earning a call-up had to be followed by performing in an England shirt.

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s Trent Alexander-Arnold can prove his worth to England while alternative right-back options are injured. Photograph: Cesar Cebolla/PressInPhoto/Shutterstock

The message from Tuchel was that he has had no sleepless nights over his World Cup squad. He wants to bottle the brotherhood, the team spirit. Fine, but there are technical and tactical flaws to address. There was an interesting pause from Tuchel when a reporter linked the selections of Alexander-Arnold, Alex Scott and Cole Palmer to whether England had enough forward passers at the World Cup. The memory of Tuchel’s comment after the Argentina game about ball possession not being part of England’s DNA lingers.

After his appointment Tuchel talked about England needing to tap into the pace and power of the Premier League. At the World Cup, though, the only time they really went full throttle was during the second half of the win over Croatia in their opening game. Otherwise they were overly reliant on stout defending and moments of inspiration from Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham.

Quick Guide England's squad Show Goalkeepers: Jordan Pickford, James Trafford, Jason Steele. Defenders: Trent Alexander-Arnold, Jarrod Branthwaite, Trevoh Chalobah, Marc Guéhi, Lewis Hall, Ezri Konsa, Tino Livramento, Nico O’Reilly, Jarell Quansah. Midfielders: Elliot Anderson, Jude Bellingham, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Kobbie Mainoo, Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Alex Scott. Forwards: Dominic Calvert-Lewin, Eberechi Eze, Anthony Gordon, Harry Kane, Rio Ngumoha, Marcus Rashford, Morgan Rogers, Bukayo Saka. Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The frustration is England tumbled into a place where they had neither Spanish-style possession nor Premier League chaos. Tuchel would like his players to show more balance, to rest with the ball at times, but says he is more inclined to “embrace the chaos” and replicate the fury of the Croatia second half.

Easier said than done, of course, when international football is so often dominated by the smartest passing teams. England, Tuchel said, were not the “most economical” side. The intensity of the Premier League takes a lot out of his players.

There is an argument, though, that Tuchel tied his hands with his midfield choices. With Declan Rice flagging against Argentina, England needed to introduce legs alongside Elliot Anderson. There were few alternatives. Jordan Henderson had a broken wrist and is 36. Tuchel selected Kobbie Mainoo, who is nimble in tight areas, but then did not use the Manchester United midfielder.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It was an oversight from the head coach, who admits he has a duty to look at Mainoo properly this time. There were ways for England to ensure they did not end up in a grim 5-4-1 against Argentina. Myles Lewis-Skelly was playing well in Arsenal’s midfield at the end of last season. Scott was shining for Bournemouth. Lewis-Skelly and Scott have been selected this time. Tuchel remains cold on Adam Wharton.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Tuchel did not use Kobbie Mainoo (right) at the World Cup but the midfielder has retained his place in the England squad. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

There will always be contentious choices. Morgan Gibbs-White and Josh King are unlucky to be left out. Liam Delap could have been chosen over Dominic Calvert-Lewin as Kane’s deputy. But this is a good squad, with quality in all areas and an injection of youth to add excitement.

Rio Ngumoha, Liverpool’s teenage winger, is part of the new wave. Jarrad Branthwaite looks like the new Burn after edging out Levi Colwill in central defence. Lewis Hall can advance his cause at left-back and leaving Madueke out for Palmer suggests Tuchel is willing to be more versatile in attack after picking like-for-like players in every position at the World Cup.

Palmer may not run in straight, sharp lines down the flanks but Chelsea’s No 10 is a better footballer than Madueke. England have technicians. Fans do not want to see more fear. They want Tuchel to find a way to coach this group. England start their Nations League campaign with a home game against Spain next Saturday and more than 0.1% of supporters will be waiting to see whether Tuchel has learned from his mistakes.

Sports.title: We wanted to let Max Dowman bloom in the shadows but he has become hard to ignore | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
The poet Jorge Luis Borges wrote a famous short story about a society that had become so good at making maps, so obsessed with capturing every detail, that its rulers decided the only way to do the job right was to make a lifesize map of its entire empire, which could then be laid out across the actual land from coast to coast. Imagine a map of Britain the exact same size as Britain, showing every branch of Greggs, every nail bar, every vape shop in perfect detail. Only then can we really see what Britain looks like, by standing on a fake Britain laid over the top of actual Britain.

Borges was writing in the 1940s, at a time when people were fascinated by the mechanised future, with its new forms of measuring out the world: the wireless, the 30mph motorcar, the rise of Big Tape Measure. And to be fair, the mega-map is a pretty accurate vision of our own fully networked present, a place where you can snoop around a village in Mozambique from your laptop in Egham, where no one ever stops committing acts of minute self-surveillance, even if they think they’re just searching “what is beetroot?” on the internet.

Borges also hated football. “Soccer is popular because stupidity is popular,” he wrote, which probably seemed a bold statement at the time. But then Borges also didn’t live to see an episode of Wow Sports Premier League Breakfast at Breakfast with Roger McRoger and a puzzled Lee Trundle. After which, perhaps less of a surprise. But the process he describes is also a good description of what football is doing to itself. Endless data, endless analysis, no spaces or free air, matches that are just schematised movement. At times it can feel like football is out there laying a lifesize real-time map on top of itself.

In Borges’s story, the land soon begins to decay beneath the massive map – which is reassessed by later generations as insane, pointless and stupid – and left to rot in the desert. We haven’t reached this point. Nobody is de-mapping football. But it does perhaps explain why everyone gets so excited when a talent emerges that seems to be playful and human, to exist outside the grid. And also why it has felt wrong to gush too soon about Max Dowman, to fear placing the hex on him. We know how this works. Here is a fluffy new thing. Let us break him. Let us heap pressure on his shoulders. Don’t talk about Max Dowman. Let Max Dowman exist, breathe, bloom in the shadows.

So, Max Dowman then. It has become quite hard to ignore him. He was brilliant against Ipswich in midweek, and brilliant in a way that seems solid and real and comfortable with itself. Most obviously there were the two goals, both a perfect snapshot of why Dowman seems equipped to survive, more state-of-the-art than some other young players we’ve burdened with expectation.

The second goal is particularly good, five perfect little actions packed into six seconds of football. Arsenal have the ball on the edge of the Ipswich box. Dowman shows for a pass, sees it’s going elsewhere, changes his mind, and makes a three-yard sprint to create space. Finally he has the physical capacity to control a bouncing ball in that sliver of space, to move his feet so much quicker than the nearest defender it looks like a glitch in the machine, and to finish in a way that involves sifting the options and timing the shot, all without breaking stride.

View image in fullscreen Max Dowman leaves Cédric Kipré floundering to score his brilliant second, and Arsenal’s third, goal at Ipswich. Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

The first goal is on his other side, and involves a more classical piece of one-on-one deception. This is the same defender: Cédric Kipré, 29 years old, came through Paris Saint-Germain’s youth system. Dowman walks through him with a micro-feint and a switch of feet, then reels off another hilariously understated finish, doing it all while a second defender is still gathering himself to lunge, like a man operating in a different time signature to everyone around him.

This is the key point of difference, the ability to make everything stop, the fly-vision that means he sees what’s about to happen while everyone else is whirling about trying to read the charts, in the same way Lionel Messi (yes, sorry, sorry) always seems to have time to pass the ball into the net, like this is all a kickabout in a pair of sliders.

Our way of understanding young creative players has often seemed to lag behind where the game actually is, to be driven by nostalgia for what this thing used to look like. I remember the excitement over the 18-year-old Jack Rodwell’s physicality at the exact moment physicality was no longer going to be a thing, like proudly unveiling the latest horse-drawn train just as the Ford Model T rolls off the production line.

Michael Owen was brilliant at 17, but he was mainly brilliant at running very fast in a straight line and smashing the ball into the net. Plus of course there was Wayne Rooney, who emerged a pale, unformed teenager composed entirely from energy drinks and white bread, out there making the game up on the fly, as though some urban foundling had come barrelling over the advert boards with a string of sausages still dangling from his mouth.

The narrative around Rooney is that he lost this vital native quality. But Rooney adapted and survived, and clearly understood what he had to be a lot better than those of us watching. And even now creative players have to exist against this. Cole Palmer is exciting because he does surprising things that seem to be striking a blow for freedom, beauty and older people who struggle to make their email work. But his real challenge is to retain just enough of this while fitting the world around him.

Dowman is a bit different. The things that make him stand out seem to speak very easily to how football is now. Being a modern creative footballer is not jinking runs, rasping drives or dribbling across a cabbage field in a pair of cowboy boots. It’s targeted energy, high-intensity semi-freedom. Lamine Yamal and Désiré Doué have the same fast-twitch foot and brain speed, the ability to operate in micro-moments, to see patterns just ahead of time. Dowman is 6ft tall and getting stronger. He won’t be kicked to pieces. He can repeat this without taking bites out of himself.

There is still the issue of his youth. But maybe this doesn’t matter so much either. The world has changed. In the age of Rooney and Owen there was no care, no data, no softness. This is where the structures of modern football are an advantage. Dowman will be GPS’d to the last decimal point. Endless physical scientists will have a say on his output and stress levels.

View image in fullscreen Wayne Rooney and Michael Owen broke through as teenagers in an age of less data and less care. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

The money is too big. The talent is too valuable. It also comes ready to plug and play. You don’t get to this level unless you can ingest systems and briefings. You’ve already been pressure-cooked and stress-tested. What you’re being asked to do in the orderly spaces of professional football is the same thing you were asked to do in the orderly spaces of academy football, just five levels up and with more people watching.

Borges was anti-football because he saw it as inauthentic, the players no longer sports people but “actors in jerseys before the TV cameras”. And this is also fine, further evidence that boomer-dad nostalgia is one of the key archetypes of human behaviour.

Life is also different now; not harder or easier, but more instant, a series of moments, the creation of rapid-fire energy. Dowman has grown up inside this. He can parcel his time out, disappear for a bit, maybe make a show of things in the spring.

And yes, this is another way of fitting him to a model, laying a lifesize map of future Max Dowman across the present. But I strongly suspect he will be fine, and that unlike so many other things out there he’s pretty well adapted to whatever the future is supposed to look like.

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappé leaves Nike after 20 years to sign boot deal with Swiss brand On
Sports.content:
Kylian Mbappé has ended a 20-year association with Nike to sign a boot deal with the Swiss challenger company On.

The sports and leisure brand, which has previously focused on running and tennis, is planning a major move into football next year and has also appointed Thierry Henry as its football director.

Roger Federer, who also left Nike to join them towards the end of his playing career, is a shareholder of the Zurich-based company. Mbappé will also become a shareholder in On.

“From the beginning, what drew me to On was the opportunity to build something entirely new together that will help shape tomorrow’s game,” said the France captain. “I want to bring my experience and perspective into what we create, push what’s possible through innovation, and always stay true to the joy of football. We have a shared dream, and this is only the beginning.”

On is a newcomer to football and this week unveiled its first boots, the Lightspray Prototype, which will be available for the mass market from next year before a move into training kit.

Mbappé’s departure, which came at the end of his contract after the World Cup, is a significant blow for Nike, which also lost the Barcelona and Spain star Lamine Yamal to Adidas two years ago. The 27-year-old has been the face of many of Nike’s advertising campaigns.

“Kylian’s journey with Nike began when he was nine years old,” the company said in a statement. “Over nearly two decades, we’ve shared moments that shaped the game and he has been an important part of Nike Football. We are proud of what we achieved together on and off the pitch.”

Nike and Adidas dominate the football market with their boots worn by more than 40% of players at this summer’s World Cup, according to data compiled by the retailer Fútbol Emotion, with Puma accounting for about 10%.
