World.title: Could trees developed with gene-editing technology protect Florida's citrus industry?
World.content:
Could trees developed with gene-editing technology protect Florida's citrus industry?

toggle caption Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Citrus growers in Florida are planting new trees that have been modified using gene-editing technology to ward against the lethal citrus greening disease.

Growers have tried everything from tents to sprays to protect citrus trees from the bacterial infection, which has killed off many of Florida's citrus trees and led to a massive decline in the amount of citrus the state produces. Now growers are waiting to see if the genetic modifications, which the Environmental Protection Agency approved earlier this year, will keep the trees alive.

Citrus greening arrived in Florida in 2005. The disease is spread by a tiny winged insect called an Asian citrus psyllid. It attacks the trees' immune system, so they can't fight the infection. Once infected, a tree produces bitter, discolored fruit and usually dies a few years later. There's no cure.

Sponsor Message

Ron English's family ran a citrus business in Valrico, Fla., for generations until greening wiped it out, forcing them to close in 2015.

"We had some of the best looking groves around, and all the time and effort that we had spent, you just see it diminish right before you," English said.

In the late 1990s, before citrus greening arrived in Florida, growers were shipping out around 300 million boxes of fruit each season, said Matt Joyner, CEO of Florida Citrus Mutual, a trade association that represents citrus growers. By comparison, they shipped a little more than 15 million boxes during this year's season, which ended in June, he said.

Soilcea, a Tampa-based company, used CRISPR gene-editing technology to design a rootstock that resists greening. Known as CarriCea T1, it keeps a tree's immune system working, allowing growers to rely less on insecticides.

Focusing on the rootstock to fight the bacteria is key, said Soilcea CEO Yianni Lagos. He explained that although the first sign that a tree is infected is yellowing leaves, "before you even have symptoms, half the root system is already dead."

Lagos is now waiting to see what happens when the rootstock is grafted onto trees and planted.

toggle caption Catherine Welch

In a SoilCea test field, the results so far are promising. Trees with the CarriCea T1 rootstock are taller and greener.

Sponsor Message

English cares for the dozens of trees in the test field that have the modified rootstock. They were planted last summer next to trees without it.

"That's the CarriCea rootstock — see how big the leaves have filled out," English said, pointing to a tree with the modification.

The smaller tree next to it does not have the CarriCea T1 rootstock. It's smaller with yellower leaves.

"See the discoloration, that's the disease already working through the tree," he said.

The real test for the CarriCea T1 tree will be the fruit, which takes years to show up — not only how it grows, but also how it tastes.

"The data suggests it's gonna work, but until you have a 10-year-old tree, you don't know how the tree is going to perform," Lagos said.

World.title: Parents of NHL prospect hospitalized after collapse at team workout say he's a 'fighter'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The parents of an Ontario NHL prospect who is in critical condition after collapsing during a team workout say their son is "a fighter" and that they are not giving up on him.

Twenty-one-year-old Matthew Mayich, of Hamilton, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University (ASU) hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed.

"We know Matthew's a fighter and we're hoping he pulls through this," said Matthew's father, John. He and Matthew's mother, Christina, spoke to CBC News from Phoenix, Ariz.

Before the workout, Matthew was "perfectly healthy," according to Christina.

Now, their lawyer says, he’s "clinging to his life in a hospital bed."

Matthew Mayich is pictured in a St. Louis Blues jersey in a photo the team shared on Aug. 26. (St. Louis Blues)

The incident has made waves in the sports world, prompting the Professional Hockey Players’ Association to speak up about the lack of protections for young athletes.

"When athletes feel pressure to remain silent about an injury, illness, exhaustion or concern because they fear the consequences of speaking up, the system has failed them," said PHPA executive director Brian Ramsay in a statement on Sept. 10, which does not directly name Mayich.

"Athletes should never have to choose between their health and their careers. Period."

WATCH | Family wants answers: Family demands answers after hockey player collapses from 'military style' workout | Duration closed caption 2:26 The parents of Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old NHL prospect from Stoney Creek, Ont., speak to CBC News after their son collapsed after 'military style' training at Arizona State University. Mayich is in critical condition and unlikely to recover, says his lawyer.

He loved hockey but ‘he was a lot more than hockey’

Mayich started playing hockey around age five, according to John, and excelled.

He played minor hockey with the Hamilton Huskies between 2016 and 2020, and then with the Ottawa 67's. In 2023, he was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues. His parents say they were his biggest fans, along with his younger brother and older sister, travelling everywhere to support him.

"He didn't care if he was at a small rink in Hamilton or a big rink in St. Louis with a lot of people — he just loves the game," John said.

"And he wasn't just about hockey. He was a lot more than just hockey."

Mayich’s parents describe him as "a little fireball," someone who people gravitate toward.

"Ever since he was young … he just lights up the room," said John.

Hockey player got heatstroke, lawyer says

When Mayich joined the ASU hockey team, it was the next rung on the ladder while chasing his NHL team.

The recent transfer to ASU was just getting settled into a new apartment, with his family looking forward to watching him play at the university.

A drone shot of Arizona State University campus in Tempe, Ariz., on Sept. 17. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

His parents say they spoke with him briefly before the last workout, adding that he was excited and "ready to work."

Christina said one of Mayich’s teammates called her to tell her what happened, and that the family rushed to Phoenix to be by his side. They haven’t left.

"We were devastated," she said. "Heartbroken. Shocked. [It’s] just so hard to believe."

Mayich suffered heatstroke during the workout, according to the family’s Phoenix-based lawyer, Leonard Aragon, who is less optimistic than the parents that the young athlete will survive.

"I'm a lawyer, not a doctor, but I don't believe so," he told CBC News.

Workout designed to 'break the kids,' lawyer alleges

There were roughly 25 other players at the workout, according to John Mayich.

The morning session, which took place in advance of October's season opener, involved push-ups, running and drills where medicine balls were carried from one side of the field to the other, said Aragon.

The lawyer describes the session as "military-style," taking place in "overwhelming" heat and that water was withheld from players.

"[It] was designed to basically break the kids and try to put some sort of toughness or something like that into the kids at the beginning of the year," Aragon said.

He also says safety guidelines at the university were not followed.

"Protocols that ASU itself says should have been followed, such as monitoring people to see if they have heat problems or having a cool-down tub if someone has heatstroke or heat exhaustion — things like that didn't take place," he said. "And it led to this tragedy."

The university declined an interview request, citing an ongoing review.

It did not respond to questions about whether the individual who ran the workout was vetted and contracted by the university and whether there have been any consequences for the leadership team since the incident.

Instead, an ASU spokesperson referred CBC News to a statement issued on Sept. 3, stating the athletics program has "heat-illness guidelines in place" and that the morning workout included a "third party who had previously worked" with the team.

The statement said university police are investigating, "as they would anytime they are called to a serious incident."

Leonard Aragon is a lawyer representing the Mayich family. (Andrew Hernandez/CBC)

Aragon calls the university’s failure to immediately call for an independent third-party investigation "a slap in the face to the family."

John Mayich's thoughts are also with the young athletes who witnessed what happened to his son.

"It was tragic what happened," he said. "I feel for them also. It's not easy to see that."

Is enough being done to protect athletes?

Athletes are highly competitive, seeking limited spots on sports teams, which is why protections for athletes are critical, says Adam Huxley, a hockey development coach based in Wainwright, Alta.

"When there's 30 players and 20 spots, I can see where the mindset of, 'Well, if I'm not feeling great or something's not going right, I don't want to be the one that says something, because then I seem like I'm the weak link,'" Huxley told CBC News.

He says there should be better education for players so they know when they are being pushed beyond their limits. Huxley also says it should be balanced with teams being able to tell their players it's OK to speak up.

Adam Huxley is a hockey development coach and owner of Huxley Hockey Conditioning. (Samuel Martin/CBC)

"If you're in trouble, say something. If you feel like something's not going right or whatever — and that goes for the player that is involved in it, that goes [for] the teammates that are around [them], OK? And that goes for the staff," Huxley said. "Everyone's gonna learn from this."

In the statement issued by the PHPA, Ramsay said there is an obligation to keep pushing for a culture where speaking up about health and wellness is a strength not a weakness.

"That young man, on the cusp of his career in professional hockey, was failed by the system, the system that should have protected him," Ramsay said in the statement.

The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), which oversees student athletes in the United States, said a stated goal is to "ensure well-being … for college athletes."

An NCAA spokesperson declined to comment on the incident.

The NHL also did not respond to inquiries from CBC News.

Family waiting for a miracle

For now, Mayich's parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles are taking shifts at his bedside.

"Most of the kids usually come around him and they'll sing to him. There's Scripture-reading and prayers constantly. And we tell him funny stories, 'cause he was a funny guy, he was a jokester," Christina Mayich said.

"There's definitely a positive vibe in his room. There's something there that we just cannot explain. So much love, so much peace."

She says the family is taking it one day at a time.

"We're just continuing and asking the Lord to give us our miracle."

World.title: 'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith and her government expect next month's separation referendum to be the last word on the subject — but those fighting for an independent Alberta say no matter the outcome, the fight goes on.

"We're never giving up," Jeff Rath, the lawyer for a group that helped organize an independence petition, said Wednesday in an interview.

"The logic of independence is such that we're not going home when this is all over.

"Do you think we're just going to stop advocating for a free and independent Alberta?"

Cory Morgan, an organizer with the Pathway to Independence group campaigning for separation, agreed: "That's a very significant movement on something that's looking for some very serious change."

Morgan said the grievances motivating advocates are still going to be there after the referendum.

"The issue doesn't go away, but it'll change its approach," he said.

Even on the pro-Canada side, there is doubt the issue will be put to rest after voting day.

Thomas Lukaszuk, who is steering the Forever Canadian campaign vying to keep Alberta a part of Confederation, said he doesn't put it past Smith to call a second, binding referendum even if a clear majority rejects separation.

"We're making sure that we have the contingency plans put in place to carry on [campaigning] if we have to. I hope we don't. I hope we put this behind us," Lukaszuk said earlier this week.

Voters head to the polls next month to answer 10 referendum questions. Nine of them focus on giving Alberta more elbow room on immigration and constitutional issues.

The final one asks if Alberta should stay in Canada or whether it's time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The issue has roiled the province. Polls suggest a majority of Albertans want to stay in the country.

Smith has promised to vote to stay in Canada.

She has said she called the vote because of competing citizen-led petitions over whether to remain in Canada or leave.

Critics, including the NDP, say Smith has no mandate to roll the dice on Canada's future and that she is only doing so to mollify separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said a vote for separation is technically not a vote for separation, but a vote to hold another vote.

That means, he said, that regardless of the outcome, Alberta's intolerably subservient status in Canada continues. Central Canada has the majority of the population, he said, and therefore will continue to call the shots in Parliament.

"This vote won't resolve what's broken in Canada and won't fix how Albertans are treated poorly by Ottawa, so demands for fairness will continue," Wilson said.

'Ready to move forward'

Smith has said she expects the Oct. 19 vote to settle the matter.

As recently as this week, her office reiterated that in a statement following a surprising byelection loss by Smith's candidate to the Opposition NDP in what is normally a safe Calgary seat for her UCP.

"In five weeks, the referendum vote will be over, and we're confident Albertans will be ready to move forward and fight for a stronger Alberta within a united Canada," spokesperson Sam Blackett said in an emailed statement.

WATCH | Referendum debate heats up ahead of Alberta vote: Alberta referendum campaigns heat up | Duration closed caption 1:57 With a referendum on Alberta’s future in Canada only a couple of months away, groups on both sides held weekend rallies, while Premier Danielle Smith highlighted the need for Albertans to be united.

Commentators on both sides of the political spectrum say disillusionment and dismay over Smith calling the referendum played a role in Calgary-Shaw voters punishing her party at the ballot box.

Smith's office disagrees, blaming right-centre vote splitting for the NDP win.

The loss could signal larger challenges down the road for the UCP given Calgary is viewed as critical to victory in the looming October 2027 general election.

Morgan said it's not just voters, but also UCP members that Smith needs to watch out for. He said Smith's embrace of citizen initiative petitions has activated a group of activists who hold significant sway over Smith's party.

"She's going to have to give them something to sink their teeth into or they're going to come after her," he said.

World.title: As Carney's popularity soars, Conservatives weigh what to do about their own leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A number of Conservative MPs have soured on Pierre Poilievre as leader, but despite this growing angst, his position is relatively secure because there is no strong appetite to oust him and choose someone new right now, according to party and caucus sources who spoke to CBC News.

Last year, Poilievre was on the cusp of leading his party to the largest Conservative government in a generation only to fall short when the Liberals replaced an unpopular incumbent with a leader offering a new vision.

He has struggled to recover ever since, facing accusations from some critics that he's yesterday's man, and poorly placed to deal with the issue of our time: an increasingly hostile U.S. government determined to wreck Canada economically.

Poilievre earned plaudits for a series of pro-Canada interviews on U.S. television last week, but he hasn't said if he supports the government's retaliatory tariffs on American products. He says he wants to wait for an "analysis" of the expected economic costs before taking a position.

WATCH | Poilievre on the Conservatives' role as Opposition: Criticizing government's 'costly decisions' is a 'great act of patriotism': Poilievre | Duration closed caption 0:54 Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre addressed his caucus on Wednesday saying the role of the Opposition is 'holding the government accountable here at home' and that 'a country is always more than its government.'

His lines about this fight have largely focused on trying to cajole the government to bring Parliament back sooner than planned and reveal a failed trade deal that negotiators say is protected by confidentiality clauses.

Sources speaking to CBC News on the sidelines of the party's caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., describe caucus morale as low because the U.S. dispute dominates the news cycle, putting their leader and the team at a disadvantage.

One MP said Canadians simply "don't want to hear from us right now," and their relevance is in question.

Poilievre has made a career out of fiercely opposing Liberal policies he says have ruined this country. That sort of rhetoric doesn't sell as well as it used to given the current patriotic climate, this MP said.

CBC News has agreed not to name the sources so they can speak freely about internal dynamics.

But at least one MP, Jamil Jivani, who has said Canadians have thrown "an anti-America hissy fit" and that the government is overreacting to the trade war, publicly suggested he wants his leader to take a harder line.

During Poilievre's U.S. media tour, which was largely deferential to Carney, Jivani, a close friend of Vice-President JD Vance, said: "You have people who should be offering an alternative to the Liberals instead going out there to appease people in positions of power."

In this context, the party's poll numbers have fallen further. The recent performance in federal byelections — losing one seat and considerable support in two others — has only increased the sense of doom among some Conservatives.

"I think you have to be quite honest, this is not the position that we want to be in at this juncture — there’s no question about that," Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman told reporters after meeting with her caucus mates in the B.C. interior.

WATCH | Lantsman on the Conservatives' position: Conservatives not in 'position we want to be in,' says deputy leader | Duration closed caption 0:47 Conservative Party deputy leader Melissa Lantsman says her caucus is united on the issue of fighting for Canadians, and that the party's retreat in Penticton, B.C., will allow MPs to come together.

Lantsman said that given the underperformance, the party will make some "changes" to the Conservative playbook this fall.

What's unlikely to change is the leader. While some MPs say behind closed doors that they are decidedly done with Poilievre, most don't want to take the next step and trigger a Reform Act ousting, like the one parliamentarians used to remove the last leader, Erin O'Toole, sources said.

Such a move could split the party, as some of the more stridently populist members might revolt against what could be perceived as an elite-driven coup, said one MP.

Conservative MP Michael Barrett said the party base strongly supported Poilievre at his leadership review in January — Poilievre won a commanding 88 per cent of the vote — so the caucus will stick with him.

When asked if Poilievre is the best person to lead the party right now, Barrett deferred to the grassroots.

"The Conservative membership made a very strong decision this year for Mr. Poilievre to lead our party. And that's the direction that we've taken," he said in an interview.

Conservative MPs listen as Poilievre speaks at the party's caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C., on Wednesday. (Stephane Richer/CBC)

Two senior Conservatives said replacing Poilievre now would just needlessly burn through another leader given the perception that the Liberals would likely win if there's another election sometime soon.

These Conservatives posited that it's better to let Poilievre lead the party into another election, potentially lose and then resign to trigger a new leadership process. That would be less divisive than trying to remove a leader who has a strong and vocal online following, especially one who sailed through a recent leadership review, these sources said.

Another ex-campaign staffer close to Poilievre said even if a Reform Act ouster prompted the leadership selection process, Poilievre could always run again and win — given few people have expressed serious interest in the job.

While he came up short, Poilievre did lead his party to a respectable showing in the last campaign, taking 41 per cent of the vote and 144 seats, a figure that has since been whittled down by floor-crossings and defections.

Poilievre could reassure skeptical members that while things aren't looking good now, they can change on a dime in politics, this ex-campaign staffer said.

Plus, given the divisions in caucus over how to handle the U.S., as well as other longstanding divides on social issues, Poilievre is best placed to hold this disparate group together, the staffer said.

WATCH | Where do Conservatives go from here? Conservatives try to chart a way forward as Carney's popularity soars | Duration closed caption 2:03 Conservatives are discussing party priorities ahead of Parliament's return from summer break. The caucus retreat comes as widespread support for Prime Minister Mark Carney's trade strategy has left Conservatives grasping for political footing.

Chad Rogers, a longtime Conservative and a partner at the public affairs firm Crestview Strategy, said all is not lost for Poilievre.

Rogers said he is old enough to remember when some pundits claimed former prime minister Paul Martin would win a "super majority" in 2004, leaving the unpopular Stephen Harper on the Opposition benches for years.

That never panned out — Martin limped to a minority, and Harper eventually won and governed for nearly a decade.

Carney's aura could also wear off as it did for that Liberal leader some 20 years ago, Rogers said. Poilievre is struggling to punch through now, but that might not always be the case, he said.

He said Poilievre's plan to go all-in on affordability concerns during this fall sitting of Parliament could bear fruit, given that voters consistently tell pollsters it's a major issue for them.

"I don't know that I would want to be an incumbent premier or prime minister anywhere in Canada with the inflation numbers, the debt numbers. There are a number of bills soon coming due to pay," he said.

"I think as a Conservative, I have a medium-term optimism that Canadians are about to hire us back to clean up the economy."

MP Michelle Rempel Garner said Poilievre's understanding of what average Canadians are going through in an economy wracked by higher prices makes him a good leader for this moment.

"I'm proud to serve under his leadership this fall," she said.

World.title: New cat species identified for the 1st time in a century
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia's cloud forest has been identified as a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century.

The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is ‌part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America.

It was found in Bolivia's lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 46 centimetres (18 inches) long and weighs around three pounds, making it smaller than the average domestic cat.

Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species, ​and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name.

"Its fur is ​light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," said Paola Nogales Ascarrunz, a National Geographic explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology.

Little is yet known about the cat's biology and ​lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be ⁠more active at night, Nogales Ascarrunz said.

A close-up of a Leopardus tilcayo cat, the only known individual of the newly identified species living in protective captivity. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

Tiger ⁠cats are so-called cryptic species, meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, ‌said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart, of the University of Antwerp in Belgium.

Tiger cats previously had been considered a single species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species.

Only 2 live individuals found so far

Referring to the new species, Lescroart said, "Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records."

One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ⁠in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home.

Nogales Ascarrunz observes the cat at the Senda Verde animal refuge in Bolivia on Sept. 1. (Fernando Faciole/National Geographic via Reuters)

Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because "its characteristics did not match the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian cats," Nogales Ascarrunz said. "This made us wonder: What tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?"

The team analyzed DNA from 38 cats sampled across ‌several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in fact five genetically distinct species.

"We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal — subspecies or otherwise," Lescroart said.

Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.

"The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we ​estimate those lineages to have been physically separated," Lescroart said, adding that such a gap is generally considered a species-level divide in cats.

The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru's Yungas, naming it Leopardus ⁠tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca Empire that included the area it inhabits.

New species may be listed as endangered

The International Union for Conservation of Nature's red list, ⁠tracking the status of species, currently treats tiger cats as two "vulnerable" species with declining populations.

The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review ⁠will assess ⁠the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture ​of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own.

WATCH | See some of the new species discovered in 2025: See some of the new species discovered in 2025 | Duration 0:56 Scientists are discovering species more quickly than ever before. CBC Kids News contributor Manny Brennan shares some of the cool species discovered in 2025.

The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute ​in the Yungas, one of the region's most ⁠threatened ecosystems.

The mountain forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales Ascarrunz added.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study.

"There are many undiscovered species out there ⁠in the world, and they are at risk of ‌disappearing before we even discover them."

World.title: Gas prices are dropping. You can thank the 'winter blend' for that
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Drivers rejoice: gas prices in Canada are dropping, thanks to a yearly switch.

Gas prices ticked up earlier this week, reaching a national average of 194.5 cents per litre yesterday according to affordableenergy.ca , but dropped by about eight cents overnight to 186.9 cents per litre as of Friday.

The cost of gas usually goes up in the summer and comes down in the fall because of a mid-September switchover from summer-blend gasoline to a winter blend, says Dan McTeague, the president of Canadians for Affordable Energy.

The different mix of fuel is used to prevent fuel-line freezing and make engines run better in the cold.

McTeague forecasts the cost of gas could drop by another few cents over the weekend before settling.

"But that's probably as good as it's going to get unless someone … can wave a magic wand and get a lot more oil, diesel, jet fuel and gasoline into global markets," McTeague told CBC News Network.

WATCH | Gas prices drop 8 to 10 cents in some Canadian cities: Gas prices drop 8 to 10 cents in some Canadian cities | Duration closed caption 4:07 Prices for gasoline fell about eight cents per litre overnight, with some cities seeing the price for a litre fall 20 cents. It's a reversal of the overall trend of higher prices for fuel since the start of the U.S. war in Iran.

Fighting in the Middle East has all but shuttered the Strait of Hormuz and compromised the Bab al-Mandeb Strait , disrupting the flow of oil to the rest of the world. Fewer barrels flowing from the region has sent the price of oil way up: the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil soared past the $100-per-barrel U.S. benchmark last week and is now hovering around $104 US.

But diesel, on the other hand, is soaring. The average cost for a litre of diesel across Canada sat at $2.751 as of Thursday, according to Natural Resources Canada , though certain cities like Calgary hovered lower, at $2.513. Vancouver topped the three-dollar mark, with a litre of diesel costing drivers $3.055.

That's bad news even for those who don't drive, according to experts. Trucks that deliver consumer items to stores — including your groceries — as well as tractors that harvest food all tend to run on diesel.

It could mean consumers see higher sticker prices, because companies will have no choice but to pass on the higher cost of fuel to consumers, said Tej Dulat, director of government and public affairs with the Canada Truck Operators Association.

World.title: Deepfake doctors peddling bogus cures are becoming more convincing — and very little can be done to stop them
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, B.C. Provincial Health Officer Dr. Bonnie Henry became a familiar face across the country, appearing regularly at news conferences and in media clips.

Then her face and voice started popping up somewhere else: in AI-generated videos on social media, where her likeness was used to peddle supposed health products, including a prostate treatment.

"It really scared me initially, because it was so easy for people to make it look like I was saying things that were just not true," Henry recalled in a recent interview with CBC News.

Known as deepfakes, the online ads are "disturbing," she added, "because you know that people are taking things that are real and distorting them."

Henry is far from the only prominent Canadian physician whose likeness has been faked in questionable social media ads — and who has found little recourse.

Dr. François Marquis, chief of intensive care at Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital in Montreal, said he's heard from multiple patients and colleagues that videos featuring his likeness — all selling a range of pills or products — keep popping up on Facebook.

"This time I'm selling something that is supposed to fix your joints," he said, referring to the latest AI-generated ad. "And what is getting bolder is, now I'm offering $1 million if you're not a satisfied customer."

WATCH | Doctors describe 'disturbing' rise of deepfakes: Canadian doctors selling meds online? Those are AI deepfakes | Duration 1:43 Intensive care physician Dr. François Marquis discovered an AI deepfake scheme was using his face and voice to sell drugs online. Marquis is one of several Canadian physicians who've been the victims of similar AI deepfake campaigns.

Marquis and other physicians say these videos are scamming patients out of their money, putting Canadians' health at risk, and eroding public trust. Yet there's still no clear method to get deepfake videos taken down, multiple doctors agreed.

"A few years ago, when this started to happen to me, nobody had any policies, nobody knew what to do," said Henry, who eventually filed cease and desist letters to multiple parties in hopes of combating the wave of deepfakes using her voice and face.

But she says her complaints are still hitting roadblocks today.

"I think our organizations — whether it's police services, whether it's universities, whether it's employment organizations — they're not really prepared yet to support people who are going through this," she said.

WATCH | Quebec doctors issue warning over deepfake scams: Don’t fall for this deepfake scam using AI-generated images of doctors, Quebec physicians warn | Duration closed caption 2:54 Some well-known doctors in Quebec are warning people not to fall for a new scam circulating on social media. Videos have surfaced using AI-generated images of doctors selling health products.

Scams 'only going to get more convincing'

The term "deepfakes" refers to a digital likeness of a real person, including their facial movements and voice, created by AI.

The videos have exploded online in recent years, and the quality has dramatically improved, too, making fake videos of politicians, celebrities or physicians increasingly tough to spot.

One study found up to 50 per cent of people couldn't distinguish deepfakes from authentic videos about scientific subjects — and that was three years ago.

"It's only going to get more sophisticated," warned Timothy Caulfield, a researcher and professor focusing on health law and science policy at the University of Alberta.

"These kinds of scams — and that's really what they are — are only going to get more convincing."

While there's no major Canadian research yet on the prevalence of doctor deepfakes on platforms like Facebook and TikTok, a 2024 report in the British Medical Journal noted they're increasingly common in the U.K., while American policymakers are considering a bill — dubbed the "NO FAKES Act" — to combat the growing trend of AI deepfakes in the U.S.

Canadian physicians say more research and recourse is needed here as well, alongside public education to help patients avoid getting scammed.

WATCH | Nude-deepfake law came too late for Halifax woman: New AI deepfakes law 'too little, too late' for Halifax woman | Duration closed caption 2:12 Canada’s new law criminalizing the distribution of AI generated nude deepfakes comes ‘too little, too late’ for one Halifax woman, whose identity is protected under a publication ban. The man who admitted to altering a photo of her with artificial intelligence was acquitted before the law was changed.

Concern over fake drugs, dangerous health advice

Marquis recalled a victim of one deepfake scam who came looking for him in the ICU, wanting his money back for pills that were never delivered.

"It was very sad, because that person invested hundreds of dollars in those pills and never received anything," he said.

Marquis's bigger fear is patients ordering and consuming fake drugs, or following false advice to stop their medications.

Despite those risks, he routinely struggles to get deepfake videos taken down before new ones pop back up — even though he's flagged them to social media platforms, Quebec's medical college and the police.

"Basically I was told that there's nothing they can really do," he said.

WATCH | Carney deepfake ad cost this man $3,000: He lost $3,000 after falling for a fake Carney ad pushing for crypto | Duration closed caption 2:01 Lynn Phaneuf lost nearly $3,000 investing on a cryptocurrency site after watching a deepfake video that looked like a CBC News interview with Prime Minister Mark Carney pushing for crypto. Experts say these AI scams are becoming increasingly hard to spot.

Canada lacks 'co-ordinated response'

As part of an effort to clamp down on deepfakes and other AI-related security issues, the federal government has in recent years taken measures such as expanding the Canadian AI Safety Institute and introducing legislation to combat non-consensual sexualized deepfakes — dubbed the Protecting Victims Act — and AI-generated electoral misinformation.

Anyone who may have been a victim of cybercrime can file a police report or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, a federal bulletin from 2024 noted.

In a statement emailed to CBC News on Friday, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said safety is its priority.

The department pointed to its legislative plans, including Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act (PPCDA) that would give individuals the right to request that an organization dispose of their personal information — including to take down a deepfake of themselves from a commercial platform, such as social media.

It added that the new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada aims to address deepfakes as well as age assurance.

Dr. Fahad Razak, an internist at St. Michael's Hospital and Canada Research Chair in Healthcare Data and Analytics at the University of Toronto, said there still isn't a "co-ordinated" response to the problem across Canada.

"And what makes it very challenging is that a lot of the media we consume in Canada is not generated in Canada," he added. "We don't have enforcement mechanisms and the ability to save and filter out content from certain parts of the world."

WATCH | Carney deepfakes on social media: Fact check: Ads on Facebook link to Carney deepfakes | Duration 2:19 CBC’s Fact Check team has received dozens of emails flagging Facebook ads that link to deepfakes of Prime Minister Mark Carney. The fake videos are designed to scam you into sending money.

Videos selling products can be 'red flag'

For now, much of the onus to spot and avoid deepfake scams falls on the public.

"I think that any time content is being pushed to you and they're selling a product, that should be a major red flag," said Caulfield.

That's even more true for Canadian doctors supposedly selling health drugs or treatments, since provincial and territorial medical colleges enforce strict standards, noted the Canadian Medical Association (CMA) in an awareness post earlier this year.

"Although the precise rules vary, the intent is clear: doctors cannot publicly endorse health products in ads, on social media or in interviews," the CMA stated. Those products are defined by Canada's Food and Drugs Act as any regulated drugs, biologics, medical devices or natural health products.

Razak encouraged people to be highly skeptical of any videos featuring a doctor selling medical goods.

"If you think about your own physician experience, how often is a physician pulling out a drawer of material and trying to sell you something?" he said.

"That's not how our health-care system works."

World.title: Pickleball courts cause uproar in this normally quiet community in Port Stanley, Ont.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont. — all because of pickleball.

Kokomo Park is a quiet neighbourhood, with a condo building, a block of single-family homes, a playground and four public pickleball courts that are popular with some residents and their friends.

"We hang out together, we laugh together, we joke together," said Ashley Hennessey, who plays regularly at the courts. "The good thing about pickleball is it brings you out so that you're getting good healthy workout, good community and get to know people you didn't know before."

But for others, the courts are a source of constant noise.

After receiving a number of complaints, the Municipality of Central Elgin decided in July that the courts could only be used from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., a change from the previous policy of dawn to dusk.

The Kokomo Park pickleball courts sit in front of a condo building, where some residents are concerned about excessive noise. (Jack Sutton/CBC)

At a municipal council meeting on Monday, the players submitted a petition with 130 signatures, asking to change the hours to 8 a.m. to dusk, and for the municipality to conduct a noise study and include the players in future discussions.

At the same meeting, St. Catharines-based lawyer J. Patrick Maloney submitted a letter on behalf of Richard Robson, one of the condo owners, and Kokomo Affected Neighbours, a group of condo residents.

The letter threatens legal action if the pickleball courts aren't removed, claiming the use of the courts would exceed provincial noise guidelines and "contravene the general legal principles associated with the tort of nuisance."

"We understand that the pickleball users are pushing for expanded hours, which demonstrates they are not concerned with such nuisance impacts or our clients legal right to the quiet enjoyment of their property," Maloney wrote.

Maloney did not respond to a request for a statement. CBC News spoke with two of the Kokomo Affected Neighbours, but neither wished to comment.

The municipality received both communications at Monday's meeting, but no decision has been made regarding either the players' or the residents' requests.

Players at the Kokomo Park pickleball courts want to be able to play earlier in the morning because they're concerned about the heat and humidity, but the municipality shortened the hours to 9 a.m. to dusk. (Jack Sutton/CBC)

Hennessey, who started the players' petition, said he and the others want the courts to remain open earlier in the morning due to concerns over the heat and humidity, noting the "advanced age" of many of the people who use them.

"Playing in 30- to 35-degree weather is not healthy," he said. "So we come out, we play earlier in the day and to us that is a reasonable alternative."

The disagreement has led to tensions between neighbours, he said, describing multiple occasions on which condo residents have yelled at him and other players if they arrive at the courts too early or leave too late.

Hennessey said he and the other players are willing to work with the community to find a way to reduce the disruption, and he was surprised to read the lawyer's letter asking for the courts to be closed outright.

"That is absolutely not fair because what we want to hear is the joy ... the laughing, the joking, chirping each other back and forth," he said. "This is what life is about, it's supposed to be about getting along, being peaceful and having a good time."

Courts can get busy in evening, neighbour says

In 2025, Lloyd Mulroney moved into the home directly in front of the pickleball courts, fully aware they existed and were a part of the community, he said. Mulroney said he has even taken to sitting and watching from his porch some mornings, and he and his wife occasionally play.

But the courts can get busy, he said, particularly in the evenings, with upwards of 20 people playing and 15 to 20 cars in the small parking lot.

"There's a lot of cheering and activity that's happening. But if it closes down by 8 p.m., people are respectful, then that works for everybody, right?"

He said there are a lot of "camps" in the community, where the courts are concerned. Some want them gone, some don't care and some, like him, "kind of lay in the middle."

"I think it could have been dealt with a little bit better," he said. "A little bit more collaboration and a little bit more folks concerned for their neighbour."

World.title: Montreal mayor mulls legal action against Quebec after baby found at encampment
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada is threatening to take legal action against Quebec after a baby was found living with their mother in an encampment on Notre-Dame Street.

The baby, who is just over a year old, was found last Friday in a tent with their mother, according to the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM). Police officers recovered the child, who was then placed into the care of Quebec youth services (DPJ), while their mother was taken into the care of social services.

According to police, the baby's life, health and safety are not at risk, and they are currently in the care of a family member.

After saying on Thursday that the case is a sign that the province is not doing enough to address the homelessness crisis in Montreal, Martinez Ferrada doubled down on her criticism in an interview with Radio-Canada on Friday.

"I believe there are concrete actions the Quebec government can and must take," Martinez Ferrada said in French, adding that a lack of provincial funding is limiting her administration's ability to address homelessness in Montreal.

"If I have to go to court to secure that support, it is an option I am seriously considering right now," she said.

The people living in encampments along Notre-Dame Street are on land owned by Quebec, and Superior Court judges have on several occasions blocked the city's efforts to dismantle tents there.

Mathieu Morin, director of the community organization Carrefour Familial Hochelaga, says it is still extremely rare to find kids on the street, but a baby living in an encampment shows how severe the housing crisis has become.

"We are past saying this is a crisis," Morin told Radio-Canada.

Politicians respond

Quebec premier and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette said the case is heartbreaking, and that it must not happen again.

She said all levels of government need to work together to combat homelessness in Montreal and across the province, adding that she plans to meet with Martinez Ferrada in the coming days.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard echoed Fréchette's sentiment, saying that elected officials at all levels shoulder responsibility for the homelessness crisis. He also said that officials should focus more on addressing the root causes of the crisis.

Ruba Ghazal, meanwhile, expressed anger at the situation. The Qu é bec Solidaire co-spokesperson said she was shocked at the news, while arguing that more investment and political will is needed to solve homelessness in the province.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon also expressed outrage at the situation, saying that it was embarassing for Quebec. He argued for better social safety nets for vulnerable people in the province.

When asked about the situation, Éric Duhaime was more blunt. The Conservative Party of Quebec leader said he was sympathetic to people living in encampments, but he argued that encampments should be dismantled as soon as possible.

All five party leaders have agreed to participate in a forum on homelessness in 2027.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

Integrate

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issue to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Colombia’s social organizations and labor unions announce national strike in November
World.content:
Some 1,500 representatives of social organizations and labor unions agreed to begin organizing an anti-government national strike that should take place throughout Colombia either on November 11 or on November 20.

The organizations agreed to the mass mobilization during the National Gathering for the Defense of Life, Dignity, Democracy, Peace, Sovereignty, and Social Reforms that had been organized by labor unions in the capital Bogota.

The first and fundamental decision of the Meeting is to declare the most radical opposition to the illegitimate government of Abelardo de la Espriella because of the course it has imposed on the country—one of subordination to the interests of U.S. imperialism and alignment with the agenda of the international far right—which constitutes a direct threat to national sovereignty, democracy, and the rights won by the Colombian people, and an undeniable shift toward fascism. Social organizations and labor unions

In a statement, the organizations said that the national strike will be preceded by regional protests on October 10 and 14 that will seek to generate momentum for the national strike.

Indigenous organizations will additionally organize a Day of Indigenous, Afro and Popular Resistance on October 12.

A final date for the national strike has yet to be defined.

The organizations decided to call a strike to protest the government’s security and defense policy, the ending of peace processes with illegal armed groups and in defense of social reforms that had been implemented by former President Gustavo Petro.

The protests additionally seek to express solidarity with the people of Palestine, western Sahara, Iran, Bolivia and Venezuela, and reject US imperialism in the Americas.

We must categorically reject the interference of U.S. government officials in the formulation of domestic policies under the guise of so-called friendly aid, which in reality masks the ambition to intensify overexploitation, extractivism, territorial control, and the presence of foreign troops on our soil. Social organizations and labor unions

The organizations agreed to “prepare, through the most intense and massive agitation and propaganda campaign, a national strike.”

World.title: Judge suspends Colombia’s aerial fumigation pilot
World.content:
A Putumayo from the southern Putumayo province suspended the government’s announced resumption of the aerial spraying of coca, ordering information that would allow “a sufficiently informed decision on the merits.”

Earlier this week, the National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine, “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

The National Police subsequently said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo, a province inside the Amazon forest.

These announcements triggered a local foundation to sue the administration, claiming that the plans to do a pilot were in violation of the 2015 ban on aerial fumigation and threatened both locals and the environment.

The judge agreed and ordered the administration of President Abelardo de la Espriella to provide information on the environmental and health risk involved in the aerial spraying with glufosinate ammonium.

The potential implementation of the pilot plan before gathering and analyzing the studies, documents, and technical evidence cited by the administration itself as the basis for the decision could render the requested constitutional protection ineffective and jeopardize the possibility of reaching a sufficiently informed decision on the merits; Indeed, the combination of the announced imminence of the measure, the current lack of essential information needed to understand its territorial, social, and environmental scope, and the particular ecological sensitivity of the department of Putumayo necessitates preventive action aimed at preserving the effectiveness of this constitutional action. Putumayo court

The suspension of the aerial spraying comes days after De la Espriella promised US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that he would resume aerial fumigation, a notoriously ineffective way to get rid of coca.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.

He was an unabashed eccentric. Smart. Complicated. He had an entrepreneurial spirit but no real nose for business. Steve was a lawyer who wrote about politics and fruit exports. An editor with a penchant for typos. Part idealist, part cynic. A campaigner with no patience for diplomacy. He was perpetually cash-strapped, but generous. He was impulsive and impatient at times, but also deeply committed—to his various projects and causes, and to his family and colleagues. He was a teacher and a mentor. A doting father. A friend.

Goodbye Steve. Paz. And thank you.

World.title: Anti-vaccine mandate protests spread across the country, crippling Canada-U.S. trade
World.content:
Speaking to reporters at a press conference in Ottawa, Emergency Preparedness Minister Bill Blair said the blockade at Windsor’s Ambassador Bridge is particularly alarming because a quarter of all Canada-U.S. trade moves through that one crossing, which connects Canada with Detroit and points beyond.

Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of products have been held back for three days as 50 to 75 vehicles and about 100 anti-mandate protesters camp out on the main road that leads on and off the bridge.
