World.title: Kenya Residency Visa Requirements 2026: Class K Starts at 35
World.content:
KENYA · VISA

Key Facts — The retirement route Class K requires an assured annual income of at least US$24,000 from a pension or annuity.

— The age bar Applicants for the Class K permit must be not less than thirty-five years old.

— The catch The annual issuance fee is about US$1,930, roughly eight percent of the required income.

— The remote-work route Class N covers people living in Kenya and working for foreign-registered companies.

— What Class N costs It takes US$200 to apply and US$1,000 a year to hold, renewable annually.

— What comes next East African Community citizens pay nothing for these permits.

Kenya residency visa requirements are unusually explicit. The figures are published, and two of them are higher than most people expect.

Kenya Residency Visa Requirements 2026: Class K Starts at 35 Photo: Matti Blume, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Where This Fits

Kenya residency visa requirements are easier to research than most in the region. The immigration directorate publishes the classes, the thresholds and the fees.

That transparency is the useful part. It also means the numbers are harder to talk around than in countries where the rules are discretionary.

Four routes matter for most foreigners moving to Kenya. They are Class K, Class N, Class G and the special pass.

This guide sets out what each requires, what each costs and where the awkward details sit.

Class K: The Ordinary Resident Permit

Class K is the permit for people living in Kenya on a fixed income. It is the closest thing the country has to a retirement route.

Two conditions define it. An applicant must be not less than thirty-five years of age.

They must also have an assured annual income of not less than US$24,000. That income has to come from a pension or an annuity.

The wording on source matters. The published requirement covers income derived from sources outside Kenya and remitted into the country, or derived from a pension or annuity.

The documents are conventional. Form 25 and a cover letter to the Director General open the file.

A recent colour passport photograph and the passport bio-data pages follow. So do current immigration status documents.

The document that decides the application is the proof of assured income. Everything else is administrative.

Applications are submitted through the electronic Foreign Nationals Services portal rather than over a counter.

What Class K Costs

The processing fee is 20,000 Kenyan shillings and is non-refundable. That is about US$154.

All conversions here use a rate of 129.53 to the dollar published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026. Shilling fees move against the dollar, so the equivalents drift.

The issuance fee is 250,000 shillings per year, roughly US$1,930. That is the figure most applicants underestimate.

Set it against the income requirement and the proportion becomes clear. The annual fee is about eight percent of the US$24,000 the applicant must prove.

For a retiree on exactly the minimum, the permit is a meaningful line in the budget. It is charged every year rather than once.

That recurring structure is the part worth planning around. A one-off cost can be absorbed, and an annual one has to be funded.

It also changes how the two routes compare. Over five years the difference between Class K and Class N runs into thousands of dollars.

Nairobi, where permit applications are filed and where most Class N holders live. Photo: This Photo was taken by Timothy A. Gonsalves. Feel free to use my photos, but please menti, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Class N: The Remote Work Permit

Kenya created a formal route for remote workers, which few countries in the region have done. Class N covers people residing in Kenya while working for foreign-registered companies.

It came into force on 16 December 2024 under Legal Notice 198 of 2024. Applications opened in April 2025.

The application fee is US$200 and is non-refundable. The issuance fee is US$1,000 a year.

The permit runs for one year and is renewable. Payment is made by card or mobile money through the same online portal.

Compared with Class K the arithmetic is different. There is no age bar and no pension requirement, and the annual cost is roughly half.

The trade is what the permit assumes about your work. Class N presumes an employer or client registered outside Kenya.

Someone earning from Kenyan clients does not fit it. That case belongs under Class G, with its heavier conditions.

What this means for a life in Kenya is that Class N separates permission to live from permission to earn locally. A permit holder who invoices clients abroad sits inside the rules; the same person billing a Nairobi company from the same laptop does not. Officers apply the distinction to the paperwork in front of them, not to job titles, so the contract and the invoices matter more than how an applicant describes the work.

Class G: Trade, Business and Consultancy

Class G covers a specific trade, business, consultancy or profession. It is the route for someone setting up or buying into a Kenyan company.

The capital requirement is US$100,000, and documentary proof is required. That is the same headline threshold Guatemala applies to its investor route.

The processing fee is about US$155 and the issuance fee about US$1,930 a year. Those figures match the Class K structure closely.

The paperwork is heavier than for the other classes. Kenyan company registration, an incorporation certificate, a tax PIN certificate and a shareholders certificate are all required.

This is a business permit rather than a residence-by-investment scheme. The company has to exist and operate, not merely hold an asset.

Mombasa, the coastal entry point where trade and consultancy permits concentrate. Photo: Ministry of East African Affairs, Commerce & Touri, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons

The Special Pass and the Community Exemption

A special pass covers temporary business, trade or professional activity. It runs for a maximum of six months.

The fee is US$200 a month for non-citizens of the East African Community. An organisation stamp or sponsorship is mandatory.

That monthly rate makes it expensive as a bridge. Six months at US$200 costs more than a year of Class N.

The East African Community exemption is the largest single discount in the system. Citizens of member states pay nothing for these permits.

For everyone else the fees are uniform and published. There is no negotiated rate and no discretionary reduction documented here.

That uniformity is worth something when planning. A published fee cannot quietly become a different fee at the counter.

What We Could Not Confirm

Three points are left open because the sources used did not settle them.

The first is the stated validity period of the Class K permit. The official page sets an annual issuance fee without naming a term.

The second is the renewal procedure for Class K, which is not described alongside the initial requirements. The third is whether the assured income test is applied gross or net of tax.

None of those is guessed at here. The immigration directorate is the authority on all three, and the portal is where a current answer can be obtained.

What Kenya Residency Visa Requirements Come Down To

Kenya sets out its terms plainly, and the terms are not cheap. That combination is rarer than it should be.

For a retiree, the binding constraints are the age of thirty-five and the assured US$24,000 a year. The annual fee of about US$1,930 then takes a real bite out of that income.

For a remote worker, Class N is the better-designed option. It costs half as much annually, carries no age bar and was written for exactly this case.

For anyone building a business, Class G asks US$100,000 and a functioning Kenyan company. It is a work permit with an investment condition attached.

Read Kenya residency visa requirements as a published price list. The advantage is that you can plan against it, and the disadvantage is that you cannot argue with it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the Kenyan Class K permit require?

An assured annual income of at least US$24,000 from a pension or annuity. Applicants must be not less than thirty-five years old.

What does Class K cost?

The annual issuance fee is about US$1,930, roughly eight percent of the income the permit requires.

Is there a permit for remote workers?

Class N covers people living in Kenya and working for foreign-registered companies. It takes US$200 to apply and US$1,000 a year to hold, renewable annually.

Do regional citizens pay the same fees?

No. East African Community citizens pay nothing for these permits.

World.title: Morocco Residency Visa Requirements 2026: The Ninety-Day Line
World.content:
MOROCCO · VISA

Key Facts — When it applies A residence permit becomes compulsory once a stay passes 90 days in the country.

— What it is called The document is the certificat or carte d’immatriculation, issued through the police.

— The catch The law has no category written for retirees or investors, so both apply as visitors.

— What you must show A home-country criminal record, a medical certificate and documented means of support.

— Where you apply The Bureau des Etrangers at a police prefecture, or the Gendarmerie in rural areas.

— What comes next The permit lapses after six months of absence, whatever validity it carries.

Morocco residency visa requirements begin with a date rather than a form. Ninety days is the line.

Morocco Residency Visa Requirements 2026: The Ninety-Day Line Photo: "Parlement Rabat" by Taha ahh, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Where This Fits

Morocco residency visa requirements are less about a visa than about a deadline. Most Western nationals do not need a visa to arrive at all.

What they need is a residence permit once the stay gets long. The rules around that permit are specific, and some of them are not obvious.

This guide covers the permit itself. When it is required, what it is called, what documents it takes and how long it lasts.

It also covers two points that catch people out, which are the missing categories and the bank account decision.

The Ninety-Day Line

Nationals of most Western countries enter Morocco without a visa. The permitted stay is 90 days.

The limit is framed as a maximum within a six-month window. A tourist stay cannot exceed three consecutive months in any six-month period.

Once a stay passes that line, a residence permit stops being optional. It is required rather than advisable.

That is the practical trigger for everything below. Anyone planning to stay longer should start the file before the ninety days run out, not after.

What the Permit Is and Where You Get It

The document is a certificate of registration, the certificat or carte d’immatriculation. It is handled by the police rather than by a consulate.

In urban areas the application goes to the Bureau des Etrangers at the local police prefecture or central police station. In rural areas it goes to the Gendarmerie.

The office is the one local to where you actually live. That is why a lease or an equivalent proof of address has to come first.

Applications are made in person. You receive an interim receipt, the recepisse, on the day.

The card itself follows weeks later. The cost is modest and paid locally.

Casablanca, where many residence applicants first deal with Moroccan paperwork. Photo: Milamber's portfolio, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Documents

The list is consistent across sources and it is longer than most people expect. A legalised copy of the passport is the starting point.

Eight photographs are required, taken within the previous three months. Proof of address follows, which can be a lease, a utility bill or a hosting attestation.

A medical certificate is required, confirming the absence of contagious disease. So is a criminal record extract from the country of origin.

Proof of financial means is required in every category but one. A bank attestation showing the balance of a local Moroccan account is the usual form.

Documents are generally submitted as notarised copies. Two notarised copies of each is the standard expectation.

The only documented exception on means is for applicants aged sixteen to eighteen declaring an intention to settle. Everyone else shows money.

The Categories, and What Is Missing

Morocco’s framework for foreigners is Law 02-03. It sets out discretionary mentions rather than entitlements.

The mentions named in that law are visitor, student, work, family regrouping and long-term medical treatment. Each is granted at the administration’s discretion.

There is no statutory mention for a retiree, and none for an investor. That is the single most consequential fact in this guide.

A retired person moving to Morocco does not apply under a retirement route, because there is not one. They apply as a visitor and satisfy the means test.

An investor is in the same position. Capital brought into the country does not create a residence category of its own.

Sources differ on the total number of categories in current practice. One official page refers to eight, while the statute names five, and that discrepancy is not resolved here.

What this means for a life in Morocco is that the permit category matters less at the start than the paper trail behind it. A retiree who can show a pension, a lease and a clean record usually moves through the same prefecture counter as a worker with a contract; the difference is which box the officer ticks. Applicants who arrive with documents translated and legalised before their ninety days expire describe the process as slow but predictable. Those who start the paperwork late describe the same office very differently.

Validity, Renewal and Absence

The permit is issued for a period between one and ten years. It is renewable for the same period it was granted.

The range is wide because the term is discretionary. A first permit is commonly short, and longer terms follow a record of renewals.

Renewal requires a Moroccan criminal record certificate, the casier judiciaire. It is obtained from the Ministry of Justice in Rabat with birth and passport copies.

One rule overrides the stated validity. The permit lapses after six months of absence from the country.

That matters for anyone intending to split the year between two countries. A ten-year card does not survive a seven-month trip.

Daily life in Casablanca continues around the permit process, not inside it. Photo: Sharon Hahn Darlin, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Bank Account Decision

This is the part that is irreversible, and it is rarely explained before arrival. Moroccan bank accounts come in convertible and ordinary forms.

A convertible dirham account is funded by selling foreign currency, by transfer from another convertible account, or by investment deposits. Money in it can be converted and sent out again.

Money that enters as ordinary dirhams never becomes convertible. That status is fixed at the moment of deposit.

So funds must arrive through banking channels as foreign currency to keep the option of leaving later. Cash converted at a bureau and then deposited does not qualify.

One day you may sell a property or wind down and leave. This single mechanical detail decides whether the proceeds can follow you.

What We Could Not Confirm

Three points are left open because the sources used did not settle them.

The first is the exact fee schedule for the permit. It is described as modest and paid locally, without a published figure.

The second is the number of categories in current administrative practice, where an official page and the statute do not agree. The third is the penalty for failing to register after ninety days.

None of those is guessed at here. The prefecture handling your file is the authority on all three.

What Morocco Residency Visa Requirements Come Down To

Entry is easy and staying is procedural. The ninety-day line is the moment the process becomes compulsory.

The documents are conventional except for their volume and the notarisation. Building the file takes longer than submitting it.

The two traps are structural rather than bureaucratic. There is no retiree or investor category, and the bank account status cannot be changed later.

Tax residency is a separate question with its own tests. They are a permanent home, a centre of economic interests, or 183 days in any 365-day period.

Residents are taxed on worldwide income, and non-residents only on Moroccan-sourced income. The residence permit and the tax test are not the same thing.

Read Morocco residency visa requirements as a deadline, a document list and one irreversible banking choice. The first two are work, and the third is the one to get right before arriving.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do I need a residence permit in Morocco?

A residence permit becomes compulsory once a stay passes 90 days in the country.

What is the permit called, and where do I apply?

The document is the certificat or carte d’immatriculation, issued through the police. Applications go to the Bureau des Étrangers at a police prefecture, or to the Gendarmerie in rural areas.

What do I have to show?

A home-country criminal record, a medical certificate and documented means of support.

Is there a retirement or investor category?

No. The law has no category written for retirees or investors, so both apply as visitors. The permit lapses after six months of absence, whatever validity it carries.

World.title: Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight: Free Under the Arches, Angra at Vivo Rio, September 18, 2026
World.content:

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Fafá de Belém Under the Arches, Free She opens the fourth Amir Haddad theatre festival at the Arcos da Lapa at 10 p.m. with her Guitarradas do Pará show. Entry is free, the bill starts at 7 p.m., and the forecast has the rain gone by then.

Tonight at a Glance — Free at 10 p.m. Fafá de Belém with guest Manoel Cordeiro at the Arcos da Lapa, Praça Cardeal Câmara.

— Free at 8 p.m. Mart’nália opens the Próxima Parada Samba season at the Palácio Capanema, Rua da Imprensa 16.

— Angra at Vivo Rio Doors 7 p.m., show 9 p.m., R$150 full or R$75 half, about US$29 and US$15.

— Samba in Lapa Dani Coimbra at Carioca da Gema, R$35 or about US$7, with two sets on a Friday.

— A silent film with a live score Quarteto Kalimera play Nosferatu at the Sala Cecília Meireles, 7 p.m., R$40 or about US$8.

— Weather Between 17 and 25 degrees, showers in the afternoon and a dry, cloudy evening.

— No football Flamengo went through last night, so the Maracanã is dark and Lapa has the city to itself.

Tonight, Friday 18 September 2026, Rio runs one of its fullest free programmes of the year. The Semana de Arte and a new theatre festival overlap, and all times below are Rio time, four hours behind London.

What’s On Tonight in Lapa

Fafá de Belém opens the fourth Festival de Teatro Amir Haddad under the Arcos da Lapa at 10 p.m. She brings her Guitarradas do Pará show, with the guitarist Manoel Cordeiro as guest, and entry is free.

The bill under the arches starts earlier than that. Baque Mulher, Bárbara Vento with Carimbaby and the Festa Xêpa fill the stage from 7 p.m. onwards.

Rio de Janeiro Nightlife Tonight — Friday, September 18, 2026 Photo: Carlos Lucio, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

A few hundred metres away, the Circo Voador has Samba do Sacramento with Hugo Ojuara from 8 p.m. Tickets run from R$60 at half price, roughly US$12, through Eventim.

The Sala Cecília Meireles takes the other direction entirely. Quarteto Kalimera play a live score to Murnau’s Nosferatu at 7 p.m., for R$40 or about US$8.

That programme also ran last night, which is unusual for the hall. Tonight is the second and final showing.

Samba at Carioca da Gema

Carioca da Gema on Avenida Mem de Sá has Dani Coimbra tonight. The house describes her as a singer, actor and dancer whose repertoire runs from samba to jazz, pop and xote.

She is one of the voices of Empolga às 9, a Rio street carnival bloco. A bloco is a neighbourhood carnival group that parades through the streets rather than the Sambadrome.

Entry is R$35, about US$7, the Friday and Saturday rate. Tuesday to Thursday costs R$30, roughly US$6, and holiday eves are charged at the Friday rate.

Tickets go through Zig, linked from the venue’s own listing. The Zig page itself shows no price, so that R$35, about US$7, comes from the house information rather than the seller.

The Start Time Needs Checking

The venue publishes two different Friday timings on the same page. Its entry for tonight gives 7.30 p.m., while its standing Friday block gives doors at 6.30 p.m. and a main show at 9.30 p.m.

Neither figure carries a correction, so we report both rather than choose. The gap between the two published start times is two hours.

The published door is 6.30 p.m., which makes 7.30 p.m. a time half an hour into the happy-hour set. Arrive at 7 p.m. for the early show or 9.30 p.m. for the main one.

Telephone (21) 98556-0834 if the exact hour matters. Tables reserved in advance are held until 9 p.m.

This is not carelessness peculiar to one bar. Small Rio houses run their websites alongside the kitchen, and a fixed weekly block rarely matches a per-event field.

Free Music Across the Centre

Mart’nália sings at the Palácio Gustavo Capanema at 8 p.m., on Rua da Imprensa 16 in the Centro. Entry is free with no ticket, subject to capacity, and a vinyl set follows at 10 p.m.

The concert opens Próxima Parada Samba, an occupation of the building built around a tribute to Beth Carvalho. It is the strongest free bill of the Semana de Arte so far.

At Praça XV, the Festival Sotaque Carregado runs a fair from 5 p.m. until half past eleven. Orquestra Voadora play at half past six and BNegão at half past seven, with a samba circle at half past eight.

The XXI RioHarpFestival gives two free concerts today. A naval wind sextet with the harpist Giovana Sanches plays the Espaço Cultural da Marinha at half past twelve. The Camerata do Uerê follows at the Palácio Tiradentes at 6 p.m.

Several smaller rooms are also free. Fausto Fawcett is at the Teatro Glauce Rocha at 7 p.m. and Amanda Magalhães at Arte SESC Flamengo at the same hour.

Angra, Theatre and the Rest of the Ticketed Night

Angra play Vivo Rio tonight, performing Holy Land in full for the album’s thirtieth anniversary. Doors open at 7 p.m. and the show starts at 9 p.m., with Throw Me To The Wolves supporting.

Tickets are R$150 full and R$75 half, about US$29 and US$15, and the show is for over-18s. The venue sits at Avenida Infante Dom Henrique 85 in the Parque do Flamengo.

Thaís Fraga’s trio marks more than thirty years of bossa and jazz at the Vinicius Show in Ipanema, at 8 p.m. Entry is R$120 full and R$60 half, roughly US$23 and US$12.

At the Teatro João Caetano on Praça Tiradentes, the musical O Neguinho da Beija-Flor plays at 7 p.m. Stalls are R$80 full and R$40 half, about US$16 and US$8.

Rio Gastronomia runs at the Jockey Club in Gávea from 6 p.m. until midnight, from R$80 or roughly US$16. ArtRio is open at the Marina da Glória until 9 p.m., at R$100 full or about US$19.

What the Weather Will Do to Your Evening

Today runs between 17 and 25 degrees Celsius, with showers in the afternoon and a 56 per cent chance of rain. Forecasters put the total at under two millimetres.

The useful part for a night out is what happens after dark. The forecast has cloud but no rain overnight, which matters for the free outdoor bills under the Arcos and at Praça XV.

Sunset falls at 5.48 in the afternoon. That leaves a long evening and a mild one by Rio standards for September.

The Rest of the Weekend

Andrezão do Cacique plays Carioca da Gema tomorrow, with doors at 8.30 p.m. and the main show at 10 p.m. Entry is R$35 again, about US$7, and the house then closes on Sunday and Monday.

The MIMO Festival takes over the Circo Voador tomorrow and Sunday, free both nights. Saturday starts at 8 p.m. and Sunday at 6 p.m., with Tiken Jah Fakoly, Fernanda Abreu, Capicua with Emicida and Tinariwen among the names.

MIMO also shows fourteen free films at the Cine Santa Teresa across the two days, from 4 p.m. Entry is first come, subject to capacity.

The Semana de Arte do Rio has been running since 16 September and continues until the 27th. The Centro Cultural Lavradio at Rua do Lavradio 15 is free from Wednesday to Sunday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

That building is a five-minute walk from Carioca da Gema. It is the easiest way to see the festival’s daytime side before the evening starts.

Where to Go

Arcos da Lapa — Praça Cardeal Câmara The eighteenth-century aqueduct that gives Lapa its outline, used as an open-air stage. Tonight it opens the fourth Amir Haddad theatre festival. Tonight Fafá de Belém with Manoel Cordeiro at 10 p.m.; the bill starts at 7 p.m.

Entry Free, no ticket.

Also on Baque Mulher, Bárbara Vento with Carimbaby and Festa Xêpa from 7 p.m.

Festival Fourth Festival de Teatro Amir Haddad, running 18 to 25 September.

Address Praça Cardeal Câmara, Lapa. Metro Cinelândia, then a short walk.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa A two-storey samba house on Avenida Mem de Sá, open since 2000. The room is small and the tables sit close to the stage. Tonight Dani Coimbra. The event entry gives 7.30 p.m.

Friday block Doors 6.30 p.m., happy-hour set 7 p.m., main show 9.30 p.m.

Entry R$35, about US$7, Friday and Saturday; R$30, roughly US$6, Tuesday to Thursday.

Tables Held for reservations until 9 p.m., then released.

Tickets Through Zig, linked from the venue’s own event page. Zig does not show the price.

Address Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Centro. Metro Cinelândia, then a short walk.

Vivo Rio — Parque do Flamengo A 4,000-capacity hall inside the Modern Art Museum complex, facing Guanabara Bay. Tonight it hosts a thirtieth-anniversary metal show. Tonight Angra performing Holy Land. Doors 7 p.m., show 9 p.m.

Entry R$150 full, R$75 half, about US$29 and US$15.

Support Throw Me To The Wolves.

Age Over-18s only.

Address Avenida Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo.

Palácio Gustavo Capanema — Centro The 1940s modernist ministry building designed with Le Corbusier’s involvement, now a cultural centre. Tonight it opens a samba season in tribute to Beth Carvalho. Tonight Mart’nália at 8 p.m., then a vinyl set at 10 p.m.

Entry Free, no ticket, subject to capacity.

Season Próxima Parada Samba, part of the Semana de Arte do Rio.

Address Rua da Imprensa 16, Centro.

Money and How Paying Works

We convert at 5.1521 reais to one US dollar. That is the closing sell rate the Banco Central published for Thursday 17 September, the last business day before today.

Entry at the samba houses is a fixed price rather than a per-artist one. Food and drink are billed separately, at the table.

Bars usually add a service charge of about 10 per cent, called serviço. Brazilian law makes it optional, and staff remove it if you ask.

The free concerts tonight are genuinely free, with no ticket and no registration. They fill on a first-come basis, so arriving early is the only currency that helps.

Getting Home Safe

A 10 p.m. start under the Arcos will outlast the metro on some lines. Check the last train for your own line on the MetrôRio site, and plan a car if you stay to the end.

Rideshare is the reliable way out of Lapa after midnight. Book from inside the venue and wait in a lit, busy spot.

Keep your phone in a pocket on the quieter streets around Mem de Sá. The avenue stays busy, and the side streets do not.

Tonight’s free bills are outdoor and crowded, which is safe in the middle and thinner at the edges. Stay where the lights and the people are.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is free in Rio tonight?

Fafá de Belém under the Arcos da Lapa at 10 p.m., Mart’nália at the Palácio Capanema at 8 p.m., the Festival Sotaque Carregado at Praça XV from 5 p.m., and two RioHarpFestival concerts at half past twelve and 6 p.m.

What time does the show at Carioca da Gema start?

The venue publishes two figures. Its event entry gives 7.30 p.m., and its standing Friday schedule gives doors at 6.30 p.m., a happy-hour set at 7 p.m. and the main show at 9.30 p.m.

How much is Carioca da Gema?

Entry is R$35, about US$7, on Fridays, Saturdays and holiday eves. Tuesday to Thursday costs R$30, roughly US$6.

How much are the Angra tickets?

R$150 full and R$75 half price, about US$29 and US$15. Doors open at 7 p.m. and the show starts at 9 p.m. at Vivo Rio.

Is there football in Rio tonight?

No. Flamengo drew 1-1 with Independiente del Valle at the Maracanã last night and went through 3-1 on aggregate to face Estudiantes in the semi-finals.

Will it rain tonight?

Showers are forecast for the afternoon, with a 56 per cent chance and under two millimetres of rain. The evening is expected to be cloudy and dry.

What is on tomorrow?

Andrezão do Cacique at Carioca da Gema, doors 8.30 p.m. and show 10 p.m. for R$35 or about US$7. The MIMO Festival is free at the Circo Voador from 8 p.m.

Sources: Carioca da Gema, events and house information, retrieved 18 September 2026; Dani Coimbra and Andrezão do Cacique ticket pages on Zig; Vivo Rio event page for Angra; Sala Cecília Meireles programme; Riotur event calendar for Circo Voador; Eu Rio on the Amir Haddad festival and Fafá de Belém; Folha do Leste on Mart’nália at Capanema; Rota Cult on the Festival Sotaque Carregado and the Centro Cultural Lavradio; Pressenza on the RioHarpFestival; MIMO Festival programme; Climatempo forecast for Rio de Janeiro; Banco Central PTAX close, 17 September 2026.

World.title: Cost of Living Arequipa Peru 2026: Less Than Half of Lima
World.content:
PERU · COST OF LIVING

Key Facts — What rent costs A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$362 a month, and US$241 outside it.

— Against the capital Lima charges about US$767 for the same flat, more than twice the Arequipa figure.

— The catch The average net salary is about US$629, so central rent still takes nearly three-fifths of it.

— What bills cost Basic utilities average about US$24 a month, the lowest figure in this series.

— What eating out costs A meal at an inexpensive restaurant averages about US$3.56.

— What comes next The figures rest on 23 contributors, so treat them as indicative rather than exact.

Cost of living Arequipa Peru is the cheapest entry in this series. The utility bill is where the gap becomes hard to believe.

Arequipa's Plaza de Armas. A central one-bedroom costs less than half the Lima equivalent. Photo: PsamatheM, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Where This Fits

Cost of living Arequipa Peru produces the lowest figures in this series of city guides. That holds on rent, on bills and on eating out.

Arequipa is Peru’s second city, built in white volcanic stone at around 2,300 metres. It is not a small town or a resort.

The comparison that makes the point is with Lima rather than with anywhere abroad. The two cities sit in the same country under the same currency.

What follows sets out the figures, converts them, and then tests them against the local wage.

Less Than Half of Lima

A one-bedroom apartment in the centre of Arequipa averages 1,218 soles a month. That works out at about US$362.

All conversions here use a rate of 3.37 to the dollar, published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026. Sol prices move against the dollar, so the equivalents drift.

The same flat in central Lima averages about US$767. Arequipa is therefore cheaper by more than half on the single line most people check.

That is a wider internal gap than most countries show between their first and second cities. It is the practical case for looking beyond the capital.

The trade is not nothing. Lima has the international airport, the largest job market and the bulk of the country’s professional services.

Arequipa answers with climate and scale. It is large enough to have what a city needs and small enough to cross without planning around traffic.

The altitude is the other variable. At around 2,300 metres the air is thinner than most arrivals expect. That is a health question rather than a cost one.

The Plaza de Armas in Arequipa. The colonial centre carries a premium of about half over the outlying districts. Photo: PsamatheM, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

What Housing Costs

Outside the centre a one-bedroom averages 812.17 soles, about US$241. The discount for leaving the middle is roughly a third.

A three-bedroom in the centre averages 2,488 soles, close to US$739. Outside the centre it falls to 1,440 soles, about US$428.

A family-sized flat in central Arequipa therefore costs about what a one-bedroom costs in central Lima. That comparison is the one worth carrying.

The central premium here is real but moderate. It is narrower than Curitiba’s 42% and far narrower than the gap in the small expat towns covered earlier.

That suggests a housing market shaped mainly by local demand. Where foreign money dominates, the central premium tends to be much wider.

The Bills Are the Surprise

Basic utilities for a standard apartment average 81.67 soles a month. That is about US$24.

Set that against the same line elsewhere in this series. Nassau runs about US$397.50, Punta del Este about US$114 and Curitiba about US$99.

Arequipa therefore costs roughly a sixteenth of the Nassau figure. That is the widest single gap recorded across these guides.

Part of the explanation is the climate. At this altitude the city needs little heating and almost no air conditioning.

Broadband adds about 80 soles, close to US$23.75, and a mobile plan around 34.98 soles, about US$10.39. Connectivity costs roughly what the electricity does.

Laguna de Salinas in the Arequipa region. Altitude shapes the climate, and it keeps the heating and cooling bill small. Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons

Food, Transport and Schooling

A meal at an inexpensive restaurant averages 12 soles, about US$3.56. That is the lowest figure in this series by a clear margin.

For comparison, the same line is US$6.50 in Boquete, US$6.81 in Antigua Guatemala and US$38.75 in Nassau. Arequipa is an order of magnitude below the island.

Local transport costs one sol a trip, roughly US$0.30. Petrol runs about 5.15 soles a litre, close to US$1.53.

Preschool is reported at about 257.50 soles a month, near US$76. For a family that is the kind of line that decides a city.

None of these figures is a rounding error against rent. Together they make the difference between the two Peruvian cities larger than rent alone suggests.

A single person eating out daily would spend about US$107 a month at that price. The same habit in Nassau would cost more than a thousand.

That is the kind of gap that changes how a person lives rather than only what they pay. Eating out stops being an occasion here.

Rent Against the Local Wage

The average monthly net salary in Arequipa is 2,117.60 soles, about US$629. A central one-bedroom averages about US$362.

Rent therefore takes close to three-fifths of the average net wage. That is a heavy share by any standard.

It is still a better ratio than most of this series. In Antigua Guatemala, Boquete and Punta del Este, central rent exceeds the average wage outright.

The difference matters for what kind of city this is. Arequipa is priced by people who live and work there, not by visitors or foreign buyers.

For someone arriving on a foreign income, that has a practical consequence. Your money goes further here than in places where foreign money has already set the price.

What We Could Not Price

Three items are not stated here because the source did not carry a dependable figure.

The first is the monthly transport pass, which the data lists as unavailable rather than free. The second is health cover, which varies by provider and age.

The third is altitude adjustment, which is not a cost but is a real factor at 2,300 metres. Some arrivals need weeks rather than days.

The first of those is the only one that changes a budget, and single fares suggest it would be modest.

What Cost of Living Arequipa Peru Comes Down To

This is the cheapest city covered in this series, and the margin is not narrow. Rent, bills and eating out are all the lowest recorded.

The utility line is the one that stands out. At about US$24 a month it is a sixteenth of what the same bill costs in Nassau.

Against Lima, the case is straightforward. A family-sized flat in the centre costs roughly what a single person pays in the capital.

The honest qualifier is the wage. Local salaries are low enough that rent still takes most of a typical pay packet.

That is also why the city stays affordable to outsiders. Nothing here has been repriced upward by foreign demand.

Read cost of living Arequipa Peru as Peru without the capital-city premium. What you give up is the airport and the job market, and what you gain is most of your budget.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does rent cost in Arequipa?

A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$362 a month, and about US$241 outside the centre.

How does Arequipa compare with Lima?

Lima charges about US$767 for the same flat, more than twice the Arequipa figure.

How does rent compare with local wages?

The average net salary is about US$629 a month, so central rent still takes nearly three-fifths of it.

What do bills and eating out cost?

Basic utilities average about US$24 a month, the lowest figure in this series. A meal at an inexpensive restaurant averages about US$3.56.

World.title: Cost of Living Punta del Este 2026: Half Again Above Montevideo
World.content:
URUGUAY · COST OF LIVING

Key Facts — What rent costs A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$1,094 a month, and US$815 outside it.

— Against the capital That is roughly 49% above the Montevideo figure for the same size of flat.

— The catch The average local net salary is about US$1,031, below the cost of a central one-bedroom.

— What the season does Reported three-bedroom rents outside the centre span US$598 to US$2,789.

— What bills cost Basic utilities average about US$114 a month, and a cheap restaurant meal about US$13.

— What comes next The figures rest on 29 contributors over 18 months, with some lines estimated.

Cost of living Punta del Este is a resort price attached to a small permanent population. The season is inside every figure.

Punta del Este. Rent runs about half again above Montevideo, and the summer season sits inside every average.

Where This Fits

Cost of living Punta del Este is usually answered with a comparison to Montevideo. That comparison is the right starting point and it is unflattering.

Punta del Este is a resort on the Atlantic coast with a small permanent population and a very large summer one. Its housing market is built for the second group.

A resident arriving outside the season sees one set of prices. The published averages blend both, and that blending is worth understanding.

This guide gives the figures, converts them, and then says where the seasonality is hiding inside them.

The Premium Over Montevideo

A one-bedroom apartment in the centre of Punta del Este averages 44,170.45 Uruguayan pesos a month. That is about US$1,094.

All conversions here use a rate of 40.36 to the dollar, published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026. Peso prices move against the dollar, so the equivalents drift.

The same flat in Montevideo averages about US$732. Punta del Este therefore carries a premium of roughly 49% over the national capital.

That is unusual. In most countries the capital is the expensive address and the coastal towns are the discount.

Uruguay inverts it because its coast is an international market. Buyers and renters from Argentina and Brazil price this stretch, not Uruguayan salaries.

The marina at Punta del Este. Housing here is priced against seasonal demand rather than local wages.

What Housing Costs

Outside the centre a one-bedroom averages 32,882.85 pesos, about US$815. The discount for leaving the middle is roughly a quarter.

A three-bedroom in the centre averages 78,240.63 pesos, close to US$1,939. Outside the centre the average falls to 51,396.51 pesos, about US$1,273.

Those averages are comfortable to quote and misleading to rely on. The reported ranges tell a different story.

A central one-bedroom is reported between about US$897 and US$1,494. That is a spread of two-thirds around a single description.

For a three-bedroom outside the centre the reported range runs from about US$598 to US$2,789. The top is more than four times the bottom.

The Season Is Inside the Numbers

A spread that wide is not noise. It is the summer season and the winter one recorded in the same average.

Punta del Este fills in January and February and empties afterwards. A property let by the week in season and by the year out of season produces two incompatible prices.

For someone planning to live here year-round, the practical consequence is straightforward. Annual leases are negotiated against a landlord’s alternative, which is the summer let.

That is why long-term tenants often sign contracts that exclude the peak weeks. It is a local convention rather than an oddity.

Anyone comparing this town with a mainland city should hold that in mind. The averages here describe a market with two modes, not one.

The same logic applies to services. Restaurants and shops that open for the season price accordingly, and some simply close afterwards.

Winter in Punta del Este is quieter and cheaper than the averages suggest. Summer is dearer and more crowded than they suggest.

Los Dedos on Brava beach. The resort’s permanent population is a fraction of its summer one. Photo: M M from Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Bills and Groceries

Basic utilities for a standard apartment average 4,612.50 pesos a month, about US$114. That sits above Curitiba and far below Nassau.

A meal at an inexpensive restaurant averages 525 pesos, roughly US$13.01. That is twice the Antigua Guatemala figure and a third of the Nassau one.

Groceries are ordinary by Uruguayan standards. Milk runs about 46.33 pesos a litre, close to US$1.15.

A loaf of bread averages 99.70 pesos, about US$2.47. A dozen eggs run 172.24 pesos, near US$4.27.

Eggs stand out as expensive relative to the rest of the basket. Otherwise the daily shop is not where the resort premium lands.

That pattern is worth noting because it is the opposite of Nassau. There the import bill reaches every line, and here it reaches almost none.

Uruguay produces most of its own food, and Punta del Este is two hours from the capital. The premium is paid for the address, not for the supply chain.

Rent Against the Local Wage

The average monthly net salary in Punta del Este is 41,625.33 pesos, about US$1,031. A central one-bedroom averages about US$1,094.

Rent on an average central flat therefore exceeds the average net wage. That is the same pattern found in Antigua Guatemala and Boquete.

The mechanism is identical in each case. Housing is priced by people earning elsewhere, and wages are set by the local economy.

What differs here is the seasonal layer on top. In the other two towns the foreign demand is year-round, and here it is concentrated in eight weeks.

For a year-round resident that concentration is an opportunity as much as a problem. The off-season is when the negotiating position improves.

It also means the town has a different character depending on when you arrive. Judging it on a January visit is judging a different place.

What We Could Not Price

Three items are not stated here because the source did not carry a reliable figure.

The first is the purchase price per square metre. In a market this seasonal that needs a local valuation rather than an average.

The second is the split between summer and annual rents. That is the single number most useful to a year-round tenant, and it is not published.

The third is the cost of health cover, which varies by mutualista and by age. None of the three is estimated here.

The seasonal rent split in particular would change the picture more than any figure above.

What Cost of Living Punta del Este Comes Down To

This is the most expensive address in Uruguay, and the premium over Montevideo is about half again on rent. That is the headline and it holds.

Daily costs are not where the premium sits. Utilities, groceries and a cheap meal are recognisably Uruguayan.

Housing carries the whole difference, and housing here is a seasonal asset. The published averages flatten a market that has two distinct prices.

The practical advice for a year-round resident is to negotiate out of season. Expect the peak weeks to be treated separately in any contract.

For anyone weighing this against Montevideo, the trade is clear enough. You pay about half again on rent for the coast and the season.

Read cost of living Punta del Este as a coastal price list with a calendar attached. The address is expensive, and when you sign matters as much as where.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does rent cost in Punta del Este?

A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$1,094 a month, and about US$815 outside the centre.

How does that compare with Montevideo?

It is roughly 49% above the Montevideo figure for the same size of flat.

Can locals afford those rents?

The average local net salary is about US$1,031 a month, which sits below the cost of a central one-bedroom.

How much does the season move prices?

Reported three-bedroom rents outside the centre span US$598 to US$2,789. Basic utilities average about US$114 a month and a cheap restaurant meal about US$13.

World.title: Cost of Living Nassau Bahamas 2026: Where the Bills Bite Hardest
World.content:
BAHAMAS · COST OF LIVING

Key Facts — What rent costs A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$1,490 a month.

— The inversion Outside the centre the same flat averages US$2,000, above the downtown figure.

— The catch Utilities average US$397.50 a month, several times what the same bill costs in Central America.

— What people earn The average net salary after tax is about US$3,356 a month.

— What eating out costs An inexpensive restaurant meal averages US$38.75, close to six times the Antigua figure.

— What comes next The data rests on 11 contributors, so every figure here is indicative.

Cost of living Nassau Bahamas is high in the way island economies are high. The electricity bill is where it shows.

Nassau from the air. Rent is high, and the monthly power bill is the line that separates the city from the mainland. Photo: "Nassau, Bahamas aerial view" by Quintin Soloviev, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Where This Fits

Cost of living Nassau Bahamas is the most expensive entry in this series of city guides. That is worth stating before any individual figure.

The Bahamas is an island economy that imports most of what it consumes. Prices reflect freight, duty and a small domestic market.

The headline that catches most newcomers is not rent. It is the monthly utility bill, which behaves unlike anywhere else covered here.

This guide separates the lines that are merely high from the one that is genuinely unusual.

The Currency Question Does Not Arise

The Bahamian dollar is held at parity with the United States dollar. One buys one.

For a foreign resident that removes exchange-rate risk from the budget entirely. Prices quoted locally are already in the currency most readers think in.

It also means the figures below need no conversion or dating against a rate. They are directly comparable with the dollar figures elsewhere in this series.

That is a genuine simplification. It is also the end of the good news on cost.

What Housing Costs, and the Inversion

A one-bedroom apartment in the city centre averages about US$1,490 a month. That is roughly double the Lima figure and three times the Curitiba one.

Outside the centre the same flat averages about US$2,000. That is the detail worth pausing on.

In almost every city, moving out of the middle lowers the rent. In Nassau the reported average moves the other way.

The explanation is what lies outside downtown on New Providence. Waterfront and gated developments sit away from the commercial centre, and they are not cheap housing.

So the usual strategy of trading location for space does not work here in the same form. The cheaper stock is downtown, not beyond it.

Anyone budgeting should treat neighbourhood rather than distance as the variable. The centre-and-outskirts framing borrowed from mainland cities misleads on this island.

The cruise port retail area. Visitor-facing prices and resident prices are not the same market, but they share a supply chain.

The Utility Bill Is the Real Story

Basic utilities for a standard apartment average US$397.50 a month. That figure covers electricity, heating, water and rubbish.

Set it against the same line elsewhere in this series. Curitiba runs about US$99, and both Antigua Guatemala and Boquete sit near US$58.

Nassau therefore costs roughly four times the Brazilian figure and close to seven times the Central American ones. The gap is larger than the gap on rent.

The cause is structural rather than seasonal. Electricity on the islands is generated largely from imported fuel, and air conditioning runs most of the year.

For a household budget that single line is worth more attention than the choice between two flats. A US$300 monthly difference outweighs most rent negotiations.

It is also the line most often omitted from relocation estimates. Rent is advertised and power is discovered.

Eating and Everyday Prices

A meal at an inexpensive restaurant averages US$38.75. In Antigua Guatemala the same line is US$6.81, and in Boquete US$6.50.

That is close to a six-fold difference for the cheapest category of restaurant meal. It is not a comparison between fine dining and street food.

The mechanism is the same as for utilities. Food is largely imported, and the domestic market is too small to spread fixed costs.

For a resident this pushes cooking at home from a preference to an economy. The saving is proportionally far larger than in a mainland city.

It also changes how a visitor’s impression translates. Prices that feel like holiday prices are simply prices here.

Bay Street in 1901, in a hand-coloured photochrom print. The island’s dependence on imported goods is older than its tourism industry. Photo: "Bay Street, Nassau, Bahama Islands-LCCN2008679534" by unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain.

Rent Against Wages

The average monthly net salary in Nassau is about US$3,356. That is the highest average wage in this series by a wide margin.

A central one-bedroom at US$1,490 takes about 44% of it. Adding the average utility bill brings housing and power to roughly 56% of the average net wage.

That is a heavy load, though not the extreme seen in the small towns covered earlier. In Antigua Guatemala and Boquete, central rent alone exceeds the average wage.

The Bahamas pays more and charges more, and the two move roughly together. That is a different structure from a town where foreign money has outrun local income.

For someone arriving on a foreign salary, the practical reading is that Nassau is expensive but not distorted. You are paying island prices in an economy that also pays island wages.

How Thin the Data Is

The figures here come from crowd-sourced reporting, and the Nassau base is small. It rests on 133 price entries from 11 different contributors.

The data was last updated on 19 June 2026. Eleven contributors is among the thinnest samples in this series.

That matters most for the rent inversion described above. A reported average built on few observations can be moved by a handful of expensive listings.

The utility and restaurant figures are more robust as a signal, because the gap to other cities is so large. An error of thirty percent would not change the conclusion.

The safest use of this page is directional. Nassau is expensive, power is the standout line, and the specific rent figures should be checked against current listings.

What We Could Not Price

Three items are not stated here because no reliable figure was available.

The first is property purchase prices, which the source did not carry for this city. The second is health cover, which varies by provider and age.

The third is the cost of shipping household goods to the island, which for a relocation is a one-off but substantial figure.

Each of those can exceed a year of the rent difference between two flats.

What Cost of Living Nassau Bahamas Comes Down To

Rent is high, and it is the number most people plan around. It is not the number that will surprise them.

The utility bill is the line that separates Nassau from every other city in this series. At about US$397.50 a month it is a second rent.

The second surprise is that moving out of the centre does not reliably save money. The cheaper housing is downtown.

Against that, wages are the highest recorded in this series. The ratio of rent to income is less punishing than in the small expat towns.

Read cost of living Nassau Bahamas as an import bill rather than a property market. What you pay for is distance from a mainland, and it shows up in the power bill first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does rent cost in Nassau?

A one-bedroom in the centre averages about US$1,490 a month. Outside the centre the same flat averages US$2,000, above the downtown figure.

Why are utility bills so high?

Utilities average US$397.50 a month, several times what the same bill costs in Central America. That single line is what reorders the budget.

What do people earn, and what does eating out cost?

The average net salary after tax is about US$3,356 a month. An inexpensive restaurant meal averages US$38.75.

How reliable are these figures?

The data rests on 11 contributors, so every figure here is indicative rather than precise.

World.title: Investing in Guatemala as a Foreigner in 2026: Two Taxes Just Went
World.content:
GUATEMALA · INVESTING

Key Facts — What it takes Investor residency requires at least US$100,000 in property, business capital or a deposit.

— How income is taxed Guatemala taxes only income arising inside the country, under Decreto 10-2012.

— The catch The two largest reliefs are 2026 decrees, and one of them has not taken effect yet.

— Inheritance tax Decree 6-2026 abolished it outright in March 2026, with gifts to close relatives exempt.

— Property tax Decree 18-2026 takes the residential rate to zero from 8 January 2027.

— What comes next Permanent residency needs five continuous years, and naturalisation more than ten.

Investing in Guatemala as a foreigner became materially cheaper in 2026. The reliefs are new enough to verify rather than assume.

Guatemala City. Residential property tax falls to zero from January 2027, and inheritance tax went in March 2026. Photo: "Guatemala, Guatemala City - panoramio" by randreu, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

Where This Fits

Investing in Guatemala as a foreigner rarely appears on shortlists next to Panama or Costa Rica. The tax position deserves a second look.

Guatemala taxes territorially, sets a low bar for investor residency, and removed two taxes during 2026. That combination is unusual in the region.

The qualification matters as much as the headline. Both removals arrived by decree this year, and one of them is not yet in force.

This piece sets out what applies now, what applies from January, and what still has to be confirmed.

The Investor Route

Investor residency requires a minimum of US$100,000. The threshold can be met by combined properties rather than a single purchase.

Qualifying assets are broad. They include residential or commercial real estate, capitalising a business, buying an existing business, or bank deposits earmarked for investment.

The framework sits in Decreto 44-2016, the migration code, with rules in Acuerdo Gubernativo 83-2019. Those rules were reformed by Acuerdo IGM-016-2025.

Applications go to the Instituto Guatemalteco de Migracion. Processing runs two to four months.

The permit is temporary and renewable, and its validity depends on the fee paid. One year costs US$200, two years US$300, and three to five years US$500.

After five continuous years of temporary residency an applicant can move to permanent status. Naturalisation comes later, after more than ten years as a resident.

Antigua Guatemala. Property is the most common qualifying asset for the investor residency route. Photo: "Agua Volcano in Antigua Guatemala" by Chad Davis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Territoriality Is the Foundation

Guatemala’s income tax law is Decreto 10-2012, the Ley de Actualizacion Tributaria. It taxes only income generated inside the country.

Tax residency is triggered by more than 183 days in a year, or by having your economic centre in Guatemala. Residency does not pull worldwide income into the net.

That distinction is the important one. In many territorial systems residency starts a clock or narrows the exemption, and here it does neither.

Foreign pensions, offshore dividends and international investment income stay outside the Guatemalan base. That holds regardless of how long someone has lived in the country.

For employment income earned locally, the scale is short. It is 5% up to 300,000 quetzales a year, about US$39,300, and 7% on the excess.

All conversions here use a rate of 7.64 to the dollar published by open.er-api.com on 18 September 2026. A standard deduction of 48,000 quetzales applies, about US$6,300, with an extra 3,024 quetzales, about US$400, for 2026.

What a Business Pays

A business chooses between two regimes, and the choice is consequential. The profits regime taxes net profit at a flat 25%.

It is filed annually with quarterly advance payments. The simplified regime works on gross receipts instead.

There the rate is 5% up to 30,000 quetzales a month, about US$3,930, and 7% on anything above. Filing is quarterly.

A small-taxpayer option exists below 150,000 quetzales a year, roughly US$19,600, at a flat 5%. That rate replaces both income tax and value added tax.

Standard value added tax is 12%. The choice of regime is not a formality.

For a low-margin business the gross-receipts regime can cost more than the profits regime. For a high-margin one it can cost considerably less.

The decision should be made on projected margin rather than on projected turnover. It is the most consequential filing choice a small business makes here.

Two Taxes That Just Went Away

Decree 6-2026 abolished inheritance tax outright in March 2026. Gifts to relatives within the second degree are exempt as well.

Decree 18-2026 sets the residential property tax rate to zero. That takes effect on 8 January 2027.

Commercial property keeps a tiered charge. It runs at three per thousand up to 500,000 quetzales of value, about US$65,400.

Between that and one million quetzales the rate is six per thousand. Above one million, roughly US$130,900, it is nine per thousand.

Taken together these are significant for anyone holding property across generations. They are also the newest part of the framework.

The practical point is the effective date. A residential purchase completed now still meets the old regime until January.

Guatemala City. Residential property tax falls to zero from January 2027 under a decree passed this year. Photo: "Guatemala, Guatemala City - panoramio" by randreu, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What Investment Income Pays

Capital gains are taxed at a flat 10%. That applies to gains arising inside Guatemala.

Dividends are charged at 5% for residents and 10% for non-residents. The gap is small by regional standards.

These rates are modest, and they sit on top of a base that excludes foreign income entirely. For a holder of local assets that is a light overall load.

The picture is different for anyone whose income is already foreign. For them Guatemala is not a tax play so much as a place the tax system ignores.

That distinction decides what kind of structure makes sense. Holding foreign assets through a Guatemalan company converts exempt income into taxable local income.

The usual mistake is to incorporate locally because residency was obtained locally. The two decisions are separate and should be taken separately.

What We Could Not Price

Four points are open and are not presented as settled here.

The first is whether Decree 18-2026 will take effect on schedule. It was passed this year and applies from January 2027.

The second is how the investor threshold is valued in practice, since property is assessed at purchase. The third is the current schedule of notarial and registry costs on a purchase.

The fourth is how the two 2026 decrees interact with existing assessments. New law of this kind usually takes a cycle before the practice settles.

None of that argues against the country. It argues for written confirmation rather than relying on a summary, including this one.

What Investing in Guatemala as a Foreigner Comes Down To

The entry price is low. US$100,000 across property or business capital is among the more accessible investor thresholds in the region.

The tax base is narrow and stays narrow. Residency does not expand it, which distinguishes Guatemala from its neighbours with three-year and eleven-year clocks.

Two meaningful taxes have been removed inside a single year. That is a real change and it is also a young one.

The sensible approach is to treat the pre-2026 rules as the baseline and the reliefs as confirmed extras. Confirm the effective dates before they form part of a purchase decision.

Read investing in Guatemala as a foreigner as a low bar with fresh paint. The structure underneath is stable, and the newest layer is still drying.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does investor residency in Guatemala require?

At least US$100,000 in property, business capital or a deposit.

How is income taxed?

Guatemala taxes only income arising inside the country, under Decreto 10-2012.

What changed on inheritance and property tax?

Decree 6-2026 abolished inheritance tax outright in March 2026, with gifts to close relatives exempt. Decree 18-2026 takes the residential property rate to zero from 8 January 2027.

How long until permanent residency or citizenship?

Permanent residency needs five continuous years, and naturalisation more than ten.

World.title: A Special Season to Rediscover Río Celeste
World.content:
Hideaway Río Celeste, a 5-star hotel that combines the beauty of nature with the allure and wellness of Río Celeste

Its Kantala restaurant is open to the public

For those who live in Costa Rica and are looking to explore and enjoy some of the country’s most iconic landscapes and natural wonders, you cannot miss the opportunity to visit the Bijagua area. This emblematic destination is home to Tenorio Volcano National Park and the breathtaking Río Celeste waterfall. It is also a habitat for the iconic tapir and a place of extraordinary natural beauty, perfect for relaxation and reconnecting with nature.

Located in this area is Hideaway Río Celeste, a 5-star hotel whose greatest highlight is its private trail leading to the river, where guests can enjoy a refreshing swim. In addition to accommodation, the hotel offers delicious and varied dining options, as well as a SPA featuring a sauna, steam room, and massage stations.

This is the perfect season for Costa Rican residents and domestic travelers to enjoy this paradise, as special rates are available from September 1 through October 31. This preferential rate allows guests to choose between staying in a Garden View Casita for US$245 plus VAT per night, or a Forest View Casita for US$315 plus VAT per night, with both options based on double occupancy.

The promotion also includes a full breakfast for two and a US$50 credit per reservation to be used at the new PRANA Spa, a wellness space offering exclusive therapies inspired by natural elements.

Gabriela Mora, General Manager of Hideaway Río Celeste, explains: “We want to invite Costa Ricans and residents to rediscover the extraordinary beauty we have within our own country. At Hideaway Río Celeste, we believe there is a unique sense of wellbeing that comes from combining comfort and genuine hospitality with the restorative power of the rainforest. Our wish is for every guest to slow down, reconnect and leave feeling renewed, while knowing that their experience takes place in an environment deeply committed to protecting the biodiversity that surrounds us.”

The experience is designed to restore balance between body, mind, and spirit through a comprehensive selection of activities and experiences. During their stay, visitors can embark on a guided nighttime walk to observe the fascinating local wildlife, participate in yoga classes surrounded by lush vegetation, enjoy sunrise birdwatching tours, take guided walks through the local flora, and explore the reserve’s private trails leading to a branch of Río Celeste.

The resort also offers facilities designed for relaxation and vitality, including a swimming pool, three outdoor jacuzzis, a Jungle GYM, and opportunities to explore local cuisine or unwind with holistic spa treatments.

The culinary offering is equally diverse. The hotel features Kantala Restaurant, specializing in fusion cuisine. Kantala is open to the public, and guests can make reservations to enjoy a delicious lunch or dinner. Mandarina Restaurant focuses on Asian cuisine. Café Romance offers coffee classes, fine pastries, and beverages. The property also features Cantina El Delirio, as well as a delicious BBQ experience by the pool.

This special promotion is valid exclusively for Costa Rican nationals and residents and is subject to availability. Those interested in making a reservation or obtaining more information can contact the hotel via WhatsApp at +506 6061-7193 or email reservations@riocelestehideaway.com.

World.title: Why the Same Costa Rica Highways Keep Washing Out
World.content:
Costa Rica has spent more than ₡86 billion patching and rebuilding roads after floods, slides, and storm damage — and the Comptroller General says too little of that money went into stopping the next washout. The Contraloría General de la República (CGR) used that figure to describe a pattern, not a one-off invoice.

After an emergency, crews go back to the same cut in the mountain or the same river crossing, put the asphalt down again, and wait for the next tropical wave. What often never happens, the audit says, is a serious look at risk: Is this slope going to go again? Does this culvert match the water that actually shows up in September? Should this stretch be redesigned instead of resurfaced?

A companion CGR review this week made the same point in broader language. Vital public infrastructure — roads, the power grid, reconstruction jobs, even fuel facilities — still runs in react mode when the climate hits. Resilience is talked about. It is not built in as a rule.

If you drive around Costa Rica, you already know the plot. Route 32 drops a hillside and Cambronero or a mountain side road closes overnight. A river takes a shoulder on the way to the beach and then the cones come out. The news alert goes to your phone and then a few weeks later the lane reopens, and the next wave is already on the IMN map.

The comptroller’s complaint is that this loop is now a budget line. Emergency rebuilds look urgent and visible. Drainage, slope work, and climate-risk studies look slow and boring — until the same kilometer fails again and the bill is larger than the first repair. None of this means every pothole is a scandal. Storms will keep tearing at a steep, wet country. What the CGR is flagging is the missing middle step: measure the risk before the storm, then spend on the fix that lasts.

For anyone who lives here visits us, here’s the point. Rainy-season travel plans still need a Plan B on the big corridors — 1, 27, 32, and the South Pacific laterals — because the state is still better at rebuilding after the slide than at preventing it. For taxpayers, ₡86 billion is the price tag on that habit.

In the end, Costa Rica is not only fighting the weather but also paying twice when it treats the weather as a surprise.

World.title: Benque Viejo comes alive with National Pride as students celebrate Belize’s 45th Independence
World.content:
Benque Viejo comes alive with National Pride as students celebrate Belize’s 45th Independence

By Zoila Palma: The streets of Benque Viejo del Carmen came alive today with a vibrant display of patriotism as students, teachers and parents took part in a colorful parade celebrating Belize’s Independence. With red, white and blue filling the streets, the event showcased the creativity, national pride and civic spirit of young Belizeans.

Students marched proudly in a variety of patriotic displays, including uniforms inspired by the Belize Defence Force (BDF), reflecting the aspirations of young people who dream of serving and protecting Belize and its sovereignty.

Others rode bicycles creatively decorated in the national colors, while colorful dance groups brought energy and excitement to the parade.

The parade also featured posters and displays highlighting Belize’s currency, national symbols and other elements that represent the country’s identity.

Students proudly showcased the keel-billed toucan and other national symbols, while creative costumes and presentations celebrated Belize’s rich culture, history and natural beauty.

Parents and teachers joined the celebrations, cheering on the students and adding to the festive atmosphere throughout Benque.

Mayor Jorge Rosales encouraged the students to continue demonstrating civic pride and good citizenship, while also expressing pride in their identity as Belizeans and being proud Benqueños.

Area Representative Miguel Guerra also commended the students for their patriotic display, emphasizing that they represent the future of Belize. He expressed pride in seeing young Belizeans celebrate their country and demonstrate their love for Belize through creativity, participation and national pride.

The vibrant parade served as another reminder that Belize’s Independence celebrations are not only about honoring the nation’s past, but also about inspiring the next generation to value, protect and contribute to the country they will one day lead.

World.title: Sea of red, white and blue: students across Belize celebrate National Pride
World.content:
Sea of red, white and blue: students across Belize celebrate National Pride

By Zoila Palma: Schools across Belize came alive today with a vibrant display of patriotism as students took part in a nationwide school rally celebrating the country’s culture, identity, national symbols and natural beauty.

Dressed in red, white and blue, students proudly waved Belizean flags, wore patriotic hats and Belize-themed shirts, and carried colorful banners showcasing the nation’s national symbols.

Some schools brought Belize’s wildlife to life through creative costumes, including the keel-billed toucan and various marine animals, highlighting the rich biodiversity that makes Belize unique.

In Benque Viejo del Carmen, Breaking Belize News journalist Zoila Palma was on the ground to cover the celebrations, where the spirit was vibrant and proudly Belizean.

Students, teachers and members of the community joined in the festivities, transforming the streets into a colorful celebration of national pride.

The creative displays also offered a reminder of Belize’s natural treasures, from its tropical forests and iconic wildlife to its marine ecosystems and diverse sea life.

Through their costumes, banners and performances, students demonstrated that patriotism can also be expressed by appreciating and protecting the country’s natural resources.

Across Belize, the school rallies provided students with an opportunity to celebrate what makes the nation special as Belize continues its 45th Independence Anniversary celebrations.

World.title: Police officer reported missing from Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Police officer reported missing from Orange Walk Town

By Breaking Belize News Staff:Officials are asking the public for assistance in locating 24 year old Kenyon Barrow, a Belizean police officer from Orange Walk Town who has been reported missing.

According to a missing person notice issued by Crime Stoppers Belize, Barrow was last seen on Saturday, September 12, 2026.

He is described as being of Creole descent, with a dark complexion and approximately 5 feet 6 inches tall.

No information has been provided on what Barrow was wearing when he was last seen or the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

Crime Stoppers Belize is urging anyone who may have seen Barrow or who has information that could assist in locating him to come forward.

Information can be provided anonymously by calling Crime Stoppers at 922, using the P3 Tips app or contacting the nearest police station.

World.title: IOM donates ATV, radios and field equipment to Belize Defence Force
World.content:
IOM donates ATV, radios and field equipment to Belize Defence Force

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Defence Force has received a new package of equipment from the International Organization for Migration aimed at strengthening field operations and border security capabilities.

The initial contribution includes one All Terrain Vehicle, portable field stoves and radios.

According to the Belize Defence Force, the equipment will improve mobility, communication and logistical support for personnel carrying out operations in the field.

The ATV is expected to give soldiers better access to areas where conventional vehicles may face difficulties, while the portable stoves will support personnel during extended deployments.

The radios are also expected to strengthen coordination between teams operating in remote areas.

The Belize Defence Force says the donation represents the first phase of support from the International Organization for Migration, with additional equipment expected to follow.

Officials say the continued partnership will contribute to efforts to strengthen border protection, security operations and support for personnel working in the field.

The Belize Defence Force thanked the International Organization for Migration for what it described as a meaningful contribution to Belize’s security forces.

World.title: Motor Solutions offers ZXAUTO GrandLion pickup at special $92,000 price
World.content:
Motor Solutions offers ZXAUTO GrandLion pickup at special $92,000 price

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Motor Solutions LLP is promoting the ZXAUTO GrandLion, a full size 4×4 pickup aimed at drivers looking for power, technology and comfort in one package.

The GrandLion is currently being offered at a special price of $92,000, with all duties and taxes included.

The pickup comes equipped with a 2.3 litre turbo diesel engine paired with an 8 speed automatic transmission, giving drivers a combination designed for both work and everyday driving.

Other features include coil spring suspension, a 360 degree view camera and a modern cabin with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity.

The GrandLion also comes 4×4 ready and includes a three year warranty.

Motor Solutions says the vehicle is suited for job sites, long distance driving and weekend adventures, while still offering the technology and comfort expected from a modern pickup.

Interested customers can schedule a test drive or request additional information by contacting 610 3398 or 626 7439.

World.title: BTL not worried about Starlink competition, CEO explains why
World.content:
BTL not worried about Starlink competition, CEO explains why

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Telemedia Limited CEO Ivan Tesucum says the company does not view satellite internet provider Starlink as a direct competitor to its internet services in Belize.

Speaking in an interview with 7 News Belize, Tesucum described Starlink as a “complementary service” and pointed to BTL’s extensive fibre network as one of the company’s key advantages.

Tesucum said BTL has more than 2,000 miles of fibre infrastructure distributed throughout Belize and argued that fibre technology allows the company to deliver high speed connectivity directly to homes.

“We see Starlink as a complementary service, not a competing service,” Tesucum told 7 News Belize.

The BTL CEO explained that Starlink relies on satellite technology, while BTL’s terrestrial fibre network provides a different method of delivering internet connectivity.

Tesucum said BTL’s network passes more than 100,000 homes across the country and maintained that the company’s internet prices remain affordable.

His comments come as satellite internet has expanded the options available to Belizean consumers, particularly in locations where traditional telecommunications infrastructure may be less accessible.

BTL, however, is positioning its fibre infrastructure as a central part of its strategy as the company moves into its next phase of development.

The company recently reported a record $36.9 million net profit for the 2025 to 2026 fiscal year and says its future plans include strengthening network reliability and accelerating technology adoption.

Interview credit: 7 News Belize.

World.title: BTL reports record $36.9 million net profit as shareholders approve dividend
World.content:
BTL reports record $36.9 million net profit as shareholders approve dividend

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Belize Telemedia Limited says it recorded a $36.9 million net profit for the 2025 to 2026 fiscal year, marking what the company described as a record financial performance.

The results were announced as BTL held its 20th Annual General Meeting on September 17.

According to the company, net profit has increased by 581 percent from $5.4 million at the beginning of its five year strategic period.

Earnings per share also increased from $0.07 to $0.70, while cash and cash equivalents grew to $62.8 million.

BTL reported that its long term debt declined significantly over the same period, falling from $77.8 million to $15.6 million.

Shareholders also approved a $0.37 per share dividend for the fiscal year that ended March 31, 2026.

The telecommunications company says it has expanded its operations during the past five years and now operates more than 180 mobile sites nationwide. Its portfolio includes mobile, broadband, fixed telephony, television and financial technology services.

Chief Executive Officer Ivan Tesucum said the financial results reflect progress made in strengthening and transforming the company.

Looking ahead, BTL says its next strategic phase will focus on network reliability, operational efficiency and increased adoption of technologies including artificial intelligence, automation, cloud services, cybersecurity and advanced analytics.

The sale comes just days before Belize celebrates its 45th anniversary of Independence on September 21.

With gatherings, cookouts and family meals expected throughout the long Independence weekend, the promotion gives shoppers an opportunity to stock their refrigerators and freezers while taking advantage of reduced prices.
