World.title: Sydney v Fremantle player ratings: Brightest stars and stunning moments on a night of agony and ecstasy
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Sydney v Fremantle player ratings: Brightest stars and stunning moments on a night of agony and ecstasy

Loading

Some fairytales just don’t come true. After the events of past month in Melbourne, the second-on-the-ladder Swans couldn’t have seemed further away from another grand final berth. But what happened since – despite missing a host of their best players after they were handed season-ending suspensions by the Swans for failing to meet the club’s standards after their round 23 win over Essendon – has been nothing short of remarkable. On Friday night, they finished just 13 points shy of the decider as the Dockers roared home. Marc McGowan (Sydney) and Steve Barrett (Fremantle) run their eye over every player in from the preliminary final at the SCG.



Shai Bolton and Isaiah Dudley celebrate a crucial goal in their thrilling win over Sydney. Getty Images Sydney (2) Hayden McLean: Relieved Brodie Grundy in the ruck and comfortably won those stints against Mason Cox. His intercept marking was also a feature. 6/10 (4) Brodie Grundy: Grundy took the first-half honours against Luke Jackson and was a key reason the Swans started so well, but the star Docker rose to the occasion after half-time. It was a great ruck battle. 6.5/10



(6) Logan McDonald: McDonald was excellent again, after kicking six goals in the Swans’ qualifying final drubbing of the Lions. He was often Sydney’s deepest forward and constantly presented, and was rewarded with a game-high three goals. 8/10 Logan McDonald loomed as a potential match winner for the Swans. AFL Photos (8) James Rowbottom: Had a series of defensive efforts that led to Angus Sheldrick’s third-quarter goal and there is never any question on his effort. 6.5/10 (9) Jesse Dattoli: A quiet night for the second-year Swan, who otherwise grabbed his opportunity late in the season. 1/10 (11) Tom Papley: Papley was sensational in the opening half, whether kicking or setting up goals, executing diving smothers or stealing handballs. But he would have loved a better return than 1.3. 8/10



(12) Angus Sheldrick: Sheldrick is as tough as nails and kicked a goal in the third quarter, but won only 12 disposals. 6/10 Related Article AFL 2026 Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides (13) Jai Serong: Who would have picked the ex-Hawk at the start of the year to be a centre-bounce midfielder in a preliminary final? Serong’s been a bargain recruit and was a strong performer on the night. 7/10 (15) Sam Wicks: Wicks won enough of the ball, but was a bit sloppy with his disposals, and wasn’t quite as good defensively as usual. 5/10 (16) Braeden Campbell: Started the game strongly, including a terrific snap for a goal, and seemed headed for a big night, but faded dramatically before getting a few touches late. 4/10



(21) Errol Gulden: Had an early turnover that gifted Fremantle a goal, but quickly returned to his dominant self that extended his purple patch. Gulden’s 36 disposals were seven more than any other player, but probably wasn’t quite as damaging as usual. 8.5/10 (24) Dane Rampe: Returned to the captaincy after Callum Mills’ ACL rupture, and typically gave his all in what may have been his last game. Copped a huge fend-off from Patrick Voss in the last quarter before the Docker’s key goal. 6/10 Joel Hamling and Mason Cox to toe-to-toe. Getty Images (25) Billy Cootee: Had a second-quarter handball blunder that almost cost the Swans a goal, but was part of the Swans’ ground-wide defensive effort. 3/10 (27) Justin McInerney: One of many Swans who faded badly in the final term, picking up just one of his 14 disposals. Sydney rolled the dice in selecting him for his first match since June, and he was OK without doing a great deal. 5/10



(29) Joel Hamling: The premiership-winning Bulldog and ex-Docker grabbed a few intercept marks and spent time on Jye Amiss and Voss. Can hold his head up high. 7/10 Tom McCartin keeps a close eye on Patrick Voss. AFL Photos (30) Tom McCartin: Big moment early with a goal-saving tackle on Voss and finished with a game-high 11 intercept possessions, which sums up how strong he was aerially. Conceded a goal to Jackson with a no-look hack kick in his defensive 50. 7.5/10 (32) Harry Kyle: Kyle did not look out of place down back and looks a promising prospect who will play further afield in the future. 6/10 (33) Caiden Cleary: Cleary’s turnover off a risky corridor kick when the game was in the balance late could have been incredibly costly. His tackling pressure was good, but didn’t win a heap of the Sherrin. 5/10



(34) Matt Roberts: Roberts was a solid performer without having a major impact. He has played much better games than this. 6/10 James Rowbottom and Charlie Curnow were left heartbroken with the result. AFL Photos (35) Charlie Curnow: It was not Charlie’s night. Outside of a brilliant hanger over Oscar McDonald, which preceded his sole goal, Curnow failed to have his usual impact when the Swans needed him most. 2/10 (40) Tom Hanily: Did his best work in the first quarter, when his repeated strong efforts were rewarded with an opportunistic goal. But he had only four touches after quarter-time. 3/10 (43) Lewis Melican: Lost contact with Mason Cox in the final term when the ex-Pie marked and kicked Fremantle ahead, then dropped a mark before Isaiah Dudley’s sealing goal. Was solid in the first three quarters. 4/10



(44) Jake Lloyd: Lloyd did as he has throughout his career, providing strong rebound out of defence and generally using the ball well. 7/10 View post on X Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: After seeing off Oisin Mullin’s tag a week ago, Serong got away from Rowbottom, before Sydney dispensed with the run-with role at half-time. The lion-hearted midfielder misfired with 0.3 but set others up with his 28 disposals and 10 clearances. 7.5/10



(5) Heath Chapman: His aerial game was sturdy, and he used the footy neatly off half-back, aside from one obviously costly moment, which resulted in a third quarter goal which sparked Sydney’s resurgence. 6/10 (6) Jordan Clark: Had 490 metres gained, with his customary dash out of defence, but that was offset by some imprecise use of the footy and below-par decision-making. 5/10 (8) Andrew Brayshaw: A typically industrious display in the centre square. Brayshaw’s disposal was a tad off in the preliminary final heat, but his heart and head – covered in blood approaching three-quarter-time – could never be questioned, amassing a team-high 29 touches. 7/10 View post on X (9) Luke Jackson: A week after destroying Geelong, Jackson was always going to be in for a more challenging night against Grundy. Still, “the Unicorn” narrowly took the individual honours, booting two important goals and letting Grundy know about it. 7/10



Related Article AFL 2026 How ‘a pair of footy nerds’ unlocked Shai Bolton’s X-factor (10) Shai Bolton: Constantly hurried in the first half and unsighted in the third term, Bolton came alive in the fourth. He booted two final-quarter goals, his shift from midfield to deep forward proving a masterstroke. He also laid eight tackles. A cameo by his standards, but what a cameo. 7.5/10 (13) Luke Ryan: Generated rebound out of defensive 50 and rarely wasted the footy. He was important down the stretch and went at 94 per cent disposal efficiency. 7/10 (16) Murphy Reid: That trademark craftiness, creativity and poise – all of it was absent in the first half. Reid was under the pump against Sydney’s hounding pressure, before bouncing back to his best with some key, deft touches after the break. 7/10 They’ve done it: Murphy Reid, Caleb Serong and Hayden Young are through to a grand final. Getty Images



(17) Judd McVee: Had the challenging task of minding Papley and, after a more than rough start, held his own. 6/10 (18) Mason Cox: Won his share of hitouts but was unimpactful around the ground ... until his moment came. The big fella’s strong mark and goal put the Dockers in front in the final term. 5/10 (20) Patrick Voss: Talk about a mixed bag. He’d conceded three free kicks by the time he finally registered his first touch, after the half-time siren. Then in the second half, he showed why he belongs on the big stage. Voss produced the fend-off of the year with a vicious “don’t argue” on Rampe, before kicking a massive goal during the fourth-quarter barrage. 5/10 View post on X (21) Oscar McDonald: Had the job on the other McDonald and conceded three goals, before coughing up another when matched up on Curnow. He started well, but faded considerably. 3.5/10



(23) Karl Worner: His pressure across half-back was important and his ball use was solid, if not as pristine as it was in the semi-final. 5.5/10 (24) Jye Amiss: He jagged a brilliant, team-lifting left-foot goal early in the third term, but generally found the going tough against Sydney’s backline. 4.5/10 (25) Alex Pearce: Kept Curnow largely under the thumb for the large stretches they were matched up on each other. The skipper was quiet offensively, but his defensive efforts were sound. 5/10 (26) Hayden Young: A magnificent third term, capped by a stunning goal on the three-quarter-time bell, sparked Fremantle. Young was involved in most of Fremantle’s scoring chains, whether rotating through the middle or lurking across half-forward. You’d argue his goal was the biggest kick in Dockers history. Outstanding. 8.5/10 View post on X



(28) Neil Erasmus: Kicked the first goal of the night with a smart snap and was solid on his wing, aside from a few shaky moments. 6/10 (32) Michael Frederick: Failed to get a possession in the first quarter, before kicking a goal in the second. His outside run and tackling pressure were important in the second half. Twin brother Martin will line up for Sturt in this Sunday’s SANFL grand final at Adelaide Oval. It could be a big week coming up for the Frederick family. 6/10 (34) Corey Wagner: The experienced utility provided contest and run. He stood up in the first half when not many of his mates did. 6.5/10 (35) Josh Treacy: Booted four on McCartin the last time these sides met, but lowered his colours this time. His usually powerful contested marking was down. Goalless, beaten, but grand final-bound. 3.5/10 View post on X



(39) Sam Switkowski: He supplied forward pressure and got involved during the comeback after being well held for the first three quarters. Has one more game left in him. 5/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: The little goalsneak’s ball use was sketchy at times, but he booted two majors, including the sealer at the death. Dudley found more of the footy than usual too, which is always a good sign. 7/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: Played predominantly on the wing and was a consistent four-quarter contributor. 7/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Swans’ rollercoaster month ends with heartbreak after Fremantle fightback
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Swans’ rollercoaster month ends with heartbreak after Fremantle fightback Vince Rugari September 18, 2026 — 10:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Sydney Swans have put their supporters through a vast range of emotions within the past month. On Friday night, they served up a new one: heartbreak. Classic, traditional sporting trauma. It turns out you don’t need to be at Optus Stadium to experience “Wharfie Time”. It doesn’t have to be a Fremantle home game for the purple haze to suddenly descend and dull the senses. It can happen anywhere, to anyone. Loading Fears that the Swans had “played their grand final” a fortnight ago were totally unfounded. From the outset of this classic preliminary final on Friday night, the Swans were rabid, aggressive, relentless, playing like their lives depended on it. Again. If their first effort didn’t stick, there was a second, third, fourth, fifth to follow. They knew where they wanted to go and wanted to get there in a hurry. Whatever concoction sustained them in that qualifying final against the Brisbane Lions, there was more of it left … until, at some point in the final quarter, the punch bowl was empty. They were out of juice. The Dockers noticed, and they went to work.



“It looked a little bit like that,” said Swans coach Dean Cox. “This time of the year, you can’t give a team any momentum, and they took it.” For three quarters, the Dockers were nowhere near it. Everyone knew they were the better side considering Sydney’s long list of absentees, but the Swans played like the better side, and the scoreboard reflected it. Yet they had left the door ever so slightly ajar for Freo, hitting the post four times and letting a number of other key opportunities slip, particularly in the first quarter. Swans players Tom Papley, Errol Gulden and James Rowbottom after Friday’s loss to Fremantle. via Getty Images Hayden Young’s goal for Fremantle on the three-quarter-time siren reduced Sydney’s margin to a manageable 21 points and restored in themselves a modicum of belief. So who pushed the “Wharfie Time” button? You can take your pick, but it may well have been Patrick Voss, aka “the Prancing Pony”, who had hitherto been playing like a donkey. His only possession for the entire first half was a set shot after the half-time siren which did not even make the distance.





The Swans tried to hold on throughout the 10-minute arm wrestle that followed Voss’ goal, but they were cooked, and they knew it. Goals from Shai Bolton, Mason Cox and Isaiah Dudley finished them off, and the pain was etched all over the faces and bodies of Sydney’s players when the final siren eventually sounded and put them all out of their misery. “I’m just extremely proud of everyone uniting, galvanising and coming together to try and get our season to the last game, and we fell short,” Cox said. Related Article AFL 2026 Dockers storm into grand final after SCG thriller, but star of the show calls his goal ‘a fluke’ “It’s hard to say it’s a missed opportunity when you play a really good footy team. Prelims are big games and there’s a lot at stake because there’s a grand final next week. We missed the opportunity to take those moments to put ourselves in a grand final. The older players, they certainly understand that they don’t just come around every year. Some of the young ones, they just [think], ‘How good is it to be a part of it, and I’m learning everything, and I’ll grow from playing in them,’ but they’re hard to get to.” So the ride ends here. After a month defined by the scandal at the Pullman Hotel and the on- and off-field fallout, the Swans can be immensely proud of the way their remaining players have gallantly defended the club’s colours and culture, as well as disappointed that it couldn’t take them all the way. They will never know how far they could have gone if “the Pullman Five” had simply behaved themselves that night, and that hurts, too.



What happens next for those players remains to be seen, and in any case will be largely determined by Victoria Police. But during their absence, the Swans found something else: Proof that whatever this club is supposed to stand for is bigger than any individuals, and sturdy enough to survive the damage they caused. Now they can try and build again. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Mounting calls for venues to cancel Ben Cousins speaking tour
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWADomestic violence Mounting calls for venues to cancel Ben Cousins speaking tour Hannah Murphy September 19, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former West Coast Eagles player and convicted domestic violence perpetrator Ben Cousins is facing growing calls to cancel his ongoing speaking tour dates, among concerns he has failed to fully take accountability for abusing his former partner. Ben Cousins carries the 2006 Premiership Cup around the field with former teammates in 2026. Getty The calls come after the George Hotel in Ballarat earlier this week opted to cancel Cousins’ tour date, saying the venue had failed to consider the former West Coast Eagle player’s previous domestic violence convictions when booking him to speak. “We recognise that decisions about who is given a public platform carry particular significance for women, victim-survivors and others affected by domestic violence,” the hotel said in a statement. “We understand why members of our community have questioned what this event represents and whether their experiences and concerns were adequately considered.”



Cousins has a number of scheduled dates for his speaking tour, which is being organised by local business Z Entertainment. Cousins has been convicted of persistently stalking his former partner and violence restraining order breaches. On October 3, he is scheduled to speak with former Richmond Tigers player Dustin Martin at the Camfield pub outside Optus Stadium at an event billing the pair as “two of the greatest to ever play the game”. The Camfield across from Optus Stadium. “Ben Cousins. The PRINCE: One of the most electrifying talents the game has ever seen… for the FIRST TIME EVER these icons share the stage and take you inside the game and their personal lives – the glory, the grind, the highs, the heartbreaks, and the moments we’ll never forget,” the  for the event reads.



Related Article AFL 2024 Ben Cousins won’t be part of the football hall of fame’s class of ’24 This masthead does not suggest any wrongdoing by Martin. The Camfield declined to comment about its decision to host the event, although the Women’s Legal Service of WA director Jennie Gray said the venue had a chance to make an impactful decision. “I think we absolutely need to follow the precedent that has been set - rightly set - by the George Hotel, and cancel his speaking engagement at the Camfield,” she said. “We need to think really carefully about who we’re putting on these platforms and the message that it sends to community. What does platforming Ben Cousins say to victim survivors who are considering escaping or reporting family violence?



“We absolutely don’t have to offer him a microphone. And maybe the microphone that we should offer Ben Cousins is one at a man’s behaviour change program.” WA’s Centre for Women’s Safety and Wellbeing’s Dr Alison Evans, who recently praised the decision to take down disgraced AFL footballer and abuser Nicky Winmar’s statue from outside Optus Stadium, said the George Hotel’s move was an important step forward. “It was very heartening to see the George Hotel be so responsive to their local community’s expectations that the Hotel be part of our collective efforts to end violence against women and children in our communities,” she said. WA Centre for Women’s Safety and Wellbeing chief executive officer Alison Evans. “There are disturbingly high numbers of women and children experiencing family, domestic and sexual violence in all communities across Australia, including in the Perth metropolitan areas.



“It’s vital that we all take this issue very seriously given the fear and harm that is caused and the lives that are lost through domestic violence homicide and suicide. We must stand together on this issue. Related Article Courts Nicky Winmar’s statue removed from Optus Stadium after assault conviction “It’s important to recognise that men who are harming and frightening women and children can change their behaviours if they are genuinely committed to doing this. But this will require their time and effort and getting the right help. “Ostracising men using violence is not the best way to prevent them from continuing to cause harm to others. “But public figures need to accept that if they are using or have used violence against women and children then the community can’t allow further harm to be caused to their victims or to other victim-survivors by celebrating them or giving them public platforms.”



The Camfield declined to comment, and directed queries to Z Entertainment. “We recognise the significant impact to victims and the wider community and condemn these actions. We encourage and support passionate advocacy for victims, and on behalf of victims, of domestic violence,” a Z Entertainment spokesperson said. “His unfolding journey is one that inspires and will be shared during the event from a heart of gratitude and incredible humility, providing genuine, tangible hope to many. We do not celebrate past indiscretions, rather provide a platform for insight to Ben’s journey and an opportunity for all that attend to learn from the experiences of another. Ben Cousins struggled with drug issues during and after his football career. AFL Photos “Ben has regrets and acknowledges he hasn’t always presented his best self, often referring to the number of chances he’s been afforded as ‘more than I’d give’.



The spokesperson said the promotion of these events, and the content within, are not a celebration of indiscretions but an insight to this incredibly unique journey showing how high-performance sport and serious personal issues can coexist. “However, there’s a vast difference from where he’s at - starting to talk about his indiscretions -to positioning him on a pedestal as the icon for rehabilitation, providing advice and guidance – the additional significant pressure aligned to this position could not be foreseen as beneficial. “We manage Ben’s engagements and content aligned to his journey, which continues to evolve.” However, Gray said they had yet to seen Cousins take any meaningful public accountability for his actions, and had often framed his domestic violence convictions as a byproduct of his drug use. “He does have a history of family and domestic violence, including instilling significant fear in his ex-partner through stalking - I’m not sure if he has taken responsibility or accountability for that,” she said.

World.title: These laws were designed to ban thugs from Perth nightspots. Have they worked?
World.content:
NationalWAPolice These laws were designed to ban thugs from Perth nightspots. Have they worked? Hamish Hastie September 19, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Powers to ban violent offenders from some of Perth’s busiest night spots have helped improve public perception of safety in those areas. However, the state’s ombudsman also found they were “error-ridden” and have disproportionately targeted Aboriginal people and the homeless. Police have used their powers to ban individuals from party precincts for anti-social, violent or threatening behaviour under the State’s new Protected Entertainment Precincts laws. Nine News Perth. WA Ombudsman Bevan Warner’s first probe into WA’s Protected Entertainment Precinct laws has found information blockages between WA Police and the law’s lead agency – Racing, Gaming and Liquor – had resulted in some serious offenders not being served their bans. He also found fears held before the laws passed in 2022 by groups like Aboriginal Legal Service WA that the bans, known as exclusion orders, would be heavily skewed toward vulnerable groups had been realised.



What are PEPs? The PEP laws were passed following an unprovoked one-punch attack which killed Giuseppe Raco in Northbridge in July 2020. Precincts the laws apply to include nightlife areas including Perth, Northbridge, Fremantle, Hillarys, Mandurah and Scarborough. The powers give police and the Director of Liquor Licensing the power to ban people committing violent acts in a PEP for as little as a day to six months for short-term exclusion orders, or to up to five years for adults and two years for juveniles for automatic and extended orders. ‘Error-prone’ methods at heart of problems



Warner found there were violent offenders who should have been given automatic exclusion orders, but weren’t, because of Racing, Gaming and Liquor’s “error-prone” method of identifying them. He said staff did not have access to police systems and had to manually gather information through exchanges with police or by checking publicly available court records. “Our monitoring also found several individuals who appear to meet the legal threshold to be automatically excluded but who had not been flagged by RGL at the end of the monitoring period,” he said. Warner also found six instances where Racing, Gaming and Liquor incorrectly notified people as automatic excluded offenders despite them not meeting legal criteria. “These errors are problematic because automatic excluded offenders are denied the right to seek a review of their status, and their freedom of movement was wrongly limited,” he said.



“The rate of omission and misclassification suggests a systemic problem rather than isolated errors and we cannot be confident that all automatic excluded offenders were excluded, when they should have been.” On short-term notices, Warner said they found instances where they were issued despite not meeting the threshold and instances where police guidelines were not applied appropriate, including when individual circumstances were ignored. Warner said he found six instances of short-term orders being issued for conduct outside a PEP area which results in five of them being quickly revoked. “Any new scheme will have teething problems, but it is important these weaknesses are fixed,” Warner said. Aboriginal people and the homeless subject to more bans



Warner’s probe showed the fears held by groups including the Aboriginal Legal Service back in 2022 that vulnerable groups would be subjected to bans more frequently had come to fruition. Related Article Police Why the ‘thug’ life could see you banned from Northbridge The PEP laws were applied disproportionately to Aboriginal people, who were the recipients of 41.6 per cent of short-term exclusion orders, despite representing 3.3 per cent of the population. “Aboriginal people informed us that the scheme also compounds prior trauma, making them feel less safe which further undermines their trust in public institutions,” Warner said. Homeless people made up 20 per cent of all approved short-term exclusion orders.



Warner cited a survey of 1000 people which found more people said they felt “safer” rather than “less safe” in PEP areas (25 per cent compared to 16 per cent), and more people said the areas felt “more welcoming” than “less welcoming” (41.9 per cent compared to 13.5 per cent). He also cited police stats that showed a lower growth of reported offences in PEP areas but said this data was “inconclusive” and may not be entirely attributable to the PEP laws. “While it is good that some people feel safer and more welcome, the available evidence does not show those changes can be attributed solely to the PEP scheme,” Warner said, pointing to other improvements in the precincts like better lighting and CCTV. A spokesman for the government said the PEP laws have been effective but said the overrepresentation of Aboriginal people and other vulnerable groups was a concern and “warrants careful attention.” “The Police Minister and the Police Commissioner have spoken about how exclusion orders can be applied consistently, giving consideration to issues raised in the report,” he said.



“The Cook Labor Government will carefully consider the report’s recommendations and work to strengthen the scheme so it remains both effective in improving safety and fair for all Western Australians.” Editor's pick One Nation One Nation’s WA leader says they can’t vet everyone after alleged neo-Nazi hands out how-to-vote cards Automatic exclusion orders apply to anyone who commits a violent offence in a PEP area, like murder, manslaughter, assault, rape, and drink-spiking. In three years, 47 automatic exclusion orders were issued – 41 of those because of an offence committed in Perth or Northbridge. WA Police made 737 applications for short-term exclusion orders in the period and 77 per cent were approved by a senior police officer.



The number of short-term orders increased dramatically over the past three years from 137 in 2024 to 365 in 2025 including 190 involving weapons which Warner said was likely attributable to knife-wanding laws which came into effect at the end of 2024. Warner made seven recommendations including allowing the Director of Liquor Licensing to have access to relevant WA Police information to identify offenders subject to an automatic notice quickly. He also recommended police should always consider individual circumstances when deciding to seeking a short-term order.

World.title: Under new (yet old) management, Lady of Ro is a throwback to how restaurants used to be
World.content:
Review Eating outSubiaco Under new (yet old) management, Lady of Ro is a throwback to how restaurants used to be Straight-shooting Greek flavours, an upbeat room, BYO: this buzzy Subiaco eatery has all the makings of your new favourite restaurant. Max Veenhuyzen September 19, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

1 / 4 Octopus: a Hellenic classic. Matt O'Donohue 2 / 4 There are no “deconstructed” dishes at Lady of Ro. Matt O'Donohue 3 / 4 Lady of Ro’s magnificent soufra. Matt O'Donohue 4 / 4 Lady of Ro is a throwback to what restaurants used to be like. Matt O'Donohue Previous Slide Next Slide 14.5 / 20 How we score Lady of Ro Greek$$$$ We need to talk about the soufra at Lady of Ro: the continental European restaurant in Subiaco that resurfaced in May after a short hiatus. We need to talk about those wispy ruffles of crisp phyllo pastry. We need to talk about the comforting, just-sweet-enough custard that gets poured into the cake and soaks into said ruffles like Brylcreem into hair. And we need to talk about how these two buds, ably assisted by the sweetness of crushed pistachio and cinnamon sugar, bring the best out of each other, Rocky Balboa and Apollo Creed style.



Lady of Ro’s Dan Goodsell and Paul Zammit. Matt O'Donohue But most important of all, if we’re going to lionise one of Perth’s most high-profile cakes, then we also need to talk about Despina Tanner: the Greek-Australian cook that introduced our city to the joys of this twice-baked custard pie via landmark addresses such as John Street Cafe, Boucla and, of course, Lady of Ro. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Do you remember eating Tanner’s soufra – or airy chocolate ricotta cake; or Sicilian-style apple tart; or any of her other baked glories – at these famous places? Then I think you’ll appreciate the current iteration of Lady of Ro: two animated, tightly packed rooms that are low of light, but high of volume thanks to guests that are absorbed in conversation rather than their screens. The kitchen gives it to us straight. Dishes are not deconstructed, reconstructed or obstructed, but as advertised.



Related Article Good Food hat 15 / 20 Review The timeless appeal and polish of Balthazar Saganaki is fried handmade haloumi hit with honey. Crisp and floury potatoes are lifted with the intriguing fragrance of za’atar. Fast-moving staff hustle and bustle. In short, today’s Lady of Ro has much in common with the neighbourhood eatery that Tanner and her husband Brian unveiled in 2014. An operation in thrall with the algorithm this is not. Rather, this is a place that calls to mind what restaurants were like back in the day, largely because it’s being run by Jaycinta Zammit, Paul Zammit and Daniel Goodsell: hospitality veterans that know back-in-the-day very well. (The Tanners, meanwhile, have left the building and now live on Kastellorizo: the Greek Island Despina and most of Perth’s Greek community can trace their lineage to.)



Wise heads know not to mess with winning formulas. Here, that means family-style dining and retaining established dishes that management should probably scribble on blackboard menus in paint rather than chalk. Good-sized octopus is slow-cooked in olive oil and then blackened on the kitchen’s hardworking charcoal grill. Braised lamb shoulder is another benefactor of the twice-cooked treatment and rightly considered another signature. (The chook, sadly, was overcooked and under seasoned on my visit.) Lady of Ro’s Greek heritage remains strong. Matt O'Donohue While Lady of Ro identifies as a continental restaurant, the site’s Greek heritage remains strong.



Although Hellenic cuisine is synonymous with lamb and seafood, many of my highlights at Lady of Ro were plant-based in nature. The char and murky sweetness of well-charred cabbage suggests vegetables benefit just as much as any protein from the two-stage braise and grill treatment. Terrific dips make already pleasing pita bread even more desirable. The meagre sounding “village eggplant” hints little at the rush of savour unlocked by grilling whole eggplants and red capsicums raw-dog on coals and combining them with the honeyed sweetness of slow-cooked garlic. The fava dip, meanwhile, is made not of dried broadbeans, but yellow chickpeas patiently cooked till they surrender into a dense, creamy vortex of flavour. Related Article Exclusive An ambitious Margaret River cellar door and dining room opens this month. Here’s what’s on the menu



While current management have retained a lot of the OG’s DNA, they’ve also found moments to inject themselves into the story. Urns, tablecloths, plates and other heirlooms from Jaycinta’s Italian grandmother feel right at home in this homely space. Her husband, meanwhile, has been quietly streamlining dishes. (While Paul hasn’t directly referenced his Maltese heritage, his hefty gogges – think of them as Greco ricotta gnocchi – were inspired by his school days in Sydney’s multicultural Redfern and swapping lunch boxes with the other kids.) Although seasoning can occasionally drift, generosity is the name of this kitchen’s game. More is more. Flavours are uncomplicated, yet not uncouth. I never got to eat my Indonesian-Chinese grandmother’s cooking when she was in her prime, but dining at Lady of Ro chimes with a lot of what I imagine dinner cooked by yiayia – the Greek word for grandmother would be like. (Yiayia’s Table, meanwhile, is the apt name of the value-packed $88 set menu which gets you a heroic, Iliadic quantity of food). As it was from the beginning, BYO is still available and feels especially welcome in these price-conscious times. Even better, Goodsell’s passion for wine shines through in the service: good glasses, cute coolers and a genuine enthusiasm that suggests he just wants you to enjoy yourself rather than try to sell you another bottle of claret.



Related Article Opinion A ‘modern Asian fusion’ pop-up is coming to Perth. Does our dining scene really need it? Max Veenhuyzen Restaurant critic and food writer While Goodsell’s focus is on the now, he (and the Zammits) are also looking to the future and have recruited some young, but promising talents. Admittedly, the current nature of hospitality often requires venues to hire green staff, but based on the meal I had, this shade of green is pretty good. Could there be a potential future custodian of Lady of Ro among the team? Maybe. Maybe not. Regardless, it’s reassuring to know that newcomers are learning and being taken under the wings of industry veterans and getting what seems like solid on-the-job training. While Paul oversees the menu and takes care of preparing dishes, the kitchen is run by Michaela De Matos in his absence.



The waitstaff move with purpose and the vim of youth while soaking up and absorbing the wisdom of old heads. Just like a certain cake we were just talking about. The low-down Atmosphere: A likeable Greek restaurant that hums, sounds and thrills like they used to. Long live Lady of Ro! Go-to dishes: Soufra ($17), fava and cashew dip with pita ($17), slow lamb with vine leaves ($46). Drinks: BYO ($12 per bottle). Cost: About $180 for two people, excluding drinks. Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.title: Head’s 75-ball hundred leads Australia to ODI series triumph
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Head’s 75-ball hundred leads Australia to ODI series triumph Ian Chadband September 19, 2026 — 2:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Travis Head has returned to his blistering best after a lean spell with a 75-ball century to help power Australia to a convincing 84-run victory over Zimbabwe in Harare and wrap up their ODI series triumph. Stand-in captain Mitch Marsh, who cracked a fine half-century himself, saluted “a complete performance” as the world champs found a new gear following their opening win on Tuesday and moved into a 2-0 series lead with a match still to come. Batsman Travis Head plays a shot in the second ODI against Zimbabwe. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Head hadn’t mustered more than 26 in any of his last eight knocks in all cricket, including Tests and IPL fare, but the left-hander was back at his intimidating best on Friday (Saturday AEST) as he crushed 112 off 84 balls to spearhead Australia’s formidable 6-356 after being asked to bat. In reply, the hosts never looked like challenging as the return of Josh Hazlewood (2-48), and a couple of wickets apiece for the spin trio of Adam Zampa, Cooper Connolly and part-timer Matt Renshaw, ensured Zimbabwe could muster only 272 off their 48.3 overs.



Connolly, able to bowl his left-arm spin again after five months when he was unable to do so because of back trouble, delivered another fine all-round performance. The left-hander built on the magnificent start provided by Head and captain Mitch Marsh, who put on a thunderous opening stand of 130 off 19 overs, as he followed up with 78 off 69 balls. Rising star Ollie Peake then chipped in with 41no off 18 balls, with three sixes, to give the innings a rousing finale. Australia’s bowler Adam Zampa, left, celebrates with teammates after bowling Zimbabwe’s batsman Innocent Kaia. AP Photo/Wonder Mashura Connolly also took a catch and the final two wickets of Zimbabwe’s innings off successive balls to finish with 2-25. It also proved a landmark day for Australia’s premier white-ball spinner Zampa (2-62) as he picked up his 200th ODI wicket.



Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Renshaw’s maiden ODI century was great. But can he fire in Tests against South Africa when it counts? The only downside for Australia, who are using this trip to Africa as a reconnaissance mission before next year’s defence of their ODI World Cup, was an injury to paceman Billy Stanlake, who went down with a side strain in his fifth over. “No update yet on Billy, but hopefully he’s OK,” reported Marsh afterwards. “I thought it was a complete performance from the boys. “The way Travis batted gave us a platform for the middle-order, and it was great to see Cooper Connolly and Peakey play roles like that.



“Then, when big Billy went down, our part-time bowlers and allrounders really stepped up in those conditions. They all loved it ​and were keen for it.” Hazlewood’s recall also brought real control, the veteran quick and Stanlake coming in to replace Xavier Bartlett and Spencer Johnson. Related Article Test cricket ‘There’s a reason I’m still here’: Labuschagne’s vow in fight to save career But might things have been very different if Marsh hadn’t been dropped at backward point by Wessly Madhevere off Blessing Muzarabani’s first ball of the game after Zimbabwe had inserted Australia? After that, the aggressive openers simply took the game away, hitting three sixes apiece as they raced to 78 off the 10-over powerplay, with Head going on to make his eighth ODI ton after Marsh had brought up his 21st half-century off 52 deliveries with a maximum.



Head’s 112 was the highest one-day score by an Australian against Zimbabwe, while Josh Inglis backed up with 21, Alex Carey 20 and first-match centurion Renshaw 15. Excellent captain Sikandar Raza top-scored for Zimbabwe with 45 while his fellow 40-year-old Brendan Taylor, who only on Tuesday replaced India great Sachin Tendulkar as the ​longest-serving ODI player, amassed 39 but while the hosts’ top-order got starts, none could kick on. The final match of the series will be played at Harare on Sunday before the tour rolls on to South Africa for three ODIs and three Tests. World.title: Dockers storm into grand final after SCG thriller, but star of the show calls his goal ‘a fluke’
World.content:
Fremantle skipper Alex Pearce spoke to Kayo Sports post-game.

On making the grand final:

“It was hard to put into words. The game threw so much at us, and we were down for so long, but we just hung in their and hung in there. I didn’t have a sense of relief, it was just joy and pride. We were able to play our best footy when the pressure was at its highest, we were calm, went through our gears and individuals stepped up in the big moments.

Alex Pearce of the Dockers celebrates with fans. Getty Images

On whether it will sink in that he will captain the Dockers in the grand final next weekend:

“Probably not, well, actually it will. I’m human and I dream. I daydream about what it will be like. But I’m very conscious of that because wanting it doesn’t make it happen and dreaming about it doesn’t make it happen. Playing the footy we did in the last quarter will go along way to getting us the result we want.

On how the team will handle grand final week:

“As boring as it sounds, we will get through this, reset, review the game and look at what we did poorly and what we can improve on and how we were able to play our best footy in the end.
