World.title: How the NRL's most underrated player explains the Knights
World.content:
In the modern rugby league landscape it's hard for any NRL player to be truly underrated.

Coverage of the game is more granular and intense than ever before and the rise of fantasy sports means every statistical contribution comes into focus, which makes it difficult for anyone to slide under the radar.

But Mat Croker, the man who explains how Newcastle have managed to find themselves in a sudden-death final against the Warriors on Sunday, has managed it after putting together a season of low-key excellence that makes him worthy of the title.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

The lock forward is the only Knight to have played every game this year and his ball-playing in the middle of the field is the straw that stirs the drink for their dynamic attack.

"I'm the link man to our halves and making sure our weapons out wide, guys like KP [Kalyn Ponga] and Braddy [Bradman Best] and Gags [Dane Gagai] get the ball if the cues are there in the defender," Croker said.

"If they're not, just go through the middle."

The 27-year-old makes his job sound simple, and maybe it is, but that's not the same as easy. If it was, someone else would be doing it.

Croker is a microcosm of Newcastle's turnaround from wooden spooners to the brink of the club's first preliminary final since 2013 because, like his team, he knows his strengths and has been empowered to play to them.

There are more explosive and dazzling players at the Knights but Croker's passing, communication and structure helps give them the opportunity to explode and dazzle. He is the rock on which you can build a church that worships attacking football.

Mat Croker has been a fixture at the back of the scrum for Newcastle. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

Newcastle lead the league in tries from their own half with 31. More than a quarter of those begin with Croker at first receiver, setting shape and creating time for the men outside him.

Like the other things Croker does well — chasing kicks, leading line speed in defence, slowing down the ruck — his impact in attack is a hard thing to quantify with numbers. But if you know what you're looking for, it becomes impossible to miss.

Sidelined halfback Dylan Brown believes it's invaluable and that Croker is part of the reason the Knights have been able to stay on their feet and make it to the second week of the finals despite a heavy injury toll.

Mat Croker has enjoyed the best season of his NRL career. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"He understands the game really well. His footy smarts, when to play it out the back and when to run — he knows he's not the biggest player on the field but he knows how to find a gap and he knows when the spine needs the ball," said Brown.

"We've had all these new players come in but we still have the core. We still have Mat Croker and Phoenix Crossland, they haven't changed all year, and the more the ball goes through their hands the easier it's going to be for the rest of the team.

"You need that. Every team needs those guys."

It's been a season of great improvement for Croker, who notched his 100th NRL game earlier this year.

Since his debut in 2021 he has been a solid contributor for the Knights and a good clubman who mainly came off the bench, starting just 13 of his 82 appearances prior to this year.

Mat Croker spent much of his early years coming off the bench. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

But after working closely with new coach Justin Holbrook and attack coach Steven Hales over the summer, Croker was given a chance to start in the club's trip to Las Vegas in Round 1.

He has since transformed from honest toiler to a genuine ball-playing lock, a coalfields remix of the sophisticated passing middle that every decent team needs.

"Ever since day one they've put a lot of responsibility on my shoulders and I'm really grateful they've done that because I think it's brought out the best football of my career," Croker said.

"Back in Vegas they backed a hunch and took a bit of a punt of me to start and I've had the luxury of starting every game since. That's a lot of faith and I try to repay it."

The greatest compliment you can pay a middle forward is to say "he's got a bit of footy in him" and Croker has proven he's got more than most.

Newcastle can progress to their first preliminary final since 2013 with a win on Sunday. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

The skills were always there, he just needed the chance to unlock them.

"Without being arrogant, I always felt like I had some skills with passing and I'm not a barnstorming forward, so I had to work around that and find other ways to improve," said Croker.

"The ability to pass and show and go was part of that — the cues, I've worked really hard with Halesy and Justo to see those.

"He's said the same thing to me for 28 games — if they're tight, move it, and if they're not go through it."

In sticking to that mantra, Croker has become to Newcastle what his opposite number on Sunday, reigning Dally M Lock of the Year Erin Clark, is to the Warriors or what Cameron Murray is to last week's vanquished foes, South Sydney.

Croker had a strong game in that one, leading the way for Newcastle's depleted pack by holding the middle together and making 42 tackles without a miss, and says he was inspired by the prospect of taking on Murray.

"I was coming up against a good 13 in Cameron Murray, who's one of the best players in the whole competition," Croker said.

How Knights finals rookie shut down Souths Newcastle was not short of heroes in its sudden-death finals win over South Sydney, but no player stood taller than 21-year-old backrower and play-off debutant Jermaine McEwen.

"I'm not saying I played over him but I knew I had a big challenge because we play similar roles and I tried to embrace that challenge without the two front-rowers I've beside me all year.

"I had to use my leadership a bit more and I'm proud of how I did it."

Repeating the dose against Clark and the Warriors in front of 50,000 fans at Eden Park is a tall order but few dare write the Knights off.

They're dangerous because they've had a whole season of learning how to play to their strengths, like they did against South Sydney and like Croker has all year to become the NRL's hidden gem.

If they pull off the upset, look for Croker at the heart of it and if he is he sure won't stay underrated for long.

World.title: Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Ryan is the most eyebrow-raising omission from Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players, for games against Brazil in Brisbane on September 25 and Townsville on September 28.

The 34-year-old lost his starting spot to young goalkeeper Patrick Beach at the World Cup, then was bizarrely substituted on for the round-of-32 penalty shootout against Egypt.

The Socceroos skipper, capped 105 times, said after that loss he was only told he might replace Beach as extra time kicked off, though Popovic has since insisted Ryan knew that was a possibility pre-match.

Tony Popovic's Socceroos are set to face Brazil in Brisbane and Townsville. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Levante goalkeeper Ryan has been omitted despite a strong start to the La Liga season.

"We know what Maty Ryan is to Australian football," Popovic said.

"A player that has a distinguished career, continues to have one, over 100 caps.

"But we'd like to have a look at another keeper."

Pressed on how Ryan, who the Socceroos boss also dropped in his first games in charge in 2024, had taken the omission, Popovic said: "He's good.

"He's the ultimate professional that he is, and that's why he's had such a distinguished career.

"He's still available for us, and he's certainly not out of the picture moving forward."

Uncapped St Mirren goalkeeper Jacob Chapman replaces Ryan, joining Beach and Paul Izzo in the squad.

Untried left-back Kasey Bos, younger brother of injured star Jordan Bos, has been called up along with fellow untested defender Dylan Leonard, 19.

Former A-League sensations Marcus Younis (Brondby IF) and Eli Adams (Gamba Osaka) earn maiden call-ups alongside Kealey Adamson (QPR), Chapman and Yaya Dukuly (NK Celje) after impressive stints overseas.

"They've been rewarded for the hard work they've put in to get an opportunity overseas," Popovic said.

"They've had to go through the struggles when you go outside of your comfort zone.

"You go through the ups and downs; not playing, playing, injuries, and that helps you grow.

"And these players get mentally tougher; they know how to handle the difficult situations in games, and I believe they all deserve an opportunity."

Sixteen players from the 26-man World Cup squad return.

Star left-back Jordan Bos (knee) and central defender Cam Burgess (Achilles) are unavailable.

Court battle looms for Socceroos star Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle as the Socceroos star's lawyer confirms he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

Cristian Volpato (hamstring) is sidelined with injury.

The Sassuolo attacker was last week fined $722 for driving with cocaine in his system in July. Volpato has maintained his innocence and will challenge the charges in court.

Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek return after missing the World Cup through injury while Alex Robertson has been recalled.

Cameron Devlin, Nishan Velupillay, Mathew Leckie, Ajdin Hrustic, Kai Trewin and Awer Mabil have been omitted.

Aziz Behich is the only A-League Men player in the squad.

The Socceroos could have played up to four games this window but have settled for two, which Popovic said allowed players to get back to their clubs.

"We feel that with the games in November, we'll be ready for the Asian Cup," he said.

AAP

World.title: A-League season start under threat with referees on strike
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It is seemingly a rare occurrence indeed that Australian football does not find itself in some degree of turmoil.

So it is perhaps of little surprise that as the A-League Men's and Women's seasons fast approach, the code is once again lurching towards another crisis.

The nations top referees have been on strike since September 4, citing "significant changes to the elite refereeing structure" proposed by Football Australia (FA).

The change would see the referees contracted directly by the league, instead of FA.

The Professional Football Referees Association (PFRA) says those changes would be "detrimental to individual referees and represent a drastic step backwards for the professional refereeing program".

The A-League seasons begin in four weeks. And the parties are, as things stand, at something of a stalemate.

The APL and FA have all told ABC Sport they are continuing to work together with the aim of reaching a resolution.

The referee's body said in a statement earlier this month that it would "continue to engage with Football Australia with the aim of resolving the outstanding matters and returning its members to the field as soon as an acceptable outcome can be reached".

As players and supporters at all levels know, without referees there can be no game, so how have we got here?

Who runs the A-Leagues?

The A-League Men and A-League Women seasons get underway in mid-October. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

To get into the weeds of this dispute, we can go back to the 2020 decision to decouple the A-League from Football Australia.

FA relinquished full control to a newly formed body, the Australian Professional Leagues, after a long period of agitation from both the clubs and world body FIFA about governance issues within the game.

In practice, this meant handing over the commercial reins of the A-Leagues to the clubs, in line with many other professional football leagues around the world, such as the Premier League, Bundesliga and J-League, among others.

The clubs believed the separation from the national governing body would help the competition's long-term viability.

The reality has been somewhat different.

In 2024, half of A-League Men players said they were "dissatisfied" with how the competition had been managed by the APL, and close to half said they had "low trust" in whether it could improve the league.

That same year, APL slashed the annual distribution to the clubs from close to $2 million to just $530,000 on account of an increasingly worrying financial outlook.

That followed a frankly disastrous plan to sell off grand finals to Sydney and rapidly declining interest and attendances.

Since then, the stalled expansion drive and the removal of failed club Western United and last month's breakdown of talks between the league and the players over the collective bargaining agreement have added to an environment of intense distrust.

Why are the referees on strike?

The referees are not striking about on-field behaviour. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Since the league unbundled from Football Australia, the sport's governing body has still provided the referees to the league, with the APL reimbursing FA for those costs.

Now, Football Australia has proposed that it will only pay for matches that come under their jurisdiction: the Australia Cup and Australian Championship.

That means the APL has to pay the referees to officiate its competitions directly, which FA says is the APL's responsibility under the contract it has signed with the league.

However, this is one of the issues that the PFRA has railed against, arguing in essence it would be a conflict of interest to officiate the clubs, who are in effect their employers.

"Such an arrangement would place referees in an unacceptable position of potential conflict and raise serious concerns regarding the integrity and impartiality of the refereeing program," the PFRA said in a statement.

The referees would prefer the formation of an independent referees body, as is the case in England with Pro Ref, formerly known as PGMOL.

The PFRA added that the proposed structure was "untenable" and that referees "cannot grow without trust [or] succeed without independence".

Football Australia said there were no issues around the integrity with their proposal, and that it was consistent with FIFA regulations.

The PFRA also said match officials who officiated in trial matches involving A-League clubs had not been paid their outstanding match fees by FA, which was refuted by FA, which said there were no outstanding debts owed.

Have games been affected?

Referee Rowan Fisher took charge of the Australia Cup semifinal. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Football Australia was forced to fly in four Singaporean referees for the Australia Cup semifinal clash between Sydney FC and Melbourne Victory on September 9.

Young Australian referee Rowan Fisher, who does not have any A-League experience, took charge of the second semifinal between South Melbourne and Lions FC earlier this week.

It is understood that there is no risk of the Australia Cup final between South Melbourne and Melbourne Victory on October 10 not being played.

This is due to a group of referees that have signed a contract with FA despite the stand-off.

The second season of the second-tier Australian Championship, which kicks off on Thursday October 15, is also not expected to be at risk.

Both those competitions are administered by FA.

However, no assurances have been given about the A-Leagues, Men and Women, which both start that same weekend.

'Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services'

One could understand the A-League referees not wanting to rush back… (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

The nation's referees are clear they want to get back to the business of refereeing.

But they feel their voices need to be heard.

"Our members have delivered an overwhelmingly clear message. They are seeking certainty around their employment, payment of outstanding amounts, and a clear and sustainable structure for professional refereeing in Australia," PFRA president Evgeny Vizelman said in a statement.

"We do not take the decision to stop officiating matches lightly. Our members want to officiate football, prepare for the upcoming season and positively contribute to the success of football in Australia.

"Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services.

"Taking ourselves off the field hurts. There comes a point where people have to stand together and say the way they are being treated is not good enough."

World.title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.

Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.

In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.

At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.

Netball Australia was not idly watching.

As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.

This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.

This is the third year the First Nations Tournament has run. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.

Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.

Embraced in Alice Springs

Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.

Gabby Coffey says it means a lot to bring Indigenous netballers together for the tournament. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.

She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.

Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.

"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.

While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.

The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.

Coffey (left) played for Birmingham in England's top competition. (Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.

Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.

"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.

"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."

Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.

"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."

Visible Indigenous role models key

Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.

"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.

Coffey says it is important to have visible role models. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.

"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.

"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."

She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.

A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.

Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.

Scarlet Jauncey is representing Western Australia, and has captained the Black Swans. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.

"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.

Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.

"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.

In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.

"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.

"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."

Jauncey in action during this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".

"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.

Cultural safety means listening to community

Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.

It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.

Ali Tucker-Munro is Netball Australia's general manager for First Nations. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.

"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."

Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.

"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.

"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."

Players have enjoyed coming together in Melbourne for this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.

The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes

Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.

"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.

"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.

"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.

"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

World.title: From African shepherd to Australia's marathon record holder
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia's men's marathon record holder, Haftu Strintzos, thrives on hard work but still finds it hard to believe where life has taken him.

Born in eastern Tigray in northern Ethiopia, he grew up standing barefoot in fields for hours, helping provide for his family from dawn to dusk.

"I feel as though I have lived a double life in a way," he said after celebrating his 27th birthday in Melbourne.

"I consider myself very privileged to live this life.

" I spent my early days as a shepherd, herding goats and sheep through the mountains of my local village. I grew up without a TV or running water. "

In his remote community, 2,300 metres above sea level, the only source of information he had until age 10 was a mobile phone.

Haftu lost both biological parents by the time he was six, and was taken in by his maternal grandmother, living with his aunt and cousins.

A Greek Australian aid worker by the name of Maria Strintzos came calling, meeting Haftu in 2007 at the age of eight.

Aid worker Maria Strintzos adopted Haftu Strintzos in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

After decades working across Ethiopia, she asked him if he'd like to be her son, adopted him and helped him migrate to Melbourne in 2011 — more than 12,000 kilometres from the mountains of Tigray.

Today, Haftu speaks five languages (Tigrinya, Amharic, Greek, Japanese and English), holds a Master of Electrical Engineering from Villanova University in the USA and recently broke the national marathon record.

Feeling the 'weight of the world'

Maria always felt compelled to help others. Growing up in South Melbourne in the 1960s, she found strength in the local Greek community, even while migrant families faced racism.

"We had absolutely everybody there. As much as I loved growing up there, it built a strength in me," she said.

Haftu Strintzos would walk barefoot from the mountains of eastern Tigray to the village with his blind grandmother, Shifta, to meet his future mother, Maria. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"I grew up knowing what social injustice and inequality looked like."

Her aid work took her through Indonesia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, supporting famine relief, water schemes, food security, women's empowerment and communities affected by conflict, spending 35 years around wars and disease, but also hope, in the Horn of Africa.

But something different about young Haftu stood out.

He would walk barefoot through dry riverbeds, guiding his almost blind grandmother, Shifta, through the mountains to meet Maria.

"He was very respectful," she said.

"And he would sit there really quietly … didn't muck around like the other kids.

"He always had this sort of sad and serious look about him. It's like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.

Haftu Strintzos took every opportunity and excelled at school, with his mother Maria Strintzos helping him go on to the US college system and graduate with a Masters of Electrical Engineering. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

"But the way he looked after his grandmother and the way the grandmother would talk about him was very moving at the time too."

With the pull of family ties in Australia, Maria found herself at a crossroads.

"I was challenged at that time because I didn't particularly want to leave Ethiopia," she said.

"I loved my life. I loved what I did … I felt like I was achieving something."

Embracing the challenge of two different worlds

Excelling at school and winning education awards, Haftu embraced every opportunity.

When he migrated to Australia in 2011, he took nothing for granted in his new environment.

Can a marathon help you beat addiction? The science says yes From addiction recovery to mental health, science is revealing why running a marathon can feel so good.

Growing up without electricity, he became fascinated by anything electrical.

Maria bought Haftu toy cars that he would unpack and dismantle.

"He literally pulled them apart with the motors, everything, and reassembled them," she said.

Having never seen a TV, he would sit on the couch for hours waiting for people to appear outside the screen.

"Sometimes I'd catch him sort of looking behind the TV because he thought there was people in there," she said.

"I still can't believe it. It was quite incredible that given his background, that he had this innate gift, something about electricity."

A reward for excelling at school, Haftu Strintzos would relish the chance to earn new stationery and school supplies in Ethiopia. (Supplied: Maria Strintzos)

Maria said she's most proud of how Haftu had risen above adversity in his life.

"Where he's come from it was a rock hut, and they would sleep on the floor and the animals were next to them," she said.

" The uniqueness of Haftu is that he's managed to retain the positive qualities of his experience. I'm in awe of him. "

But the culture shock wasn't easy; different foods, subtle racism and grappling with Western values were also some of Haftu's greatest tests.

Warming climate forcing marathon changes to keep runners cool Marathon organisers across the United States are rethinking when they hold events due to warmer temperatures.

"My biggest challenges in assimilating to Australian culture were learning the English language and motion sickness while riding in cars," he said.

"I remember a time in my early days where the only way I would not throw up while Mum drove the car was if I sat in the front passenger seat and kept my eyes on the road in front."

From a school oval to an athlete with no fear

It wasn't until he moved to Australia that Haftu realised his potential in athletics, having grown up in Tigray not knowing it was even a sport or profession.

"My PE teacher at school encouraged me to pursue it when he saw me run a cross-country race at the school oval," he said.

Adding more strings to his bow, Haftu Strintzos won the 2026 Australian Athletics Cross Country Championships in Ballarat, Victoria. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

In that school race, he just kept running and didn't stop after the finish line, such was his determination for long-distance.

"I have grown up through this sport and learned my most valuable life lessons through it," he said.

"Running helped me connect with my local community, just getting out and about and meeting like-minded people."

His talent soon attracted attention, including from Cathy Freeman, who became like a mentor and even attended his birthday party during his teens.

Training up to 190 kilometres a week under coach Adam Didyk, Haftu broke the Australian men's marathon record in two hours, six minutes and 20 seconds at the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

He became the first Australian winner in 20 years, smashed the course record and set a new Oceania record — all on his fourth attempt at the distance.

Haftu Strintzos regularly trains in Melbourne around Albert Park Lake as he prepares for global events. (ABC Sport: Damien Peck)

Didyk, who also coaches Australian women's marathon record holder Jessica Stenson, has guided Haftu remotely from Adelaide for two years.

"He's a fairly no-fuss kind of individual. He'll just take the work and get it done," Didyk said.

"He's obviously very capable when it comes to longer distances and feels confident running at the pace he needs to for the marathon; quite extraordinarily, mind you."

Didyk said Haftu's college experience and early development give him a strong understanding of racing, matched by mental strength.

"He backs himself. He has a lot of confidence in his ability, and he believes in what he can do.

"He's one of those no-fear athletes who sets a goal that looks pretty daunting, but it excites him more and more the scarier he makes it."

Having broken the Australian marathon record in July, Haftu Strintzos (third from left) is aiming for a podium at the Olympics in future years. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

Australian records are just the beginning

Haftu's talent comes as a package. Didyk said the physical ability, mental strength and calmness on race day were all put together to make good decisions, ultimately which led to the record-breaking performance at the Gold Coast Marathon.

"He's just a sensible, quite an intelligent young guy, and that all comes together to match what he can physically do as well," he said.

Haftu's calmness and patience on the Gold Coast reinforced Didyk's belief that he had world-class potential.

"There's so many positives about Haftu that he can go and achieve what no Australian has before in the marathon," Didyk said.

"He's very determined to be successful in international level … it was a phenomenally strong close.

"I think what's probably most important to us now with seeing that is if he's going to be competitive at an Olympic or World Championships level, he's going to need that ability to be able to close really fast over those last 10 kilometres.

Robert de Castella (right) held the national marathon record for 36 years until 2022. (Supplied: Australian Athletics)

"He's shown he's got the foundations to do something like that."

"Off the back of that, it started to give us the knowledge of him to go, 'that's the game he can play when he goes to a major championship, he can put himself in there and he can put himself in a competitive situation late in the race'.

"And that's ideally what we're aiming to do with him over the coming years."

From his humble beginnings in Ethiopia, Haftu's dreams of standing on an Olympic podium remain his driving force for motivation for the 2027 World Championships in China, and Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Australia hasn't had an Olympic marathon medallist since Lisa Ondieki won silver in 1988.

"I am very fortunate to have the support systems I need to help me to achieve my goals — something that not every athlete gets to have," he said.

"I want to continue to break records. After all, records are there to be broken."

Tech.title: The real story of the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s one of the most fascinating years in a while when it comes to iPhone camera upgrades. The big story of the iPhone 18 Pro is the variable aperture main lens, which lets you open the aperture up wider for better low light shots and make the aperture smaller for better depth of field in group photos. But all I can get anyone to talk about is the software upgrades: it turns out, they’re a lot more useful day to day than the aperture on a camera this small.

This week on The Vergecast, David Imel and Allison Johnson are here for a deep dive into the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera. There’s a lot to explore here, from the aperture, to the camera app’s new manual controls, to the updated imaging pipeline and the improvements to ProRAW.

After that, Hayden Field is on the show to discuss the state of the AI safety debate. Concerns are still boiling over after an Anthropic researcher quit his job to warn about the dangers of AI, and any chance for policy solutions seems to have hit a dead end. We discuss whether what’s likely to happen in the interim — third-party evaluators being embedded within the big AI labs — has any teeth, and where the safety conversation goes from here.

Finally, it’s time for a Lightning Round. We discuss Waymo’s ability to call the cops, a new ereader from Boox, and a couple of tiny retro-style cameras.

If you want to learn more about any of the topics we discussed, you can check out the stories below:

Tech.title: Gavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) is positioning the state to take the lead on AI oversight, including the potential to mandate a “kill switch” for frontier models, with a new executive order issued Friday.

Newsom’s order directs the state to convene a group of experts that will deliver recommendations within two months on how to strengthen AI safety measures in state law. Newsom wants the group to consider how the state could require AI companies to embed independent verification groups onsite for regular audits, make their transparency reports and risk assessments subject to standards of independent auditors, create a “kill switch” that’s routinely verified as effective, and make sure companies are required to report “loss-of-control incidents” like the OpenAI attack on Hugging Face as critical safety incidents. It also directs a state agency to speed up implementation of two recent laws he signed, creating a framework for independent verifiers to assess AI safety, and a state registry of AI auditors.

There’s been a flurry of bill discussions in Congress in the wake of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s post warning of a more than 10 percent chance that AI “could kill all humans” within a decade. But there’s little hope in Washington that a bill of substance could pass anytime soon given that the House is on recess until November, and the impending midterm elections make major legislation movement in the Senate similarly unlikely. At the same time, President Donald Trump has insisted, “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND ​SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”

Newsom is calling on Congress and Trump “to review and adopt the state’s framework”

Newsom’s executive order is likely not the last we’ll hear from California on this topic. On Wednesday, he floated the possibility of calling California lawmakers in for a special legislative session on AI in an interview with Politico, alongside potential executive action. He is specifically positioning the order as a model for federal action, calling on Congress and Trump “to review and adopt the state’s framework, or use its nation-leading regulation as a floor, not a ceiling, for the benefit and safety of all Americans.”

“The federal government’s abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation,” Newsom said in a statement. “We’re not waiting to act – we’re going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it’s too late. We’re going to do this thoughtfully but with urgent velocity; the stakes are too high to wait or delay action.”

Tech.title: What Hollywood thinks about existential AI warnings
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

As the tech sector sounds alarms about AI’s potential to destroy humanity, entertainment labor groups are urging the public to stay focused on what’s already happening. The Verge reached out to Disney, Netflix, Amazon, Lionsgate, and other studios who have started using AI, as well film startups focused on bringing generative AI into the mainstream to ask for their reaction to the recent warnings surrounding the technology. None have responded to our request for comment. The Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (SAG-AFTRA) and Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) did, however.

The AI tools used in entertainment production differ from the AI systems that have sparked a recent round of whistleblowing and apocalyptic declarations. They do not seem to be as existentially dangerous as the AI systems that drove former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon to quit his job and prompted Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger to insist that the technology could “kill all humans” at some point “within the next decade.”

But despite the differences between entertainment-focused AI and the models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, AI models that generate digital facsimiles of actors and attempt to replicate traditional filmmaking tools pose a threat to some human jobs. Similar to the way that the Hollywood unions advocated for protections and increased oversight around AI’s use during the 2023 strikes, Coxon’s Anthropic exit has inspired a wave of AI researchers to speak out in favor of stronger safety protocols. The heads of major AI companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and X have also called for an industry-wide slowdown on the technology’s development. While president Donald Trump has dismissed these concerns as overreactions, some other US politicians have felt pressured to take legislative action. Hollywood unions’ fight for strict rules around gen AI’s use did not stop the entertainment industry from embracing AI, but they have given Hollywood’s laborers a way to fight back in instances when they feel that AI tools are being used to harm them.

When I recently spoke with the Screen Actors Guild – American Federation of Television and Radio Artists’ (SAG-AFTRA) chief negotiator Duncan Crabtree Ireland, he told me that the union recognized early on how AI could impact its members’ livelihoods. Most people might not have been familiar with the idea of studios completely replacing human actors with digital replicas, but SAG-AFTRA understood that it had an opportunity to shape public opinion about AI in Hollywood by “speaking out about it at the earliest possible point we could.”

“We bargained for and achieved enforceable, meaningful guardrails around how this technology can be implemented by the major employers in our industry,” Crabtree-Ireland explained. “That doesn’t include companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google directly, but it does encompass all of the companies who have built up businesses around the creation of professional level entertainment content in the United States.”

Though Crabtree-Ireland believes we “should be concerned about the broader societal and social implications of AI,” he also thinks that some of the warnings about the technology being an extinction-level threat could potentially be hyperbole and overblown. Doomerism has become one of the more common ways that AI companies generate buzz around their products, but the fact that Coxon left Anthropic to sound the alarm has given Crabtree-Ireland pause. Hearing the message from “the CEOs of these companies or the billionaires who’ve made their billions off of doing the exact thing that they’re now warning us might not be good,” has left him unsure “what to trust or what to believe.” But he acknowledged that Coxon was able to achieve “traction with the public.”

“The recklessness of the tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.”

Getting people to believe that SAG-AFTRA’s fears about AI should be taken seriously was one of the union’s major goals when its members voted to strike. The key to doing that, Crabtree-Ireland told me, was leading the strike with a focused message that clearly laid out to the public what was at stake and steps that could be taken to prevent worst case scenarios. If not for that, Crabtree-Ireland thinks that the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP) might not have agreed to some of the union’s demands like requiring that studios gain permission and compensate actors for the use of their AI-generated replicas. “If that principle hadn’t been established, I think the economic incentive to use replication and to replace human performances would have been much stronger” and “would have resulted in a much greater and faster adoption of digital replication.” Had the protections not been codified, Crabtree-Ireland is confident that entertainment workers would be in a much more dire position now.

Writers Guild of America East (WGAE) executive director Sam Wheeler was much more pointed in his condemnation of the “tech oligarchs pushing AI on our society” whose recklessness “has been matched only by their rampant dishonesty.” But while Wheeler finds it hard to take AI companies’ warnings at face value, he noted that the WGAE “has long warned that unregulated artificial intelligence poses an existential threat to workers, to our democracy, and to the world.”

“Guild members have bargained meaningful AI protections into their contracts; in 2023 WGA members spent 148 days on strike before the film and television studios agreed to real safeguards for film and television writers,” Wheeler said. “But collective bargaining is not a replacement for government regulation, and we are grateful to states like New York that continue to enact meaningful regulations in the absence of federal action.”

Wheeler listed the disempowerment of workers, the degradation of the internet, the spread of disinformation, and increasing energy costs as some of the tangible societal harms AI has exacerbated. He urged policymakers not to be distracted by AI companies’ claims of ushering in an apocalypse because the real issue at hand is people behaving irresponsibly.

“These harms are the result of decisions made by human beings,” Wheeler insisted. “The WGAE believes that addressing those concrete harms and holding AI companies and their executives liable for the destruction their products cause is the surest way to safeguard against any worst-case scenarios.”

Tech.title: Security researchers used Claude to help them hack into OpenAI
Tech.content:
A team of three independent security researchers at Hacktron says it took less than 72 hours for them to hack into OpenAI employee accounts using Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.8 and 5, The Wall Street Journal reports. They were able to access OpenAI’s GitHub repository, called “Monorepo,” which reportedly contains “OpenAI’s algorithmic secrets,” according to The Wall Street Journal’s sources.

They stopped short of accessing internal code in Monorepo themselves, but sent a pull request from an employee’s Codex account to prove they gained access. They were able to get in through Discourse, the third-party service that hosts OpenAI’s community forums, by exploiting an issue with the system it uses to process HEIF images. According to Hacktron, Claude Opus 5 launched in the evening on July 24th, and by 10AM the next day they had used it to achieve RCE on Discourse Cloud and accessed OpenAI’s instance.

Their HEIF Heist project took “only one or two days” to adapt to different companies, including OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub Ent, Rails, Next.js, ImageMagick, and others, using less than $3,000 in tokens, and to their knowledge, was only detected by one target, Shopify. The vulnerabilities Hacktron reported to Discourse and OpenAI have since been fixed, and Hacktron says OpenAI paid it $6,500 for finding the bug, but as Hacktron CTO Mohan Pedhapati said to the WSJ, “I don’t think we are as strong as Chinese threat actors… We’re just three guys with Claude and Codex subscriptions.”

Tech.title: Brendan Carr’s FCC is more worried about who The View interviews than foreign governments owning Paramount
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The FCC has announced it’s waiving its rules limiting foreign equity ownership to 25 percent in the Paramount-Warner Bros. case and will allow three sovereign wealth funds run by the governments of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi to own 49.5 percent of the company.

During Brendan Carr’s tenure, the FCC has repeatedly threatened ABC, tried to block stations from airing interviews with Democrats, censored late-night TV hosts, and tried to bully journalists. However, it seems to have no qualms with repressive foreign governments owning a significant stake in a giant American media conglomerate.

In its ruling, the FCC defended the decision, saying that, because the stocks being purchased did not have voting rights, they “will not be able to wield any influence, let alone control, over decisions involving the Licensees.”

Of course, many, including the advocacy group Free Press and a number of Democrats, are not buying that. According to Variety, Free Press noted its opposition, saying that “control over for-profit, commercial domestic news media by any government is an extraordinary situation that would surely strike most Americans as unseemly, precisely because of the utility of the news media as a propaganda tool for those governments.”

Anna Gomez, the FCC’s lone Democratic commissioner, posted on X, “The FCC just let some of the most repressive governments in the world indirectly control nearly all of a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. An investment this large in one of America’s biggest media companies doesn’t just buy equity, it secures influence over what gets said and made.“

Tech.title: Lenovo’s Yoga Slim 7X is the most laptop that $1,000 can currently buy
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anyone shopping for a Windows laptop with a $1K budget should head to Best Buy, where for the rest of the day you can get a great deal on a capable Lenovo laptop. The Yoga Slim 7X is a slim 14-inch machine with a 2K 16:10 OLED touchscreen, Snapdragon’s high-end X2 Elite processor with 12 cores, plus 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. The specs are about the best you can get these days for $1,000, as worthwhile laptop deals are in short supply during RAMageddon.

The Yoga Slim 7X seems like a great alternative to spending more (and getting less) with Microsoft’s latest Surface Laptop. In fact, you’d spend $1,549 on a similar model and still get half the storage that’s in this particular Yoga Slim 7X configuration. Its Arm-based processor can run most Windows apps very well, and yields superior battery life compared to laptops with x86 processors.

The laptop includes three USB-C ports, and a hardware switch for disabling the webcam. It supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.3. It seems like a great machine for work, watching movies, or playing some games that aren’t too graphically intensive.

Tech.title: This cartridge-playing Game Boy clone is smaller and cheaper than Analogue’s Pocket
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

FunnyPlaying, a Chinese company known for its Game Boy and GBA upgrade kits, has announced a new handheld that plays original Nintendo cartridges and ROMs. The FPGB Mini’s cartridge support is limited to the Game Boy and Game Boy Color so it isn’t as capable as the Analogue Pocket that’s also compatible with the GBA and Sega Game Gear. What still makes the FPGB Mini a tempting alternative is its extremely pocketable design resulting in a handheld only slightly wider than a Game Boy cartridge, and its cheaper price.

The FPGB Mini allows for multiplayer and trading over a USB-C cable. Image: FunnyPlaying

Following recent price hikes the Analogue Pocket is now $239.99 while the FPGB Mini is currently discounted from $89.99 to $69.99 for the first batch of just 20 units that quickly sold out. However, the company is potentially planning to release more following some hardware improvements, according to Retro Dodo who’s been testing the handheld for a few days and so far seems impressed with its design and capabilities.

Like the Pocket the FPGB Mini uses field-programmable gate array (FPGA) technology to play Game Boy and GBC games as accurately as Nintendo’s original hardware does. But the FPGB Mini brings improvements like a 2.98-inch, 800x720-pixel LCD display, an 1,800mAh rechargeable battery, and a microSD slot for storing game saves, screenshots, or ROMs that can be played through emulation. The handheld’s compact size does prevent cartridges with rumble motors or other hardware additions from being used, but otherwise the FPGB Mini looks to be about as small as the Game Boy is ever going to get.

Tech.title: Flash floods can strike without warning — this new technology could change that
Tech.content:
On the morning of June 9th, Laura Lin was working from her home in Lanesville, a rural southern Indiana town about 15 miles from the Kentucky border. She was on a Zoom call, unaware that the heavy rain outside was beginning to flood her yard.

“I look over to where the barn is over there, and I see pieces of my wood floating, and I was like, ‘What?’ And I immediately was like, ‘I have to go.’ Close my laptop, and I get my kids up, and I’m like, ‘Something’s wrong,’” Lin recalls.

Lin and her family got out safely and sheltered at a neighbor’s house, but Lanesville got over 8 inches of rain within just a few hours that day, way over the threshold for what is considered “heavy” rainfall. The water was gone a few hours later.

Floods are the second-deadliest type of weather event in the United States and the deadliest globally. Just 6 inches of fast-flowing water can knock an adult off their feet, 12 inches can lift a car, and 2 feet can move larger vehicles like trucks and SUVs. A warming climate means more instances of extreme rainfall in the US, creating more opportunities for floods to occur. The deadly flash flooding in Nepal in August caused by a glacier collapse shows the power of water to devastate communities worldwide.

Fortunately, new tools are being developed to counter this threat. A new software called the Transient Artifact and Continuous Learning System (TACLS) uses satellites and machine learning to try to spot areas that could flood sooner and help the National Weather Service (NWS) make better decisions when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts.

“We didn’t get the ‘get on your roof’ warnings until I was already at that person’s house,” Lin says. “All the people in town were already flooded when they started sending out alerts, being like, ‘Get on your roof. We’re dispatching boats.’ So it was way too late.”

TACLS has the potential to help change that.

“It will help you save lives,” says Ivory Small, science and operations officer at the NWS San Diego Weather Forecast Office. Without TACLS, Small says, a storm moving into your area “could kill some folks.” With TACLS, “you can put out the warning and save some folks.”

The river near Laura Lin’s house in Lanesville, Indiana, flooded after a recent rain. New technology could provide residents with quicker warnings when the threat arises. Image: Megan Wollerton / The Verge

Follow the water

Weather forecast offices are responsible for issuing severe weather alerts, including flash flood warnings. There are 122 of them throughout the US and its territories, says Jayme Laber, senior service hydrologist for the NWS Weather Forecast Office in Oxnard, California, which oversees the LA area. Small and Laber worked closely on the TACLS project with a broader team of scientists and researchers, and they hope this new project will streamline weather alerts. To understand TACLS, it’s important to first understand how the NWS issues flood alerts.

Currently, the people working in weather forecast offices use a variety of tools to monitor flood conditions. They rely on rain and stream gauges to tell them how much water is in a certain place at any given time, Laber says. They track developing storms using satellites and weather radars. The staff monitors rainfall, but their computers also alert them when it rains more than what is considered safe for a specific area. “Based on the type of soils we have, the steepness of slopes, we have developed flash flood guidance so that we know that if we get this amount of rain in this amount of time in that area, it could result in flash flooding,” Laber says.

“It will help you save lives.” — Ivory Small

All of that, plus the years of expertise inside those buildings, determines whether or not someone presses a button to issue a flood alert for their area, Laber says.

A watch is the least serious alert. It means that there’s a chance a flash flood could happen. The watch might be issued anywhere from 12 to 48 hours in advance, Laber explains. He says local emergency teams should start working on “flood protection measures” when the flood watch is issued, so there’s enough time to prepare before people are stuck and forced to find higher ground. Response teams might review evacuation plans, set up sandbags and road barriers, and identify the highest risk areas ahead of a potential flood.

An advisory is the next level up. It might be flooding, “but it’s more nuisance-level. It’s not going to threaten life or property,” Laber says. A warning is the most serious alert. “That’s a life-and-death possibility of being swept off your feet [or] being run over by a car floating down the stream,” Small says.

The NWS differentiates a regular flood from a flash flood based on time, says Small. If an area floods in under six hours, it’s a flash flood.

The NWS has a lot of different ways to determine whether or not it needs to issue a flash flood warning, but its tech has limitations, says Yehuda Bock, TACLS project lead and research geodesist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego. The satellites the NWS uses are more detailed over oceans than land, he says. And tracking rainfall as it’s happening doesn’t give you enough lead time, “because once there’s precipitation, you’re already in the event itself,” he explains.

Deserts and other less populated areas typically have fewer rain gauges, Laber says. “We have a fairly dense network [of rain gauges], but it doesn’t cover every inch of the Earth.”

Up in the air

TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places on a map — for now, just in California — that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods. But soon, the technology will be available to every NWS office. Scientists from UCSD, the NWS, and NASA worked together to create TACLS. NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office funded the project through its Advanced Information Systems Technology program.

TACLS relies on the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), which is primarily used to predict earthquakes, says Bock. But the GNSS network, which consists of satellites and ground sensors, also happens to provide data that can help forecasters decide if they need to issue a flash flood warning. The more water vapor, or moisture, there is in the atmosphere, the longer the delay in communication between the GNSS satellites and the sensors on the ground.

The amount of moisture, or “precipitable water,” in the atmosphere tells the NWS what is actually happening in the skies leading up to a storm, Laber says.

TACLS uses satellites and machine learning to identify places that risk transitioning from rain to dangerous flash floods.

Before TACLS, Laber and his colleagues had to rely on the forecast, which wasn’t always accurate. TACLS provides real-time data about the precipitable water in the atmosphere to compare to the forecast. This helps them determine whether the storm is actually moving at the speed predicted by the weather models. “It helps us to make better decisions in our warning decision process,” Laber says.

Even with the GNSS moisture data, forecasters still need something to analyze all of it. Bhavik Chandna, a UCSD graduate student, spent about a year developing the machine learning side of TACLS using what’s called long short-term memory architecture. According to Chandna, this specific machine learning system works especially well for things like developing storms and other weather patterns that change over time.

Years of atmospheric measurements from the GNSS network, as well as data about atmospheric rivers, precipitation, and flash flood warnings, were used to train the machine learning model to understand moisture changes in the atmosphere “as a storm develops,” Chandna explains. At the same time, the machine learning system was trained to determine if the conditions are right to issue a flash flood warning.

“Machine learning sucks at some things and excels at some things,” says Joel Johnson, associate professor in the department of earth and planetary sciences at the University of Texas at Austin. Johnson, who was not involved in the TACLS project, knows firsthand the challenges of working with these types of tools. “In general, it’s very easy to have artifacts in your data, false positives. A sensor goes funky, and things like that,” Johnson says. Still, he says TACLS seems “well suited” to the task of predicting flash floods.

False positives do happen, Chandna says. “A real weather system usually affects an area, not just one isolated GNSS station. If one station shows a strong signal but its neighbors do not, that detection can be suppressed. If several nearby stations see the same pattern, we have much more confidence that it represents a real atmospheric signal,” he adds.

Chandna says TACLS is not intended to replace the forecasters who issue weather alerts. It’s just another piece of information that can assist in their decision-making, he says.

Finding a better way

TACLS software is already being used in the LA and San Diego weather forecast offices where flash flooding is a common occurrence, says Laber. “In the West, we deal with a lot more flash flooding, where it happens a lot quicker,” he explains. Today, TACLS shows them a graph with various points telling them what is going on in real time.

A newer version of TACLS with improved graphics is currently being loaded onto the NWS system and is nearly done, Laber says. It will be available to all of the NWS offices in the second half of October, he adds. This iteration has a map with detailed graphics showing how much it’s raining and whether an extreme weather event is occurring.

According to Laber, having more tools — like this latest update to TACLS — will further improve their decision-making when it comes to issuing flash flood alerts, and, in turn, maybe speed up alert times so people know there’s a problem sooner.

Laber says TACLS will likely be used the most in the Western US because the majority of the GNSS sensors are located in places known for earthquake activity. But Chandna thinks TACLS could work well elsewhere too. As long as there are some GNSS sensors and available local weather data, “we could use the same ideology that we have in our system around different parts of the world,” he says.

Small is thinking beyond TACLS. He believes ongoing research is crucial to improving how the NWS issues flash flood warnings. “We learn what’s going on a little more every time we do a storm because they’re all different,” he says. “It’s imperative that you do the research after, especially big events, and see what caused it to do what it did, and why, if it was different than what we already knew, did this occur.”

Lin’s concern is Lanesville and her home. “It would have been helpful to know [water was coming] before I was locked in. I couldn’t go anywhere,” Lin says. “If I got an alert that was like, ‘You need to get out now if you’re in lower-lying ground, this is coming.’ Yeah, that would have [been helpful]. But it came in so fast.”

Tech.title: In India, the new iPhone can arrive faster than a pizza
Tech.content:
For some iPhone buyers in India, getting Apple’s brand-new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max did not require lining up outside a store or waiting days for delivery. They needed only a few taps on a quick-commerce app to get one delivered to their doorstep in about 10 minutes.

Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy’s Instamart, and BigBasket — platforms best known in India for delivering groceries and everyday essentials in minutes — began offering the new Pro models as they went on sale in the country on Friday. The phones are, however, also available through Apple’s usual sales channels, including its stores, authorized retailers, and online marketplaces.

Putting a new iPhone on a 10-minute delivery app is not entirely new in India. Quick-commerce platforms have offered Apple’s latest devices on launch day previously as well, as they have steadily expanded beyond groceries into categories including electronics, beauty products, and fashion.

However, the market behind those deliveries is growing rapidly. India’s quick-commerce sector reached about $9 billion in the first half of 2026, per a recent report by Redseer Strategy Consultants, with the number of monthly users rising to more than 60 million from 8 million three years ago. Google and Deloitte separately estimate the market could reach $50 billion by 2030, with non-food products such as electronics, fashion and beauty accounting for 45% of spending.

There were signs of strong demand on launch day. BigBasket said it delivered more than 300 iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max units in the first hour of sales. Instamart told TechCrunch that Bengaluru led the iPhone 18 Pro-series orders on its platform, followed by Delhi. The Burgundy 256 GB iPhone 18 Pro was Instamart’s most popular variant, accounting for nearly a third of its sales.

Nonetheless, within hours of launch, availability of the new iPhones became patchy. TechCrunch found the iPhone 18 Pro models sold out on some quick-commerce platforms and in some locations, while they remained available for delivery elsewhere in cities including Delhi and Bengaluru.

Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, said the launch-day deliveries showed that quick commerce could work as a channel for premium smartphones in India’s biggest cities, even though volumes remain small compared with overall iPhone sales.

The ability to fulfill high-value smartphone orders provides an “early proof of concept,” Pathak told TechCrunch. “The key question is whether this launch-driven demand can translate into regular smartphone purchases through quick-commerce platforms.”

Navkendar Singh, associate vice president at IDC, said India stood out globally for this kind of quick-commerce delivery and was particularly suited to such purchases because consumers in major cities had built trust in the platforms by using them regularly for everyday purchases. Official tie-ups between brands and the platforms also gave consumers greater confidence in buying expensive products through them, he told TechCrunch.

For a product like the iPhone, the appeal also comes down to “instant gratification,” Singh said, allowing buyers to avoid queues outside stores or waiting several days for an online order to arrive. Still, he cautioned that quick commerce was not yet a significant sales channel for smartphones. Its role around new iPhone releases is largely a “launch-day marketing phenomenon” that “creates good noise around the launch,” he said.

Tech.title: Google’s new ‘CC’ is an AI agent that helps families run their households
Tech.content:
Google is testing a new product designed to help families coordinate with the support of an AI agent. This week, the search giant introduced a new version of CC, an AI agent designed to work across email, calendar, chats, and tasks. With the update, CC now focuses on keeping families organized, planning for the day ahead, and even handling family-specific tasks, like signing permission slips, creating shopping lists, or crafting weekly meal plans.

The move to make CC more family-focused comes as a number of AI startups are experimenting with how to best fit agentic AI into consumers’ lives. Some AI tools, like Ollie and Fambot, for instance, have aimed their services directly at helping parents and families.

Google’s CC, meanwhile, began its life as a productivity agent that connected to Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, and the wider web to understand your day, then deliver a “Your Day Ahead” briefing to your inbox. In May, the tool came to the Gemini app as “Daily Brief.”

Google said user requests showed that people wanted to use the feature more for household management tasks. They wanted AI to help them keep up with kids’ school schedules, sports practices, bills, meal plans, and more.

As a result, Google shifted CC to become an agent for families that helps run their households.

Image Credits:Google

Now, CC is getting its own Google account, so it can collaborate with family members on tasks, while also maintaining its own specific set of permissions for accessing data. Google explains that each family member chooses what they want to share — like emails about school events, sports, clubs, birthday party invites, doctor appointments, or anything else. These can be forwarded to CC via its email address, or shared automatically.

To automate sharing, users can pick the email senders whose messages they always want to share with CC going forward, like schools, travel companies, clubs, or sports teams. (CC will also suggest email senders to add on a weekly basis.)

Image Credits:Google

The company says CC currently supports up to six family members who can share information and collaborate with the agent.

Beyond email, CC can also coordinate household activities by tracking important dates and to-dos, and then automatically adding them to the calendar or a shared task list. That means, for instance, every time the orthodontist sends an email confirmation of your next appointment or the school announces a teacher workday, CC can put it on the shared calendar.

Image Credits:Google

What’s more, the agent can manage select tasks on a family’s behalf, like filling out permission slips or activity registration PDFs, making school supply shopping lists, planning weekly meals, figuring out drive times between activities, creating shared Docs or Sheets, and more. It will even ask for missing details, as needed, and update its group memory so it can be more helpful going forward.

Google notes that CC runs on its own isolated cloud computer, powered by Gemini and Google’s agentic harness, Antigravity. The experiment is only available for U.S. users with a personal Gmail account, who are ages 18 and up.

That’s a big drawback for the time being because it means older kids, like tweens and teens, can’t use the service unless they lie about their age on their Google accounts. It also means they can’t use it with their school-provided emails, despite the fact that many attend schools that run everything on Chromebooks and Google apps and have inboxes filled with school-related updates.

CC could help larger households, where parents have to coordinate with each other and with other adults, like grandparents, caregivers, nannies, or adult children still living at home, which tends to be more common these days.

Existing CC users will be invited via email in the coming days to upgrade their accounts, Google says, while new users can join a waitlist to access the AI agent.

Tech.title: Joby Aviation’s 3,100-mile autonomous flight signals its push beyond electric air taxis
Tech.content:
An aircraft equipped with Joby Aviation’s autonomy technology flew more than 3,100 miles across the United States without a human pilot taking control at any point, the company said Friday.

The flight not only demonstrated the capabilities of Joby’s autonomy tech, but also showed that the company’s ambitions extend well beyond its pursuit of electric air taxis. Joby said the autonomous aircraft it’s not done yet, and will make its way back to the West Coast with stops in various cities, including Louisville, Kentucky, and Salt Lake City, over the next two weeks.

Joby Aviation said the cross-country trip, which it described as the “first-ever autonomous flight across the United States,” included autonomous taxiing, takeoffs, navigation, and landings. The aircraft was remotely supervised from Joby’s headquarters in California and Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina. A pilot was on board for compliance, but Joby said the aircraft performed the entire operation autonomously.

Joby, which used a converted Cessna Caravan aircraft for the trip, said the flight demonstrated that its autonomy technology could handle different environments and missions, including medical transport, disaster response, and defense logistics.

It also showcased the potential for a second business for Joby, which is best known for developing electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft for an eventual urban air taxi service. Joby has spent years developing and seeking type certification from the Federal Aviation Administration for its all-electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, which will be used to carry passengers on short trips in urban areas.

While Joby’s electric air taxi service gets much of the attention, the company has a longstanding relationship with the U.S. Department of Defense and is increasingly pushing deeper into the military sector.

Its autonomy stack, which is designed to be retrofitted onto a wide range of conventional aircraft, is part of that strategy. The company plans to first bring to market a regional airframe equipped with the autonomy stack, which could be used for defense missions as well as commercial freight transport. That effort has been supported by a $17 million Air Force contract with AFWERX.

Joby took its most meaningful step into defense in August when it acquired Resonant Sciences for $500 million in cash and stock. Ohio-based Resonant Sciences, which makes radio frequency and sensor systems, is now part of a dedicated defense business within Joby that includes several projects such as the development of turbine-electric and hydrogen-electric aircraft, and an autonomy technology stack.

Last year, Joby signed an agreement with defense contractor L3Harris Technologies to “explore opportunities” to develop a new class of aircraft — specifically, a gas-turbine hybrid vertical take-off and landing aircraft that can fly autonomously — for defense applications.

Tech.content:

A week after an Anthropic researcher’s doomsday warning rattled the AI world, the company’s CEO Dario Amodei has outlined his plan to “pace the frontier” of AI development. The proposal leans on independent safety evaluators and coordination between AI labs in democratic countries, and it’s already picked up some industry support, along with some pointed pushback from Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
